It is fine as an internal implementation of the outbox; it is not a data product. Publish domain events with business meaning, shaped deliberately — the anti-corruption layer applies here exactly as it does to a legacy integration.

The analytics path: one stream, two destinations

Events serve operational consumers and analytical ones, and the two want completely different things. Trying to satisfy both from one pipeline is a common and expensive mistake.

Sink connectors, not custom code

Kafka Connect has maintained sinks for S3, BigQuery, Snowflake, Iceberg and Elasticsearch. Writing your own consumer to land Parquet files is a solved problem you would be re-solving badly.

Schema carries through

Avro plus a registry means the lake gets typed, evolving data rather than untyped JSON blobs. This is where the registry pays back a second time, and where JSON topics become an analytics tax.

Do not let analytics drive the event design

"Can you add these twelve fields so the warehouse doesn't need a join" turns a domain event into a database dump. Give analytics a separate enriched topic if they need one — built by a Streams job you own.

Shipping a breaking schema change

Sooner or later a change is genuinely incompatible. The playbook is expand/contract again — the same shape as a database migration, run across consumers you may not control.

PhaseProducerConsumersDuration
0 · MeasureList every consumer group on the topic; contact the owners—Before anything else
1 · ExpandAdd the new field alongside the old; populate bothUnchanged — the schema is still compatibleOne release
2 · MigrateUnchangedEach consumer switches to the new field on its own scheduleWeeks — the long pole
3 · VerifyMetric: is anyone still reading the old field?—Until the metric is zero
4 · ContractStop populating the old field, then remove itUnaffected — nobody reads itOne release

When expand/contract is impossible

A change to the meaning of the topic itself — different granularity, a different key, a fundamentally different shape. Then it is a new topic:

  1. Create orders.order.placed.v2.
  2. Dual-publish to v1 and v2 from the same transaction.
  3. Consumers migrate one at a time and confirm.
  4. Monitor v1 consumer groups until none remain active.
  5. Announce a sunset date, stop publishing v1, delete it later.

The version in the topic name is what makes this routine instead of a coordinated outage.

What not to doChange the schema, tell people in a chat channel, deploy on Friday. The consumers you know about will cope; the batch job that runs monthly and the partner integration nobody documented will fail silently, and you will hear about it in three weeks from a finance reconciliation.
The metric that makes step 3 possibleMonitor active consumer groups per topic and per schema version. Without it, "has everyone migrated?" is answered by asking around, which means v1 is never retired and you maintain both forever.
Dual-publish from one transactionBoth records go into the same outbox transaction, so v1 and v2 can never diverge. Publishing v2 from a separate job that reads v1 introduces lag and a second failure mode at exactly the moment you need confidence.

Living with three versions in flight

During a migration — and after a replay — a consumer sees several versions of the same event type. Handling that deliberately is what keeps the migration a background activity rather than an event.

Upcasting: normalise on the way in, handle one shape
@Component
class OrderPlacedUpcaster {

    /** Every version is converted to the current internal shape at the boundary.
     *  The handler below never sees a v1 payload. */
    OrderPlaced upcast(JsonNode raw) {
        int version = raw.path("eventVersion").asInt(1);
        return switch (version) {
            case 1 -> fromV1(raw);      // v1 had 'total' in major units, no currency
            case 2 -> fromV2(raw);      // v2 added currency, still 'total'
            case 3 -> fromV3(raw);      // v3 renamed to totalMinor
            default -> throw new UnknownEventVersion(version);   // → DLT, loudly
        };
    }

    private OrderPlaced fromV1(JsonNode n) {
        return new OrderPlaced(
            n.get("orderId").asText(),
            Money.ofMajor(n.get("total").asDouble(), "GBP"),    // the assumption, documented
            n.path("occurredAt").asText());
    }
}

One class holds every historical shape, and the business logic holds none. That is the property worth paying for: your handler stays readable even when the topic has four years of history in it.

The tolerant-reader rules

  • Ignore unknown fields. Never fail on a field you did not expect — that turns every additive producer change into your outage.
  • Never assume field order or the absence of new ones.
  • Read only what you need. A consumer that deserialises the whole payload into a mirror of the producer's model is coupled to all of it.
  • Fail loudly on an unknown version, not on an unknown field. One is a real incompatibility; the other is normal evolution.
Upcasters are permanentYou can never delete one while the topic still holds events of that version — and with compaction or long retention, that can be indefinitely. This is the hidden long-term cost of event-driven systems, and it is the main reason event sourcing is a heavier commitment than a plain event stream.
Test every versionKeep a fixture file per historical version and a test that upcasts each one. It takes minutes, it documents the history better than any wiki page, and it is what makes a four-year-old replay safe to run.

Securing an event platform

Four layers, and the one that gets skipped is authorisation — a cluster where every application can read every topic is a data-governance finding waiting to be written.

LayerMechanismProtects againstNote
Encryption in transitTLS on every listenerNetwork interceptionTable stakes. Costs some CPU unless offloaded
AuthenticationmTLS, SASL/OAUTHBEARER, SASL/SCRAMUnknown clientsOAuth aligns Kafka with your existing IdP — Kafka 4.1 added jwt-bearer
AuthorisationACLs per principal, topic and operationKnown clients reading what they should notThe layer most often left wide open
Encryption at restDisk encryption, or field-level in the payloadStolen disks; broker operatorsField-level is the only one that protects data from the platform team
ACLs: least privilege, per application
# inventory service: read orders, write its own events, use its own group
kafka-acls --add --allow-principal User:inventory-service \
  --operation Read --topic orders.order.placed.v1
kafka-acls --add --allow-principal User:inventory-service \
  --operation Read --group inventory-order-reservation
kafka-acls --add --allow-principal User:inventory-service \
  --operation Write --topic inventory.stock.reserved.v1

# Deny by default at the cluster level:
#   allow.everyone.if.no.acl.found = false
# Anything not explicitly granted is refused — the setting that makes ACLs mean something.
Personal data in events is foreverA customer's name and address in a topic with 90-day retention exists in 90 days of segments, in every consumer's local copy, in the lake, and in every backup. A deletion request cannot reach any of it.

Two defences: minimise — put ids in events and let consumers look up what they are entitled to — or crypto-shred: encrypt personal fields with a per-subject key and delete the key. The events remain; their contents become unreadable.

The quiet risk of a shared clusterA topic with no ACL on a permissive cluster is readable by every application in the estate, including ones from other departments with different data-handling obligations. In a bank that is a control failure, not a configuration preference — and it is invisible until an audit.
Principals from the platformUse mTLS certificates issued by a service mesh or a workload-identity system rather than long-lived SCRAM passwords in config. Rotation stops being a project, and a compromised credential expires on its own.

Platform governance: topics, quotas and self-service

A shared Kafka cluster with no rules becomes unusable at around a hundred topics. With the wrong rules it becomes a ticket queue. The paved-road model from the architecture deck applies directly.

Topic provisioning as code

# topics/orders.yaml — in the owning team's repo, applied by CI
- name: orders.order.placed.v1
  owner: checkout-team
  partitions: 24
  replication: 3
  config:
    min.insync.replicas: 2
    retention.ms: 604800000
    cleanup.policy: delete
  schema: schemas/order-placed-v1.avsc
  compatibility: BACKWARD
  consumers: [inventory, payment, search, notification]

Reviewed in a pull request, applied by a pipeline, and the same file generates the catalogue entry. No ticket, no console clicking, and every topic has an owner by construction.

Quotas: stop one client taking the cluster

kafka-configs --alter --entity-type clients --entity-name analytics-backfill \
  --add-config 'producer_byte_rate=10485760,consumer_byte_rate=52428800'

A backfill job replaying six months of history will saturate the cluster and degrade every production consumer. A quota makes it slow instead of making everyone else slow.

The standards worth setting centrallyNaming convention · envelope fields · default partition count and replication · compatibility mode · required ACL model · mandatory DLT per consumer · trace propagation on. Six or seven rules, enforced by the pipeline that provisions topics, cover almost everything that goes wrong.
Orphan topicsTeams reorganise; topics do not. Run a quarterly report of topics with no producer traffic, no active consumer group, or an owner who no longer exists. Deleting them is usually blocked on nobody being willing to confirm they are unused — which is what the consumer-group metric is for.

What to alert on in an event-driven system

The instinct is to alert on broker health. The things that actually hurt customers are further along, and they are all measurable.

SignalMeansPage whenOwner
End-to-end staleness p99How out of date the slowest consumer's view isAbove the stated SLO for that flowThe consuming team
Consumer lag per partitionFalling behind, or one stuck partitionRising trend, or any partition flat and non-zeroThe consuming team
DLT depthBusiness events not happeningGreater than zeroThe consuming team
Oldest unsent outbox rowEvents not reaching the broker at allOlder than ~30 sThe producing team
Rebalance rateAn unstable consumer groupMore than a few per hour with no deployThe consuming team
Under-replicated partitionsA broker is unhealthy or laggingNon-zero for more than a few minutesPlatform
Offline partitionsData unavailable right nowImmediatelyPlatform
Replication slot lag (CDC)WAL not being consumedBefore the disk fills — this can stop the databasePlatform + producing team
Lag alone is a poor alertA lag of 50,000 is fine on a topic doing 20,000/s and a disaster on one doing 5/s. Alert on estimated time to drain — lag divided by consumption rate — which is dimensionally the thing you care about and comparable across every topic.
The two SLIs to put in front of the businessFlow completeness: of the orders placed in the last hour, what fraction reached a terminal state. Flow latency: p99 time from order placed to confirmed. Both are in the product's language, both are measurable from events you already have, and both catch problems that every technical dashboard shows as green.

Consumer lag is climbing — the diagnostic order

Six checks, cheapest first. The mistake is scaling consumers before knowing which of these it is, which usually makes the problem worse by triggering a rebalance.

#CheckIf yes
1Is lag on all partitions or one?One → hot key or a stuck consumer. Do not scale; find that partition
2Did producer volume jump?A legitimate spike — scale out, or let the buffer absorb it if time-to-drain is acceptable
3Is the rebalance rate elevated?The group is thrashing. Look at max.poll.interval vs handler duration, and pod restarts
4Has handler latency risen?A downstream dependency slowed. Fix there; the consumer is a symptom
5Are consumers at the partition count already?You cannot scale further without adding partitions — make handling cheaper instead
6Are errors and retries up?Retries multiply effective processing time. Check the DLT and the retry topics
The commands to run first
# Lag per partition — the single most useful command
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group inventory
#  TOPIC   PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG   CONSUMER-ID
#  orders  0          918224          918230          6     consumer-1-a3f…
#  orders  7          901003          962847          61844 consumer-4-9cd…   ← here

# Is anything consuming at all?
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $B --describe --group inventory --members

# What is that consumer's thread actually doing?
curl -s localhost:8081/actuator/threaddump | jq '.threads[]
  | select(.threadName | contains("KafkaConsumer")) | {threadName, threadState}'
A consumer with no member idIf --describe shows lag but the CONSUMER-ID column is empty, nothing is consuming that partition — the group has no live member for it. That is a dead or unstarted consumer, not a slow one, and scaling will not help.
The fastest real fix, usuallySwitch to a batch listener with a bulk write. Five hundred individual inserts become one statement, and a consumer that handled 2,000/s handles 20,000/s with no new infrastructure and no partition change. Check this before adding pods.
Do not raise max.poll.interval.ms to stop rebalancesIt hides a slow handler and delays detection of genuinely dead consumers. Reduce max.poll.records so a poll's work finishes quickly instead.

Replay and reprocessing: the playbook

Replay is the superpower of a log-based system and the fastest way to cause a second incident. Four scenarios, each with a different safe procedure.

1 · Drain a DLT after fixing a bug

  1. Fix and deploy the consumer first. Confirm new traffic is clean.
  2. Consume the DLT with a purpose-built job, not the main listener.
  3. Republish to the main topic, or apply directly — whichever preserves idempotency.
  4. Rate-limit. Ten thousand dead letters replayed at full speed becomes a second outage.

2 · Rebuild a projection

  1. Build into a new table with a new consumer group.
  2. Let it catch up; compare against the live table.
  3. Switch reads with a feature flag.
  4. Keep the old table until you are confident.

Never reset the live group and truncate in place — you have no read model at all while it rebuilds.

3 · Backfill a new consumer

  1. Deploy with auto.offset.reset=earliest and a new group id.
  2. Apply a client quota first, so the backfill cannot starve production consumers.
  3. Expect old schema versions — your upcasters must cover them.
  4. Watch downstream systems: replaying a year of events into a database at full speed will find its limits.

4 · Reprocess after a logic bug

  1. Work out what the wrong logic already did. Emails sent, payments taken — replay will not unsend them.
  2. Reset the group to a timestamp, not an offset — timestamps are meaningful to humans and stable across partitions.
  3. Suppress non-idempotent side effects for the replay window, with a flag.
  4. Reconcile afterwards and report the delta.
Resetting a group — the group must be inactive
# Always --dry-run first. It prints what WOULD happen.
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $B --group projection-order-history \
  --topic orders.order.placed.v1 --reset-offsets \
  --to-datetime 2026-09-14T00:00:00.000 --dry-run

# Then --execute. Other options: --to-earliest --to-latest --shift-by -1000
#   --to-offset N   --by-duration PT6H
The rule that prevents the second incidentReplay re-fires every side effect the handler performs. Customers have been emailed their order confirmation four times by a well-intentioned replay. Before any replay, list what the consumer does that is not idempotent, and turn it off for the duration — deliberately, with a flag, and tell the people who own it.

Six failures, and what to do at 3am

Runbook material. Each of these has happened to every team running Kafka for more than a year.

SymptomLikely causeImmediate actionPrevention
Consumer lag rising steadily, no errorsThroughput mismatch, or a slowed dependencyCheck per-partition lag; check handler latency; scale if all partitions are behindAlert on time-to-drain; batch listeners
One partition stuck, others finePoison record blocking, or a hot keyInspect the record at that offset; confirm bounded retries route it to the DLTNon-retryable exception list; retry topics
Group rebalancing repeatedlyHandler exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, or pods restartingLower max.poll.records; check pod restarts and memory limitsStatic membership; cooperative or KIP-848 protocol
Producer errors: NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICASISR below min.insync.replicas — a broker is down or laggingThis is the cluster protecting you. Restore the broker; do not lower the setting to "fix" itAlert on ISR shrink; capacity headroom
Consumer restarted and reprocessed everythingOffsets expired, or the group id changedRely on idempotency; if unavailable, stop and reset to a known offsetStable group ids; know your offsets.retention
Events stopped arriving; broker healthyOutbox relay down, or a CDC slot stalledCheck oldest unsent outbox row and replication slot lag — the producer side, not KafkaAlert on both; they are the blind spot
The one that catches everyone"Events stopped arriving" and every Kafka dashboard is green — because the problem is upstream of Kafka entirely. The outbox relay crashed, or the Debezium connector is in FAILED state. Both are invisible from the broker's perspective, and both are why the producer-side metrics belong on the same dashboard as the consumer-side ones.
What to write down before you need itFor each critical flow: which topics, which consumer groups, who owns them, what the SLO is, how to replay safely, and what is not idempotent. One page. Link it from every alert on that flow. The value of a runbook is entirely in it existing before the incident.

Twelve event-driven anti-patterns

Each of these is common, was reasonable when it was introduced, and is expensive to unwind. Recognising them by symptom is more useful than knowing the names.

Anti-patternWhat you seeWhat it costs
Commands disguised as eventsSendEmail on a topic, one consumer, producer knows the outcomeCoupling with no owner for failures. Fan-out you can never use
Database change feed as a "domain event"CDC straight off tables into a shared topicThirty teams coupled to your schema; you can never refactor
Dual writesave(); kafka.send();Silent loss on crash. Found weeks later by reconciliation
Non-idempotent consumerA counter increment in a handlerEvery rebalance, retry and replay corrupts data a little
Unbounded retriesRetry forever, no DLTOne bad record blocks its partition and everything behind it
Event chains as workflowSix services each reacting to the last, no coordinatorNobody can answer "where is order 88421 stuck"
Event sourcing by accidentRebuilding current state by replaying a topic on every readAll the cost of event sourcing, none of the tooling
Shared consumer groupTwo applications, one group idEach sees half the events. Nobody notices for weeks
No schema governanceJSON, no registry, "we'll be careful"A breaking change reaches production and fails asynchronously
Fat events as data dumpsEvery column of the row in the payloadA published contract you can never shrink, plus a PII exposure
Synchronous call inside a consumerHandler calls three services and waitsConsumer throughput now equals the slowest dependency's latency
Events for everythingThe whole request path made asyncEvery screen must model "not yet"; debugging cost with no availability gain
The pattern behind themNine of the twelve come from treating the broker as the architecture. Kafka does not make a system event-driven any more than a database makes it well-modelled. The architecture is the event design — what is a fact, who owns it, what it means — and the broker is how it travels.

Moving an existing system to events

You almost never build event-driven from scratch — you convert something. Six phases, each shipping value on its own, none requiring a big bang.

1–2 Prepare

  • Map the synchronous calls and classify each: must succeed now, or a reaction? Only the second group moves.
  • Add the outbox to the producing service and publish events alongside the existing calls. Nothing consumes them yet.
  • Verify the event stream matches reality — counts, totals, timing — before anyone depends on it.

3–4 Shift one consumer

  • Pick the least critical reaction — search indexing, analytics, notifications.
  • Build the consumer; run it in parallel with the synchronous call, writing to a shadow table.
  • Compare outputs for a week. Then switch with a flag and remove the synchronous call.
  • Repeat for the next consumer. One at a time.

5 Harden

  • Idempotency and a DLT on every consumer before the second one goes live, not after.
  • Trace propagation across the hop — you will need it during phase 6.
  • Reconciliation job comparing source of truth to every consumer's state.
  • Runbook and alerts per flow.

6 Only then, the interesting parts

  • Projections and read models, once the stream is trusted.
  • A saga, once more than one service reacts and someone asks where things are stuck.
  • Streams, once you have a genuine stateful or windowed requirement.

Teams that start at phase 6 are the ones that end up with an event-driven system they cannot debug.

The parallel-run is the whole safety mechanismRunning the event path and the synchronous path together, comparing outputs, and only then switching is what makes this reversible at every step. It costs double processing for a few weeks. That is far cheaper than discovering in production that your event carries a subtly different meaning from the call it replaced.

Kafka, and when something else is better

Kafka is the default for enterprise event backbones and is the wrong choice more often than its popularity suggests. Honest comparison.

TechnologyModelStrong atWeak atPick it when
KafkaPartitioned, replayable logThroughput, replay, fan-out, stream processing, retention as a featurePer-message TTL, priority, complex routing, tiny deploymentsYou need a durable event backbone many consumers read independently
RabbitMQQueues with exchangesFlexible routing, per-message TTL, priorities, low latency, simple opsReplay (messages are consumed), very high throughputWork queues and RPC-style messaging with routing rules
IBM MQ / JMSQueues, transactionalXA transactions, guaranteed once-only delivery, decades of bank toolingFan-out, replay, throughput, costYou are integrating with systems that already speak it — extremely common in banking
AWS SQS + SNSManaged queue + pub/subZero operations, elastic, cheap at low volume, native DLQOrdering (FIFO queues are limited), replay, throughput ceilingsCloud-native workloads where you do not want to run a broker
EventBridge / Pub-SubManaged event busRouting rules, SaaS integrations, schema registry, no opsReplay, cost at high volume, vendor lock-inEvent routing across services and third parties, moderate volume
PulsarLog + queue, tiered by designMulti-tenancy, geo-replication, both queue and stream semanticsSmaller ecosystem, more moving parts (BookKeeper)Strong multi-tenancy or geo-replication requirements
The honest enterprise answerMost large organisations run two: Kafka as the event backbone for domain events and analytics, and an existing MQ estate for transactional integration with systems that will not change. That is not a failure to standardise — it is two different jobs. What matters is a clear rule for which goes where, written down.
Kafka's queue gap has closedKafka historically could not do per-message acknowledgement or competing consumers beyond the partition count. KIP-932 "queues for Kafka" adds share groups that acknowledge individual records and let consumer count exceed partition count. Early access in 4.0, preview in 4.1, GA in Kafka 4.2 behind the share.version feature flag (level 1 by default). On 4.2+ this is a real option for work-queue workloads instead of a second broker.

What an event-driven system costs to run

The line items that appear on the bill and in the on-call rota. Useful for a business case, and for answering "why is this more expensive than the monolith".

Worked monthly estimate

Volume
20,000 events/s × 1 KB ≈ 50 TB/month written
Replication
× 3 for RF=3 → 150 TB of writes
Storage
7 days retained, lz4 at ~4× → ~9 TB on disk
Read amplification
5 consumer groups → 5× read traffic, and cross-AZ reads are charged
Brokers
6 instances sized for network, not CPU
Plus
schema registry, Connect cluster, monitoring, and the consumers themselves

Divide by orders processed and you have cost per 1,000 orders for the event path — directly comparable to the synchronous alternative.

The costs that surprise people

  • Cross-AZ traffic. Replication and consumption across zones is charged per gigabyte and can exceed the compute bill. Rack-aware follower fetching helps.
  • Retention creep. "Let's keep 30 days just in case" quadruples storage and nobody revisits it.
  • Read amplification. Each new consumer group re-reads everything. Ten groups is 10× read cost.
  • Idle consumers. Pods beyond the partition count cost money and process nothing.
  • On-call. A broker estate needs owners, upgrades and a rota. Often the largest real cost.
Three levers that actually move the billCompression — lz4 or zstd typically cuts storage and network 3–5× for a little CPU. Retention per topic — most topics do not need seven days; some need thirty. Decide each one. Tiered storage — long retention on object storage costs a fraction of broker disk, which changes the replay conversation entirely.

The decisions, in the order to make them

Everything in this tab, as a sequence. Each answer constrains the next, and the expensive ones are all near the top.

#DecisionDefault answerCost to reverse
1Does this step need to be synchronous?Yes if the user's action should fail when it fails; otherwise an eventweeks
2Event or command?Event — a past-tense fact with no named consumerweeks
3Thin, fat or delta?Fat, with only the fields the event genuinely meansweeks — it is a contract
4What is the key?The entity whose events must stay orderedweeks — repartitioning is disruptive
5Choreography or orchestration?Choreograph within a context, orchestrate across them and past four stepsweeks
6How does the event get published?Outbox. Always. Polling relay first, CDC when volume justifies itdays
7Partition count?Peak throughput ÷ per-consumer rate, × 3 headroom. Round up generouslyweeks
8Format and compatibility?Avro + registry, BACKWARD, register from CIdays
9Retention?7 days for operational topics; compaction for reference data; long retention if rebuild is requiredhours
10Retry strategy?Bounded retries then a DLT. Non-blocking retry topics if ordering permitshours
11How is the consumer idempotent?Business key, or a dedupe table on the event id. Answer this before writing the handlerhours
12What is the staleness SLO?State a number per flow, measure it, alert on ithours
If you answer only threeMake them 6 (outbox — otherwise you lose events silently), 11 (idempotency — otherwise duplicates corrupt data) and 10 (bounded retries plus a DLT — otherwise one bad record stops a partition). Those three are the difference between a system that degrades gracefully and one that fails invisibly.

Glossary and where to go deeper

The terms that come up in design reviews and interviews, and the sources worth the time.

Terms

Offset
A record's position in a partition. A consumer group's committed offset is its bookmark.
ISR
In-sync replicas — those caught up with the leader. acks=all means all of these.
Consumer group
Both the parallelism unit and the isolation boundary. One partition to one member at a time.
Rebalance
Reassigning partitions when membership changes. Cooperative and KIP-848 make it nearly free.
Compaction
Retain the latest value per key forever. Turns a topic into a snapshot.
Tombstone
A null value on a compacted topic — the key is deleted.
Outbox
Write the event to your database in the same transaction; relay it afterwards.
Saga
A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions instead of a rollback.
Projection
A read model maintained by consuming events. Rebuildable by replay.
Upcaster
Converts an old event version to the current shape at the consumer boundary.
EOS
Exactly-once semantics — within Kafka. Elsewhere, idempotency.
Backpressure
What a system does when it cannot keep up. In Kafka, the topic absorbs it until retention does not.

Going deeper

  • Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — chapter 11 on streams is the best explanation of logs, ordering and derived data anywhere.
  • Stopford, Designing Event-Driven Systems — free from Confluent; the enterprise patterns, told well.
  • Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns — the vocabulary everyone still uses, and it predates all of this.
  • Richardson, Microservices Patterns — the definitive treatment of sagas and the outbox.
  • Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design — where domain events come from and what makes one well-formed.
  • The Kafka documentation's design section — genuinely well written, and shorter than people expect.
The three sentences worth being able to say"We design for at-least-once delivery into idempotent consumers, which gives exactly-once effects." · "Every event that must not be lost goes through an outbox, because there is no transaction across the database and the broker." · "Ordering is guaranteed per partition, so we key on the entity whose sequence matters." Those three cover most of what an interviewer is checking for, and most of what a design review needs to establish.

Thirty patterns, not one hundred and eighty problems

Nobody solves an interview problem by recalling the problem. You recognise the shape, reach for the structure that fits it, and adapt three lines. This deck takes the thirty patterns one at a time, teaches each as a reusable Java structure, and drills it on the six LeetCode problems that stress a different corner of that one idea.

30

patterns, each a self-contained topic. Nothing in one topic depends on having read another.

180

LeetCode problems, linked. Two per pattern are solved in full; the other four are shown as a delta against that pattern's own structure.

4

slides per pattern — mechanics, a dry run, the reusable structure, the six problems. Every line of code is Java 17+.

The four slides, every time

Mechanics
The invariant that holds on every iteration, and the argument for why the work is bounded. This is the part that transfers to problems not on the list.
Dry run
One concrete input traced step by step, as a diagram and a table. If you cannot trace it by hand, you do not know it yet.
Structure
The generic Java skeleton, its variants, and the exact knobs you turn per problem.
Problems
The six, each with the path from brute force to optimal — not just the finished answer.

How to use it

  • Arrow keys move through slides; C opens contents, where each pattern is its own section.
  • Work one pattern to the end before starting the next. They are deliberately independent.
  • Read the mechanics slide, then cover the dry-run table and trace the input yourself. Compare after.
  • Type the structure from memory before reading the problems. The structure is the unit of recall.
  • Copper marks the pointer or value that moved this step; teal marks auxiliary state changing.
  • Complexity is always stated as time / space, excluding the space taken by the output.
The one habit worth buildingBefore writing anything, say out loud which pattern you are using and what its invariant is. If you cannot name the invariant, you are about to write a loop you will then debug for ten minutes. Interviewers score that naming almost as highly as the code.

Each row is one self-contained topic with its own four slides. Work down the list, or jump straight to whichever pattern you are drilling — nothing below depends on anything above.

On orderThe numbering is roughly easiest to hardest, so working straight down is a reasonable default. It is not a dependency chain: each pattern's four slides stand on their own, so you can drill number 22 without having read number 9. If a pattern assumes a data structure you have not used before, its mechanics slide says so explicitly rather than pointing you elsewhere.

Read the input shape, then the question word

Pattern choice is nearly mechanical. Two features of the statement — what the input is, and what the question asks for — narrow thirty candidates down to two or three. This is an index into the list, not a grouping of it: it tells you which pattern number to open.

The trap hiding in row twoA sliding window needs the window property to be monotone: growing the window must only ever help, or only ever hurt. With negative numbers, extending a subarray can lower or raise the sum, so there is no valid shrink rule — which is why "subarray sums to K" with negatives is not a window problem at all, and belongs to a different pattern in the list.

The constraints tell you the intended complexity

Judges run on the order of 108 simple operations per second. Every problem's constraint section is therefore a direct hint at the algorithm the setter had in mind — read it before you design, not after your first submission times out.

n up toIntended complexityWhat that usually means
10–12O(n!) · O(2ⁿ·n)Permutation backtracking, bitmask DP
20–25O(2ⁿ)Subset enumeration, meet in the middle
100–500O(n³)Floyd–Warshall, interval DP, matrix chain
2 000–5 000O(n²)Grid DP, string DP, pairwise scans
10⁵O(n log n)Sorting, heaps, binary search, balanced trees
10⁶–10⁷O(n)Windows, two pointers, prefix sums, counting
10⁹ and aboveO(log n) · O(1)Binary search on the answer, maths, bit tricks

Worked example

The constraints read 1 <= piles.length <= 10⁴ and 1 <= piles[i] <= 10⁹.

The array is small but the values are enormous. A small n paired with a huge value range means the search is over the value range, not the array: the search space is the values, and each feasibility check costs one O(n) pass. Total O(n log maxV) ≈ 10⁴ × 30 = 3×10⁵ operations, comfortably inside budget. That problem is LC 875.

Two more tells worth memorising"Return the answer modulo 10⁹+7" means the count is astronomically large, so it is a counting DP and never an enumeration. "You may return the answer in any order" means the grader sorts for you, so do not spend time ordering the output.
Say this in the interview"The constraints put n at 10⁵, so I need O(n log n) or better — which rules out the pairwise approach I'd otherwise reach for." In one sentence you have demonstrated that you design against a budget rather than guessing. It reliably scores, and it costs five seconds.

Two indices that never go backwards

A sliding window answers questions about contiguous runs in one pass. The whole pattern is a bet: that when the window at [l, r] is invalid, no window ending further right can be fixed by moving l back. That bet is what turns O(n²) into O(n).

The invariant

At the bottom of every iteration, the window [l, r] is valid. The loop body has exactly three moves, always in this order:

  1. Admit a[r] into the window state — the window may now be invalid.
  2. Restore validity by evicting from the left, one element at a time.
  3. Record the answer, now that the invariant holds again.

Getting step 3 before step 2 is the single most common bug in the pattern: you measure a window that was never legal.

Why it is O(n), not O(n²)

The inner while loop looks like it makes the whole thing quadratic. It does not, and the argument is worth being able to say out loud:

l only ever increases, and it is bounded by n. So across the entire run, the inner loop executes at most n times in total — not n times per iteration. Each index enters the window once through r and leaves it at most once through l: 2n operations, amortised O(1) per step.

Being able to say that out loud is what turns "I think it is linear" into an answer an interviewer accepts.

Applies when

The answer is a contiguous subarray or substring, and validity is monotone — once a window is invalid, extending it right cannot make it valid again.

Does not apply when

Values can be negative and you are summing — extending the window may help or hurt, so no valid shrink rule exists. Also when the chosen elements need not be adjacent, since a window can only ever describe a contiguous run.

Complexity

O(n) time, since each index is admitted once and evicted at most once. O(k) space for the window state, where k is the alphabet or distinct-value count — O(1) for a fixed int[128].

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"longest / shortest substring or subarray such that…" · "contains at most K distinct" · "minimum window containing all of…" · "of size exactly k" · "after at most k replacements" · "the longest run you can make by…". If the words contiguous or substring appear alongside an optimisation word, open with a window and only abandon it if the monotonicity test fails.

LC 3 traced by hand on "abcabcbb"

Longest substring without repeating characters. The window state is a character count; the window is invalid exactly when the character we just admitted appears twice. Watch l: it moves eight times in total across the whole run, never backwards — the amortisation argument made concrete.

rcharlwindow state (counts)actionlenbest
0a0a:1admit — valid11
1b0a:1 b:1admit — valid22
2c0a:1 b:1 c:1admit — valid33
3a1b:1 c:1 a:1a:2 invalid → evict a33
4b2c:1 a:1 b:1b:2 invalid → evict b33
5c3a:1 b:1 c:1c:2 invalid → evict c33
6b5c:1 b:1b:2 invalid → evict a, then b23
7b7b:1b:2 invalid → evict c, then b13
Where brute force would have redone the workAt r=6 the naive solution restarts from l=4 and re-scans "bcb" from scratch, having already established at r=5 that "abc" was clean. The window never re-reads a settled prefix: the count map already remembers everything the rescan would have recomputed. On a string of 10⁵ characters that is the difference between 10⁵ and 10¹⁰ operations.

One skeleton, five knobs, six problems

Every variable-size window problem in this family is the same twelve lines. Memorise the skeleton, then learn which of the five marked knobs each problem turns — that is far less to carry than six separate solutions.

The canonical variable-size window · longest-valid form
/**
 * Longest window satisfying some monotone predicate.
 * Invariant: at the bottom of every iteration, [l, r] is a VALID window.
 * Each index is admitted once via r and evicted at most once via l  ->  O(n).
 */
int longestValidWindow(int[] a) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> win = new HashMap<>();   // KNOB 1 · the window state
    int l = 0, best = 0;

    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {

        win.merge(a[r], 1, Integer::sum);          // KNOB 2 · admit a[r]

        while (win.size() > 2) {                   // KNOB 3 · "the window is invalid"
            int out = a[l++];                      // KNOB 4 · evict a[l] — the exact mirror of KNOB 2
            if (win.merge(out, -1, Integer::sum) == 0) win.remove(out);
        }

        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);          // KNOB 5 · record, AFTER validity is restored
    }
    return best;
}
Variant B · shortest valid window (LC 209, 76)
// Two changes, and they always come together:
//   the while condition is inverted   (while VALID, not while invalid)
//   the record moves INSIDE the loop  (every shrink is a candidate)
int shortestValidWindow(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, sum = 0, best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        sum += a[r];

        while (sum >= target) {                 // while VALID
            best = Math.min(best, r - l + 1);   // record here
            sum -= a[l++];
        }
    }
    return best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? 0 : best;
}
Variant C · fixed size k (LC 567)
// The window grows by exactly one per step, so the shrink
// is an `if`, never a `while` — it can only ever be off by one.
int fixedWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    int l = 0, sum = 0, best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;

    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        sum += a[r];

        if (r - l + 1 > k) sum -= a[l++];       // `if`, not `while`

        if (r - l + 1 == k) best = Math.max(best, sum);
    }
    return best;
}
Variant D · counting with "exactly K"
// You cannot window "exactly K" directly — validity is not monotone.
// But "at most K" IS monotone, and:
//        exactly(K)  ==  atMost(K) - atMost(K - 1)
// Inside atMost, every window ending at r contributes (r - l + 1)
// subarrays, because every suffix of a valid window is valid too.
int exactlyK(int[] a, int k) {
    return atMost(a, k) - atMost(a, k - 1);
}

long atMost(int[] a, int k) {
    Map<Integer, Integer> win = new HashMap<>();
    long count = 0;
    for (int l = 0, r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        win.merge(a[r], 1, Integer::sum);
        while (win.size() > k) {
            int out = a[l++];
            if (win.merge(out, -1, Integer::sum) == 0) win.remove(out);
        }
        count += r - l + 1;                     // all windows ending at r
    }
    return count;
}

The five knobs, and nothing else

1 · state
int[128] for characters, HashMap for arbitrary ints, a plain sum or distinct counter when that is all you need. Prefer the array: it is faster and has no boxing.
2 · admit
One line. Whatever it does, knob 4 must undo precisely this.
3 · invalid
The only genuinely problem-specific line. Write it as a positive statement of what "broken" means, then negate nothing.
4 · evict
Write it immediately after knob 2, by copying that line and flipping the sign. Never write it later from memory.
5 · record
max after the loop for longest; min inside the loop for shortest; count += r - l + 1 for counting.
The three bugs that actually happenRecording before shrinking — you measure a window that was never valid, and the answer comes out too large. Forgetting win.remove at zero — a count of zero still occupies a key, so win.size() lies and the window never shrinks enough. if where while belongs — at r=6 in the trace, l had to move twice in one step; an if silently returns a wrong answer on exactly that input.

Six windows, six different knobs

Work them in the listed order: 3 establishes the skeleton, 209 flips it to the shortest form, 424 and 904 change only the invalidity test, 567 fixes the size, and 76 combines everything. Each row names the one knob that changes.

Anchor 1 · LC 3 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Try every pair (l, r) and test the substring for duplicates. O(n³), or O(n²) if you carry a set as r grows.
The observation
If [l, r] contains a duplicate, then so does [l, r'] for every r' > r. So once l has been pushed past a duplicate, it never has any reason to go back.
The optimisation
Keep l monotone and maintain a count array instead of rebuilding a set. Each index is touched twice.
Edge cases
Empty string returns 0; a single repeated character returns 1; the count array must cover the full ASCII range the problem allows.
LC 3 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int lengthOfLongestSubstring(String s) {
        int[] count = new int[128];       // KNOB 1 · ASCII counts beat a HashMap here
        int l = 0, best = 0;

        for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
            char in = s.charAt(r);
            count[in]++;                  // KNOB 2 · admit

            // KNOB 3 · the ONLY char that can now exceed 1 is the one
            // we just admitted, so this single test is the full invariant.
            while (count[in] > 1) {
                count[s.charAt(l++)]--;   // KNOB 4 · evict, mirroring KNOB 2
            }

            best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);   // KNOB 5 · record
        }
        return best;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 76 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Every substring, each checked against t's frequency map. O(n²·m) and hopeless at n = 10⁵.
First idea
A shortest-form window that compares the window's map to t's map. Correct, but the comparison is O(52) per step and easy to get wrong.
The observation
You never need the whole comparison — only how many characters are still missing, counted with multiplicity. That collapses to a single int.
The trick
Let need[c] go negative for surplus characters. Then need[c] > 0 before admitting means "this one actually helped", and need[c] == 0 before evicting means "losing this one actually hurts". Both tests are one line.
LC 76 · O(n + m) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public String minWindow(String s, String t) {
        if (s.length() < t.length()) return "";

        int[] need = new int[128];
        for (char c : t.toCharArray()) need[c]++;

        int missing = t.length();   // chars still uncovered, WITH multiplicity
        int bestL = 0, bestLen = Integer.MAX_VALUE, l = 0;

        for (int r = 0; r < s.length(); r++) {
            // admit: only a char we still needed reduces `missing`.
            // Surplus chars push need[c] negative, which is intentional.
            if (need[s.charAt(r)]-- > 0) missing--;

            while (missing == 0) {            // valid → shrink and record
                if (r - l + 1 < bestLen) { bestLen = r - l + 1; bestL = l; }

                // evict: giving back a char whose need was exactly 0
                // is the one that breaks coverage.
                if (need[s.charAt(l++)]++ == 0) missing++;
            }
        }
        return bestLen == Integer.MAX_VALUE
                ? "" : s.substring(bestL, bestL + bestLen);
    }
}

209 · Minimum Size Subarray Sum variant B

Path: brute force is every (l, r) with prefix sums, O(n²). The observation is that all values are positive, so the window sum rises strictly with width — validity is monotone, so a window works.

Delta: state is a single int sum; invalid test becomes while (sum >= target), and the record moves inside that loop. Return 0, not MAX_VALUE, when nothing qualifies.

Watch for: the follow-up asks for O(n log n). That variant builds a running-sum array and binary searches it for each r — worth naming even if you do not write it.

424 · Longest Repeating Character Replacement variant A

Path: brute force fixes a target letter and windows 26 times, O(26n) — already fast enough, and worth mentioning aloud. The single-pass version is the interesting one.

Delta: only knob 3 changes, to while (len - maxFreq > k) — the count of characters you would have to replace. Keep maxFreq as a running maximum and do not recompute it when shrinking: a stale-high maxFreq can only suppress a window that could not have beaten the recorded best anyway.

Watch for: that non-recomputation is the part interviewers probe. Be ready to justify it.

904 · Fruit Into Baskets variant A

Path: the story about baskets is a disguise. Two baskets, each holding one fruit type, means "longest subarray with at most 2 distinct values" — read past the narrative to the constraint.

Delta: none. This is the skeleton from the previous slide with win.size() > 2 exactly as written. Generalise the 2 to a parameter and the same code answers "at most K distinct" for any K.

Watch for: the win.remove(out) when a count hits zero — without it size() over-reports and the answer is too small.

567 · Permutation in String variant C

Path: brute force sorts every window of width |s1|, O(n·k log k). The observation: a permutation is defined entirely by its character counts, and adjacent windows differ in only two positions — so the count vector updates in O(1).

Delta: fixed size, so the shrink is an if. Rather than comparing 26 counters per step, keep a matches integer of how many letters have the right count, and adjust it by ±1 as each admit or evict crosses the target.

Watch for: the matches counter is the part worth practising. Recomputing all 26 counts each step is O(26n) and still passes, but the incremental update is what the problem is testing.

If you only drill twoDo 3 and 76. Between them they contain all five knobs, both directions of the shrink loop, and the negative-count trick that the covering problems depend on. The other four are then twenty minutes each.

Start at both ends and prove one side is useless

A sliding window walks two pointers in the same direction. Two pointers walks them towards each other, and the pattern lives or dies on one argument: at every step you must be able to prove that one of the two ends can never participate in a better answer, so discarding it is safe.

The invariant

The optimal answer always lies within [l, r]. Each step either records a candidate or strictly narrows the range — never both pointers at once, unless the step is provably neutral.

That invariant is only maintainable when the data is ordered — either literally sorted, or ordered by some property such as height or distance. Sorting first is not a preprocessing detail; it is what creates the ordering the discard argument depends on.

Total movement is bounded by n, so the scan is O(n) and the sort dominates at O(n log n).

The discard argument, in two shapes

Sum target
Array is sorted. If a[l] + a[r] < target, then a[l] paired with anything still in range is also too small — a[r] was its best remaining partner. So l can never be part of a solution: advance it. Symmetrically for too large.
Bounded by the weaker end
Container and rain-water problems. The value is capped by min(h[l], h[r]) and the width only shrinks, so keeping the shorter side can never beat what you already recorded. Discard the shorter.

If you cannot state one of these two arguments for your problem, two pointers is the wrong pattern and you will get a subtly wrong answer rather than a slow one.

Applies when

The data is sorted (or you may sort it), and you are looking for a pair, triple or k-tuple, or for a value bounded by the weaker of two ends. Also the in-place variant: a read pointer and a write pointer moving the same way.

Does not apply when

Order matters to the answer — sorting destroys the original indices, so a problem that asks you to return indices from unsorted input rules this out. Also when you need every subarray rather than every pair.

Complexity

O(n log n) dominated by the sort, or O(n) if the input arrives sorted. k-sum costs O(nk−1). Space is O(1) beyond the output and the sort's own working memory.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the array is sorted in non-decreasing order" (an explicit invitation) · "find two/three/four numbers such that…" · "return the indices of the two numbers" · "closest to target" · "container / area / trapped" · "remove duplicates in place" · "without using extra space". That last phrase is decisive: O(1) space on an array problem almost always means pointers, not a map.

LC 11 traced on [1,8,6,2,5,4,8,3,7]

Container With Most Water — the cleanest demonstration of Rule B. Area is min(h[l], h[r]) × (r − l). Width falls by one every step no matter what, so the only lever is height, and the shorter side is the one that caps it.

Why discarding the shorter bar is safe — say this out loudSuppose h[l] < h[r]. Any container using l and some r' < r has height at most h[l] and width strictly less than r − l, so its area is strictly less than the one just measured. Every remaining pair involving l is therefore already beaten, and l can be dropped with nothing lost. This is the entire proof, and interviewers ask for it far more often than for the code.

Three skeletons that cover the whole family

Converging pointers for pairs, a nested wrapper for k-sums, and same-direction read/write pointers for in-place work. The third looks unrelated until you notice it is the same bookkeeping with both pointers moving the same way.

Skeleton A · converging, sum target (LC 167, 15, 16, 18)
// Requires a SORTED array. The comparison drives which side moves.
int[] twoSumSorted(int[] a, int target) {
    int l = 0, r = a.length - 1;

    while (l < r) {
        int sum = a[l] + a[r];

        if (sum == target) return new int[]{ l, r };
        else if (sum < target) l++;   // a[r] was a[l]'s best partner: a[l] is done
        else r--;                     // symmetric
    }
    return new int[]{ -1, -1 };
}
Skeleton B · converging, weaker end (LC 11, 42)
// No sort. The ordering that licenses the discard is the HEIGHT,
// and the value is capped by whichever side is smaller.
int maxArea(int[] h) {
    int l = 0, r = h.length - 1, best = 0;

    while (l < r) {
        best = Math.max(best, Math.min(h[l], h[r]) * (r - l));

        // Discard the shorter side — it cannot do better than
        // what we just measured, because width only shrinks.
        if (h[l] < h[r]) l++; else r--;
    }
    return best;
}
Skeleton C · the k-sum reduction — one core, wrapped k−2 times
/**
 * Every k-sum is the SAME two-pointer core with nested anchors around it.
 * Sort once; each extra nesting level costs one factor of n.
 *
 *   2Sum  O(n)     the core alone
 *   3Sum  O(n^2)   one anchor  + core
 *   4Sum  O(n^3)   two anchors + core
 *
 * The three lines that matter are identical at every level:
 *   skip duplicate anchors, skip duplicate hits, move BOTH pointers on a hit.
 */
List<List<Integer>> kSum(int[] a, long target, int k, int start) {
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (start == a.length) return out;

    if (k == 2) {                                  // ---- the core ----
        int l = start, r = a.length - 1;
        while (l < r) {
            long sum = (long) a[l] + a[r];
            if (sum < target)      l++;
            else if (sum > target) r--;
            else {
                out.add(new ArrayList<>(List.of(a[l], a[r])));
                while (l < r && a[l] == a[l + 1]) l++;   // skip duplicate hits
                while (l < r && a[r] == a[r - 1]) r--;
                l++; r--;                                 // BOTH move — one alone re-finds the same pair
            }
        }
        return out;
    }

    for (int i = start; i + k - 1 < a.length; i++) {      // ---- one anchor level ----
        if (i > start && a[i] == a[i - 1]) continue;      // skip duplicate anchors
        for (List<Integer> sub : kSum(a, target - a[i], k - 1, i + 1)) {
            sub.add(0, a[i]);
            out.add(sub);
        }
    }
    return out;
}
Skeleton D · same direction, read and write
// Both pointers move right. `write` marks where the next kept
// element goes; `read` scans. No extra array is ever allocated.
int removeDuplicates(int[] a) {
    if (a.length == 0) return 0;
    int write = 1;

    for (int read = 1; read < a.length; read++) {
        if (a[read] != a[write - 1]) {   // the keep-condition: the only knob
            a[write++] = a[read];
        }
    }
    return write;                        // new logical length
}

Picking the skeleton

Sorted + target
Skeleton A. If the problem gives you the array already sorted, that is a deliberate signal.
Area, water, capacity
Skeleton B. Do not sort — sorting destroys the positions the width depends on.
Find k numbers
Skeleton C. Sort, then wrap. Use long for the running target: 4Sum with values near ±10⁹ overflows int, and that is the most common wrong answer on LC 18.
In place, O(1) space
Skeleton D. The phrase "modify the array in-place" is effectively naming this skeleton.
The three bugs that actually happenMoving only one pointer on an exact hit — the loop re-finds the same pair forever, or emits it twice. Skipping duplicates in the wrong place — the anchor skip uses i > start, not i > 0; getting that wrong drops valid triples that begin with a repeated value. Sorting when position matters — fatal in LC 11 and 42, and it silently returns a plausible wrong number rather than crashing.

Six pairs of pointers, two discard rules

167 is the bare core. 15, 16 and 18 are the same core under one, one and two anchors. 11 and 42 switch to Rule B, where the bound is the weaker end rather than a target sum.

#ProblemLevelThe twistSkeletonComplexity

153SumMediumOne anchor plus the core. All the difficulty is de-duplication.C · k=3O(n²) / O(1)

Anchor 1 · LC 15 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Three nested loops, O(n³), plus a Set of sorted triples to kill duplicates. Correct and far too slow at n = 3000.
The observation
Fix the first element. What remains is exactly 2Sum with target −a[i] — a solved problem. Sorting first costs O(n log n) once and buys the O(n) core at every anchor.
The real difficulty
Not the search, the duplicates. Sorting puts equal values adjacent, which makes de-duplication a skip rather than a hash set: skip repeated anchors, and after recording a hit skip repeated values on both sides.
Early exit
Once a[i] > 0 the smallest possible triple already exceeds zero, so break. Cheap, and it shows you are thinking about the sorted order.
LC 15 · O(n²) time, O(1) space beyond the output
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> threeSum(int[] nums) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);                       // creates the ordering the discard needs
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int i = 0; i + 2 < nums.length; i++) {
            if (nums[i] > 0) break;              // sorted: nothing ahead can reach 0
            if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;   // duplicate ANCHOR

            int l = i + 1, r = nums.length - 1;
            while (l < r) {
                int sum = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r];

                if (sum < 0)      l++;           // too small: a[l] is finished
                else if (sum > 0) r--;           // too large: a[r] is finished
                else {
                    out.add(List.of(nums[i], nums[l], nums[r]));

                    // duplicate HITS — distinct from the anchor skip above
                    while (l < r && nums[l] == nums[l + 1]) l++;
                    while (l < r && nums[r] == nums[r - 1]) r--;

                    l++; r--;                    // both, or we re-find this pair
                }
            }
        }
        return out;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 42 — the path to the solution

The right question
Do not ask "how much water sits in this valley". Ask, for each column independently: how high does the water stand here? The answer is min(maxLeft, maxRight) − h[i].
First solution
Precompute maxLeft[] and maxRight[] in two passes, then sum. O(n) time but O(n) space — a perfectly good answer, and worth stating before optimising.
The observation
You never need both maxima at once. If h[l] < h[r], then rightMax ≥ h[r] > h[l], so the water at l is fixed by leftMax alone — the right side cannot be the binding constraint.
The result
Two running maxima and two pointers: O(n) time, O(1) space. Always mention the O(n)-space version first, then this.
LC 42 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int trap(int[] h) {
        int l = 0, r = h.length - 1;
        int leftMax = 0, rightMax = 0, water = 0;

        while (l < r) {
            // Whichever side is SHORTER is the binding constraint,
            // so that side's water is already fully determined.
            if (h[l] < h[r]) {
                leftMax = Math.max(leftMax, h[l]);
                water  += leftMax - h[l];   // never negative: leftMax >= h[l]
                l++;
            } else {
                rightMax = Math.max(rightMax, h[r]);
                water   += rightMax - h[r];
                r--;
            }
        }
        return water;
    }
}

Path: the array is handed to you sorted, which is the problem telling you the intended pattern. A hash map also works in O(n) but uses O(n) space and ignores the gift.

Delta: skeleton A verbatim. The only trap is the 1-indexed return: {l + 1, r + 1}.

Watch for: if asked for an O(n log n) alternative, fix each l and binary search the remainder for its complement. Slower here, but it is the version that survives when the two pointers cannot both move.

16 · 3Sum Closest skeleton C

Path: identical scaffold to 15, but there may be no exact hit, so "found it" is replaced by "is this the closest so far".

Delta: keep bestDiff and update it before the comparison branch. The move rule is unchanged — sum < target still means l++, because closeness is still monotone along the sorted array. Return immediately on an exact hit; nothing can beat zero.

Watch for: initialise with the first valid triple, not Integer.MAX_VALUE, or the difference computation overflows.

18 · 4Sum skeleton C

Path: exactly 15 with one more nesting level. Writing the generic kSum from the previous slide once is cheaper than writing 3Sum and 4Sum separately.

Delta: two anchors, both with their own duplicate skip. Use long for the running sum and target — four values near 10⁹ overflow int, and LeetCode's test set includes exactly that case.

Watch for: the pruning if ((long) a[i] * k > target) break; turns a borderline solution into a comfortable one.

Watch for: on a tie, move either pointer; both choices are safe because the measured area is already recorded.

If you only drill twoDo 15 and 42. 15 contains the entire k-sum family and the duplicate handling that trips up most submissions; 42 contains the Rule B argument in its subtlest form, and is asked at senior level far more often than its Hard tag suggests.

You cannot go back, so send a scout ahead

A linked list gives you no indices, no length and no way to step backwards. Two pointers moving at different speeds, or the same speed with a fixed gap, recover all three — in one pass and O(1) space.

The invariant — two speeds

Move slow one node and fast two per step. Two consequences follow, and both are used constantly:

  • When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle — the length was never needed.
  • If there is a cycle, fast must eventually lap slow. Inside the cycle the gap closes by exactly one node per step, so they cannot jump past each other: a meeting is guaranteed.

That "closes by exactly one" is the whole reason the algorithm terminates, and it is what interviewers ask you to justify.

The invariant — fixed gap

Move fast ahead by n nodes first, then advance both at the same speed. The gap is preserved, so when fast hits the end, slow sits exactly n from the end.

This is how "nth node from the end" becomes one pass instead of two: you never learn the length, you just carry the offset.

Both forms are O(n) time and O(1) space, which is almost always the stated constraint. If a problem says "using only constant extra space" about a list, it is naming this pattern.

Applies when

Singly linked lists, and any structure where "next" is a function you can only follow forwards — including an array read as i → nums[i], which turns index-chasing into exactly this cycle problem.

Does not apply when

You need to move backwards, or need the k-th node from the start (that is a plain loop). If the list is doubly linked, the problem is usually easier and this pattern is overkill.

Complexity

O(n) time — phase 1 is at most L + C steps, phase 2 exactly L. O(1) space, which is the constraint these problems exist to enforce. A HashSet of visited nodes also solves 141/142 in O(n) space; say so, then give this.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"determine if the linked list has a cycle" · "return the node where the cycle begins" · "the middle node" · "the n-th node from the end" · "in one pass" · "using O(1) memory" · "the lists intersect". The pairing of linked list with O(1) space or one pass is effectively the problem naming this pattern for you.

LC 142 traced on 3 → 2 → 0 → −4 → (back to 2)

Four nodes; the tail links back to index 1, so the cycle is 2 → 0 → −4 → and the entrance is the node holding 2. Here L = 1 and C = 3. Watch phase 1 meet at −4 — not at the entrance — and phase 2 convert that into the answer in a single step.

PhaseStepslowfastWhat just happened
10A (3)A (3)Both start at the head. The loop tests after moving, so this does not count as a meeting.
11B (2)C (0)slow enters the cycle; fast is one node ahead of it around the loop.
12C (0)B (2)fast wraps D → B. The gap measured along the cycle is now 2.
13D (−4)D (−4)Gap closes by one per step, so it hits zero exactly. Meeting point M = D.
21B (2)B (2)One pointer restarts at the head. After L = 1 step both stand on the entrance. Return node B.
Why they cannot step over each otherOnce both pointers are inside the cycle, fast gains exactly one node on slow per step, so the gap runs … 3, 2, 1, 0 and must land on zero — it can never skip from 1 to −1. This is why the speeds must be 1 and 2. With speeds 1 and 3 the gap falls by two, and on an even-length cycle with an odd starting gap the two pointers can pass each other forever without meeting.

Four skeletons, and a dummy node that prevents half the bugs

Two speeds for cycles and midpoints, a fixed gap for offsets from the end, and a head-swap trick for aligning two lists. The dummy node in skeleton B is not a style choice — it is what makes deleting the head require no special case.

Skeleton A · two speeds — cycle and midpoint (LC 141, 142, 876)
// The guard `fast != null && fast.next != null` covers BOTH
// the odd and even length cases. Getting it wrong is the
// number one NullPointerException in this whole family.
ListNode middle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;

    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
    }
    return slow;        // even length: the SECOND of the two middles
}

boolean hasCycle(ListNode head) {
    ListNode slow = head, fast = head;

    while (fast != null && fast.next != null) {
        slow = slow.next;
        fast = fast.next.next;
        if (slow == fast) return true;   // compare AFTER moving
    }
    return false;                        // fast fell off: no cycle
}
Skeleton B · fixed gap from the end (LC 19)
// `dummy` sits one before the head, so deleting the head
// needs no special case: slow simply stops on the dummy.
ListNode removeNthFromEnd(ListNode head, int n) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
    ListNode fast = dummy, slow = dummy;

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) fast = fast.next;   // open the gap

    while (fast.next != null) {                     // preserve it to the end
        fast = fast.next;
        slow = slow.next;
    }

    slow.next = slow.next.next;   // slow is the node BEFORE the target
    return dummy.next;            // not `head` — it may have been deleted
}
Skeleton C · aligning two lists by swapping heads (LC 160)
// Each pointer walks its own list, then the other. Both therefore
// travel exactly lenA + lenB before meeting, which cancels the
// length difference without ever measuring either length.
//
//   a: A A A A | B B B          both cover the same total,
//   b: B B B   | A A A A        so they arrive together.
//
// If the lists never intersect, both become null at the same
// moment and the loop ends with a == b == null. The null case
// is handled by the SAME code, which is why this beats the
// "measure both lengths and skip the difference" version.
ListNode getIntersectionNode(ListNode headA, ListNode headB) {
    ListNode a = headA, b = headB;

    while (a != b) {
        a = (a == null) ? headB : a.next;
        b = (b == null) ? headA : b.next;
    }
    return a;
}
Skeleton D · reverse in place — the other half of LC 234
// Three pointers, and the order of the four lines never changes.
// Write them in this order every time and it cannot go wrong.
ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null, cur = head;

    while (cur != null) {
        ListNode next = cur.next;   // 1 · save what is ahead
        cur.next = prev;            // 2 · flip this link
        prev = cur;                 // 3 · advance prev
        cur = next;                 // 4 · advance cur
    }
    return prev;                    // the new head
}

Which skeleton, and why

"has a cycle"
A, returning a boolean. Compare after moving, never before, or both pointers start equal and you return true immediately.
"where the cycle begins"
A for phase 1, then the reset walk for phase 2. Never return the meeting point.
"the middle"
A. Decide up front whether you want the first or second middle on an even length — starting fast at head.next gives the first.
"nth from the end"
B, with a dummy. Also the right shape for "remove the head under a condition".
Two lists
C. It handles the no-intersection case with no extra branch.
The three bugs that actually happenGuard written as fast.next != null && fast != null — the order matters; testing fast.next first throws on a null fast. Comparing before moving — slow and fast both begin at the head, so a pre-move comparison reports a cycle on every list. Returning head after a deletion — if the head itself was removed, head now points at a detached node; always return dummy.next.

Six lists, four skeletons, one shared constraint

Every one of these has an easy O(n)-space solution with a HashSet or an ArrayList. Say that solution out loud first — it shows you see the trade-off — then give the O(1)-space pointer version, which is what the problem is actually testing.
