Anchor 1 · LC 739 — the path to the solution

Brute force
For each day, scan forward for the first warmer one. O(n²), which at n = 10⁵ is 10¹⁰ and hopeless.
What the brute force wastes
On a long cold spell, every day rescans the same run of cold days. The scan is repeatedly re-deriving something already known.
The observation
If day j is warmer than day i and comes after it, then day i can never be the answer for anything to the right of j — j is closer and warmer. So i can be discarded permanently the moment j appears.
What "discard" means
A stack of days still waiting, kept decreasing in temperature. Each arriving day pops everything it beats, settling those answers.
Why indices
The answer is how many days, so you need i − poppedIndex. Storing temperatures alone makes that impossible.
Edge case
Days never warmed stay on the stack and keep the 0 default — which is exactly what the problem asks for.
LC 739 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int[] dailyTemperatures(int[] temperatures) {
        int n = temperatures.length;
        int[] ans = new int[n];                    // zeros are the correct default

        // Indices of days still waiting; their temperatures
        // decrease from the bottom of the stack to the top.
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

            // Today is warmer than the day on top, so that day's
            // wait ends here. Settle it and keep going — today may
            // settle several days at once.
            while (!stack.isEmpty() && temperatures[stack.peek()] < temperatures[i]) {
                int day = stack.pop();
                ans[day] = i - day;                // the distance, hence indices
            }

            stack.push(i);
        }
        // Days left on the stack never warmed: ans stays 0.
        return ans;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 84 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Every pair (l, r), taking the minimum height between them. O(n³), or O(n²) carrying a running minimum.
The reframing
Stop enumerating rectangles. Instead ask, for each bar, what is the widest rectangle whose height is exactly that bar? Every maximal rectangle is limited by its shortest bar, so this enumeration is complete.
What that needs
For each bar, the first shorter bar to its left and the first shorter bar to its right. Those two indices give the width directly.
The insight
Both boundaries fall out of a single pass. When a bar is popped, the arriving element is its right boundary, and the item now exposed on the stack is its left boundary. No second pass is needed.
The sentinel
Iterate to n inclusive with a virtual bar of height 0. It forces every remaining bar to pop with the correct right boundary, removing the drain loop and the bugs that live in it.
Width, carefully
i − left − 1, where left is −1 when the stack empties. Deriving that from the trace once is worth more than memorising it.
LC 84 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int largestRectangleArea(int[] heights) {
        int n = heights.length, best = 0;
        Deque<Integer> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();

        // i == n is a VIRTUAL bar of height 0 that drains the stack.
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
            int cur = (i == n) ? 0 : heights[i];

            while (!stack.isEmpty() && heights[stack.peek()] >= cur) {
                int height = heights[stack.pop()];

                // Right boundary is i. Left boundary is whatever the
                // pop exposed — or -1 if this bar reaches index 0.
                int left  = stack.isEmpty() ? -1 : stack.peek();
                int width = i - left - 1;

                best = Math.max(best, height * width);
            }
            stack.push(i);
        }
        return best;
    }
}

496 · Next Greater Element I next greater

Path: the nested-loop version is O(n·m) and passes at these limits, so say it first. The point of the problem is the decomposition, not the speed.

Delta: run the template over nums2 to get every element's next greater, storing results in a HashMap<value, answer> — the statement guarantees distinct values, which is what makes keying by value safe. Then map nums1 through it.

Watch for: elements left on the stack have no greater element, so their map entry must be −1. Easiest is to drain the stack after the loop.

503 · Next Greater Element II circular

Path: the naive fix duplicates the array and runs the template on 2n elements. That works and costs O(n) extra space — worth mentioning before the cleaner version.

Delta: loop i from 0 to 2n and index with i % n. Push only while i < n: the second pass exists solely to settle leftovers, and pushing again would let elements wait forever.

Watch for: the answer here is the value, not the distance, so record a[j] rather than j.

901 · Online Stock Span previous greater

Path: keeping every price and scanning back is O(n) per call, O(n²) overall. The span is really "distance to the previous greater price", which is this pattern in streaming form.

Delta: the stack is a field, surviving between calls. Push (price, span) pairs; when popping, absorb the popped span into your own — that merged count is what makes the amortised O(1) work without storing the whole history.

Watch for: pop while topPrice <= price, inclusive. The problem counts days with a price equal to today's as part of the span.

85 · Maximal Rectangle rectangle × rows

Path: enumerating all sub-rectangles is O((rows·cols)²). The reduction is the whole problem: treat each row as the base of a histogram whose bar heights are the counts of consecutive 1s above.

Delta: maintain one heights[] array across rows — heights[c] = matrix[r][c] == '1' ? heights[c] + 1 : 0 — and call the LC 84 routine on it after each row.

Watch for: the reset to 0 on a '0' cell is what makes the histogram correct; incrementing unconditionally silently merges rectangles across gaps. Solve 84 first — this problem is unreasonable without it.

If you only drill twoDo 739 and 84. 739 makes the push-once-pop-once argument concrete and forces you to store indices. 84 is where the pattern earns its reputation: the realisation that a single pop yields both boundaries is the idea that makes the Hard tag disappear, and 85 becomes a ten-line wrapper once you have it.

A sorted spine that can also drop its oldest element

A monotonic stack discards what is dominated. A monotonic deque does that too, but adds a second eviction rule: elements that have fallen out of the window are removed from the front. Two eviction rules, two ends, and the maximum of every window becomes available in O(1).

The invariant

The deque holds indices whose values are decreasing from front to back. Two consequences follow, and both are used on every step:

  • The front is always the maximum of the current window — no scan needed.
  • Anything smaller than an arriving element is useless forever, because the newcomer is both larger and stays in the window longer.

That second point is the whole justification. A smaller, older element can never be the answer again — so it is not merely delayed, it is dead.

Three moves, always in this order

  1. Expire the front while it has fallen outside the window. This is the rule a stack cannot express.
  2. Evict the back while it is dominated by the arriving value, then push the new index.
  3. Read the front — that is the window's answer.

Each index is pushed once and removed once, from one end or the other, so the total work is 2n — amortised O(1) per element despite two inner loops.

Store indices, never values: the expiry test needs positions.

Applies when

You need the max or min over a sliding range, or a DP transition of the form dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[j]) over a moving band of j. The deque replaces the inner max with an O(1) read.

Does not apply when

Arbitrary elements are removed, or you need the k-th largest rather than the largest — those want a heap or a balanced tree. Also when the range is not contiguous.

Complexity

O(n) time by push-once, remove-once, and O(k) space for a window of width k. A heap-based solution is O(n log n) / O(n) — say that first, then beat it.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the max sliding window" · "for each window of size k" · "the absolute difference between any two elements is at most limit" (needs two deques, one for max and one for min) · "at most k steps forward" in a DP · "the shortest subarray with sum at least k" where negatives rule out a plain window. The signal is a max or min over a moving range, evaluated at every position.

LC 239 traced on [1,3,-1,-3,5,3,6,7], k = 3

The maximum of every window of width 3. The deque never holds more than three indices here, and the front is read directly as each answer — no scanning, no comparison across the window.

inums[i]expire from frontevict from backdeque (indices → values)output

Why the expiry test uses <=The window covering index i starts at i − k + 1, so an index is stale exactly when it is <= i − k. Writing < i − k keeps one element too many and silently reports a maximum from outside the window. The test fires at most once per step because only one index can newly expire, but write it as a while anyway — it costs nothing and it is the form that survives when the window width varies.

Expire, evict, read — in that order, every time

The order is not stylistic. Expiring before evicting keeps the deque small; reading last guarantees the front is both in-window and maximal. Swap any two and the answer is wrong on some input.

The template — maximum of every window of width k
/**
 * Deque holds INDICES whose values DECREASE from front to back.
 * front = the maximum of the current window.
 *
 * Each index is added once and removed once (from one end or
 * the other), so the two inner loops still total O(n).
 */
int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] a, int k) {
    int n = a.length;
    int[] out = new int[n - k + 1];

    Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();

    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

        // 1 · EXPIRE — the front has slid out of the window.
        // Window covering i starts at i-k+1, so <= i-k is stale.
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) {
            dq.pollFirst();
        }

        // 2 · EVICT — anything smaller than a[i] is dead forever:
        // a[i] is bigger AND outlives it.
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && a[dq.peekLast()] <= a[i]) {
            dq.pollLast();
        }
        dq.offerLast(i);

        // 3 · READ — only once the window is actually full.
        if (i >= k - 1) out[i - k + 1] = a[dq.peekFirst()];
    }
    return out;
}
Variant · two deques for max AND min (LC 1438)
// "Absolute difference at most limit" means max - min <= limit,
// so run one decreasing deque and one increasing deque side by
// side. The window is invalid while their fronts differ too much.
int longestSubarray(int[] a, int limit) {
    Deque<Integer> maxD = new ArrayDeque<>();   // decreasing
    Deque<Integer> minD = new ArrayDeque<>();   // increasing
    int l = 0, best = 0;

    for (int r = 0; r < a.length; r++) {
        while (!maxD.isEmpty() && maxD.peekLast() < a[r]) maxD.pollLast();
        maxD.offerLast(a[r]);
        while (!minD.isEmpty() && minD.peekLast() > a[r]) minD.pollLast();
        minD.offerLast(a[r]);

        // Here the left edge moves for VALIDITY, not for age.
        while (maxD.peekFirst() - minD.peekFirst() > limit) {
            if (maxD.peekFirst() == a[l]) maxD.pollFirst();
            if (minD.peekFirst() == a[l]) minD.pollFirst();
            l++;
        }
        best = Math.max(best, r - l + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
Variant · deque as a DP accelerator (LC 1696, 1425)
// dp[i] = a[i] + max(dp[i-k] .. dp[i-1])
// The inner max over a moving band is exactly what the deque gives
// in O(1), turning an O(n*k) DP into O(n).
int maxResult(int[] a, int k) {
    int n = a.length;
    int[] dp = new int[n];
    dp[0] = a[0];

    Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();   // indices, dp decreasing
    dq.offerLast(0);

    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        // expire: only the last k positions may be jumped from
        while (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() < i - k) dq.pollFirst();

        dp[i] = a[i] + dp[dq.peekFirst()];    // best reachable predecessor

        while (!dq.isEmpty() && dp[dq.peekLast()] <= dp[i]) dq.pollLast();
        dq.offerLast(i);
    }
    return dp[n - 1];
}

The knobs

Direction
Decreasing for a maximum, increasing for a minimum. Both at once when the question is about a spread.
Expiry rule
By age for a fixed-width window (index <= i - k); by validity when the left edge is driven by a condition, as in the two-deque variant.
What you store
Indices when you need positions or an age test; raw values when the eviction is purely by comparison, as in LC 1438.
When to read
Guard with i >= k - 1 for fixed windows, or the first few outputs come from an incomplete window.
< or <= on eviction
<= keeps the deque shorter by discarding equal values. Both are correct for a maximum; prefer <=.
The three bugs that actually happenReading before the window is full — without the i >= k - 1 guard the first k−1 answers are maxima of partial windows. Expiring with < instead of <= — keeps one stale index, so the reported maximum can come from just outside the window. Using peek() on an ArrayDeque and expecting the back — peek() is peekFirst(); always write peekFirst and peekLast explicitly here, because both ends are in play.

Six moving ranges, one sorted spine

239 is the template. 1438 runs two deques. 1696 and 1425 use it to accelerate a DP. 862 and 1499 combine it with prefix sums, which is where the pattern stops looking like a window problem at all.

Anchor 1 · LC 239 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Scan each window for its maximum. O(n·k), which at n = 10⁵ and k = 10⁵ is 10¹⁰.
The heap attempt
A max-heap of (value, index) pairs, discarding stale entries lazily from the top. O(n log n) time, O(n) space, and completely correct — offer this first, because it shows you can reach a working answer before optimising.
What the heap wastes
It keeps elements that can never win again. If a[j] ≥ a[i] and j > i, then i is dominated on both value and lifetime — yet the heap still stores it and pays log n to skip it later.
The observation
Delete those elements outright. What remains is automatically sorted, so the maximum is simply the front — no comparisons at all.
Why a deque and not a stack
Two different eviction rules operate at opposite ends: stale-by-age at the front, dominated-by-value at the back. A stack has only one end.
Edge cases
k == 1 returns the input unchanged. Guard the read with i >= k - 1. Output length is n − k + 1.
LC 239 · O(n) time, O(k) space
class Solution {
    public int[] maxSlidingWindow(int[] nums, int k) {
        int n = nums.length;
        int[] out = new int[n - k + 1];

        // Indices; their values decrease from front to back,
        // so the front is always the window maximum.
        Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {

            // 1 · expire by AGE. The window covering i begins at
            //     i - k + 1, so anything <= i - k has slid out.
            while (!dq.isEmpty() && dq.peekFirst() <= i - k) {
                dq.pollFirst();
            }

            // 2 · evict by DOMINATION. nums[i] is larger and
            //     outlives them, so they can never win again.
            while (!dq.isEmpty() && nums[dq.peekLast()] <= nums[i]) {
                dq.pollLast();
            }
            dq.offerLast(i);

            // 3 · read, but only once a full window exists.
            if (i >= k - 1) {
                out[i - k + 1] = nums[dq.peekFirst()];
            }
        }
        return out;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 862 — the path to the solution

Why the obvious window fails
With all-positive values this would be a shrink-while-valid window. Negatives destroy that: extending a subarray can lower its sum, so there is no monotone shrink rule. State this first — it is the reason the problem is Hard rather than Medium.
The reformulation
Work on prefix sums P. A subarray (j, i] qualifies when P[i] − P[j] ≥ K, and you want the largest such j to make it short.
First discard rule
Once P[i] − P[front] ≥ K, that front is answered — and no later i can do better with it, since any later window using it is longer. Record the length and remove it permanently.
Second discard rule
If P[i] ≤ P[back], that back is useless: i gives a sum at least as large from a nearer starting point. Remove it.
The result
Those two rules are exactly the deque's two evictions — but keyed on prefix values rather than on age. The deque stays increasing in P.
Edge cases
Seed with index 0 representing the empty prefix. Use long for P: 10⁵ values of 10⁵ overflows int.
LC 862 · O(n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int shortestSubarray(int[] nums, int k) {
        int n = nums.length;

        long[] P = new long[n + 1];             // long: sums reach 1e10
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) P[i + 1] = P[i] + nums[i];

        // Indices into P; their prefix values INCREASE front to back.
        Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;

        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {

            // 1 · this front is satisfied — record it and drop it.
            //     No later i can use it to make a SHORTER subarray.
            while (!dq.isEmpty() && P[i] - P[dq.peekFirst()] >= k) {
                best = Math.min(best, i - dq.pollFirst());
            }

            // 2 · a back with a bigger prefix is useless: i is both
            //     smaller and closer, so it dominates on both counts.
            while (!dq.isEmpty() && P[dq.peekLast()] >= P[i]) {
                dq.pollLast();
            }
            dq.offerLast(i);
        }
        return best == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : best;
    }
}

1438 · Longest Subarray With Absolute Diff ≤ Limit max + min

Path: a TreeMap of window counts gives max and min in O(log n) each, for O(n log n) overall — a clean, correct first answer worth stating.

Delta: two deques, one decreasing and one increasing. The condition max − min > limit drives the left edge, so expiry is by validity rather than age.

Watch for: when l advances, remove from a deque only if its front is the departing value — comparing with == on the value, not unconditionally.

1696 · Jump Game VI DP accelerator

Path: the plain DP is dp[i] = nums[i] + max(dp[i-k..i-1]), which is O(n·k) and times out. The inner max over a moving band is the deque's whole purpose.

Delta: the template with dp values in place of nums, expiring by index < i - k. dp[dq.peekFirst()] is the best reachable predecessor.

Watch for: push index 0 before the loop starts, or the first read finds an empty deque.

1425 · Constrained Subsequence Sum DP accelerator

Path: nearly identical to 1696, with one extra decision: elements may be skipped entirely, so a negative running best should be abandoned.

Delta: dp[i] = nums[i] + Math.max(0, dp[dq.peekFirst()]). The max(0, …) is the whole difference — it says "starting fresh here beats carrying a negative forward".

Watch for: the answer is max(dp), not dp[n-1] — the best subsequence need not reach the end.

1499 · Max Value of Equation algebra + deque

Path: the difficulty is algebraic, not structural. Maximise y_i + y_j + |x_i − x_j| with x_j − x_i ≤ k; since points are sorted by x, for j > i the expression is (y_j + x_j) + (y_i − x_i).

Delta: the first bracket is fixed at the current point, so you only need the maximum y_i − x_i over points within distance k — a max over a moving range, which is the template.

Watch for: expire by x-distance, not by index count: x[i] − x[front] > k. Using index age instead is the most common wrong answer here.

If you only drill twoDo 239 and 862. 239 establishes the three moves and the domination argument that justifies deleting elements outright. 862 shows the pattern applied where no window is visible at all — the deque runs over prefix sums, and both eviction rules are re-derived from the problem rather than copied. That transfer is what makes the rest of this family tractable.

Keep only k things, and know which one is worst

To find the k largest of n items you do not need to sort n things. Keep a heap of size k, and make it a min-heap — so its root is the weakest of your current best k. Every new item is compared against that root alone: beat it and you are in, fail and you are discarded immediately.

The inversion that trips everyone

For the k largest, use a min-heap. For the k smallest, use a max-heap. This feels backwards and is the single most common mistake in the pattern.

The reason: the root must be the item you are most willing to throw away. When collecting the largest values, the one you would sacrifice first is the smallest of those you hold — so that must sit at the root where it can be inspected and evicted in O(log k).

Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default, so "k largest" needs no comparator at all — which is a useful tell that you have picked the right direction.

The invariant, and the cost

After processing any prefix of the input, the heap contains exactly the best k items seen so far — never more.

Maintaining it costs one comparison against the root, plus an O(log k) push-and-pop only when the newcomer qualifies. Total O(n log k), against O(n log n) for sorting.

When k is small that gap is large — and more importantly the heap needs only O(k) memory, so it works on a stream whose length you never learn.

Applies when

You need the top k by some score, the k-th element, or a running best over a stream. Also when items arrive continuously and the total count is unknown, which rules out sorting entirely.

Does not apply when

You need the full sorted order (just sort), or k is close to n (sorting is simpler and no slower). Also when a count bounds the values — bucketing by frequency is O(n) and beats the log factor.

Complexity

O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Quickselect gives O(n) average for a single k-th query but O(n²) worst case and destroys the input; a heap is the safer default and the one to offer first.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the k-th largest" · "the top k frequent" · "the k closest" · "return any k of them" · "design a class that returns the k-th largest so far" (a stream, so O(k) memory is mandatory) · "repeatedly take the two heaviest". The phrase "k-th" next to a large n is the clearest signal in this deck.

LC 215 traced on [3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6], k = 4

The 4th largest element. The heap holds at most four values and its root is the answer-so-far. Notice how many arrivals are rejected in O(1) — that is where the running time actually goes.

Why the root is the answer, not the largestThe heap holds the k largest values, and its root is the smallest of those k. The smallest of the top four is precisely the 4th largest overall. Reaching for Collections.max(heap) here returns the 1st largest instead — a mistake that passes when k = 1 and fails everywhere else.

One bounded heap, and the comparators that configure it

The loop is five lines. Everything problem-specific lives in the comparator and in which direction the heap runs — so getting those two right is the whole job.

The template — the k largest, with a bounded min-heap
/**
 * Keep at most k items. MIN-heap, so the root is the weakest
 * of the current best k — the one to evict when something better
 * arrives.  O(n log k) time, O(k) space.
 */
int kthLargest(int[] a, int k) {
    // Java's PriorityQueue is a MIN-heap by default, which is
    // exactly what "k largest" wants. No comparator needed.
    PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();

    for (int v : a) {
        heap.offer(v);

        // Never let it exceed k. Evicting the root drops the
        // smallest, which is always the right one to lose.
        if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();
    }
    return heap.peek();     // smallest of the top k == the k-th largest
}

// The one-comparison variant: cheaper, because most arrivals
// fail the test and never touch the heap structure at all.
for (int v : a) {
    if (heap.size() < k)        heap.offer(v);
    else if (v > heap.peek()) { heap.poll(); heap.offer(v); }
    // else: discard in O(1)
}
Comparators — the part that is actually problem-specific
// k LARGEST values  -> min-heap (the default)
new PriorityQueue<Integer>();

// k SMALLEST values -> max-heap
new PriorityQueue<Integer>(Comparator.reverseOrder());

// k CLOSEST points  -> max-heap on squared distance, so the
// FARTHEST sits at the root ready to be evicted.
// Compare squared distances: no sqrt, no floating point.
new PriorityQueue<int[]>((p, q) ->
        (q[0]*q[0] + q[1]*q[1]) - (p[0]*p[0] + p[1]*p[1]));

// k MOST FREQUENT  -> min-heap on the count
new PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<Integer,Integer>>(
        Map.Entry.comparingByValue());

// MIXED KEYS — least frequent first, and among equal counts the
// LEXICOGRAPHICALLY LARGEST first, so the worst candidate is
// always at the root and gets evicted.
new PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String,Integer>>((x, y) ->
        x.getValue().equals(y.getValue())
            ? y.getKey().compareTo(x.getKey())     // reversed!
            : x.getValue() - y.getValue());
Quickselect — O(n) average for a single k-th query
// Beats the heap on average, but is O(n^2) worst case and
// REORDERS the input. Offer the heap first, then this.
int quickselect(int[] a, int k) {
    int target = a.length - k;        // k-th largest == index n-k when sorted
    int lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
    Random rnd = new Random();        // randomise or sorted input is O(n^2)

    while (true) {
        int p = lo + rnd.nextInt(hi - lo + 1);
        int pos = partition(a, lo, hi, p);

        if (pos == target) return a[pos];
        if (pos < target) lo = pos + 1;   // discard the left half entirely
        else              hi = pos - 1;
    }
}

private int partition(int[] a, int lo, int hi, int p) {
    int pivot = a[p];
    swap(a, p, hi);
    int store = lo;
    for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) {
        if (a[i] < pivot) swap(a, store++, i);
    }
    swap(a, store, hi);
    return store;
}

The knobs

Direction
The root must hold the item you would sacrifice first. k largest → min-heap; k smallest → max-heap.
Bound
Poll whenever size exceeds k. Skipping this makes it O(n log n) with O(n) memory, which defeats the point on a stream.
Comparator
The only genuinely problem-specific code. When two keys are involved, the tie-break is usually reversed relative to intuition, because the root is the loser.
When to beat it
If frequencies bound the values, bucket by count for O(n). If a single k-th query is wanted and mutating the input is allowed, quickselect averages O(n).
Streaming
Make the heap a field and keep it bounded. That is the whole design for a k-th-largest-so-far class.
The three bugs that actually happenThe heap pointing the wrong way — a max-heap for "k largest" evicts your best element every time, and the result looks plausible on small inputs. Integer overflow in a comparator — a - b overflows when the values span the int range; use Integer.compare(a, b). Forgetting to reverse the tie-break — in LC 692 the root must hold the worst candidate, so among equal counts the lexicographically largest word sorts first, which reads backwards until you remember what the root is for.

Six selections, and two worth beating

215, 973 and 703 are the bounded heap with different comparators. 347 and 692 add a counting step first — and 347 can then be solved in O(n) without a heap at all. 1046 uses a heap for repeated extraction rather than selection.

Anchor 1 · LC 215 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Sort descending and read index k − 1. O(n log n), two lines, and it passes. Say it — then explain why you would do better.
The observation
Sorting orders all n elements when you only care about k of them. The other n − k comparisons are wasted.
The bounded heap
Keep the best k seen so far in a min-heap. The root is the weakest of those, so it doubles as the admission threshold and as the running answer.
Why min and not max
Because the root must be the element you would drop first. Holding the k largest, that is the smallest of them — which is also, by definition, the k-th largest.
The O(n) follow-up
Quickselect. Partition around a random pivot; if the pivot lands at index n − k you are done, otherwise recurse into one side only. Average O(n), worst case O(n²) — mention that it mutates the input.
Edge case
Duplicates count separately: the 2nd largest of [5,5] is 5, not an error. Never de-duplicate.
LC 215 · O(n log k) time, O(k) space
class Solution {
    public int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) {
        // MIN-heap: the root is the smallest of the k largest,
        // which is exactly the k-th largest overall.
        PriorityQueue<Integer> heap = new PriorityQueue<>();

        for (int v : nums) {
            if (heap.size() < k) {
                heap.offer(v);
            } else if (v > heap.peek()) {
                // v beats the weakest one we hold — swap them.
                heap.poll();
                heap.offer(v);
            }
            // otherwise v cannot make the top k: discard in O(1)
        }
        return heap.peek();
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 692 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Count with a map, sort all entries by (count desc, word asc), take k. O(n log n) and completely correct — the expected baseline.
Why it is the interesting one
Two sort keys pointing in opposite directions: frequency descending, but ties broken alphabetically ascending.
The reversal
In a bounded min-heap the root holds the item to evict — the worst candidate. So the comparator must sort worst-first: lowest count first, and among equal counts the alphabetically largest word first, because that is the one that loses.
Why that reads backwards
The heap order is the inverse of the output order. Writing the comparator as if it were the output order is the standard failure, and it produces answers that are right on counts and wrong on ties.
The final step
Draining a min-heap yields worst-first, so the result must be reversed before returning.
Edge case
Use compareTo on the strings, not == or equals alone — you need an ordering, not equality.
LC 692 · O(n log k) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public List<String> topKFrequent(String[] words, int k) {
        Map<String, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
        for (String w : words) freq.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum);

        // The ROOT must hold the WORST candidate, so this comparator
        // is the reverse of the output order:
        //   lower count first, and among equal counts the
        //   alphabetically LARGER word first — it loses ties.
        PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Integer>> heap =
            new PriorityQueue<>((x, y) ->
                x.getValue().equals(y.getValue())
                    ? y.getKey().compareTo(x.getKey())
                    : x.getValue() - y.getValue());

        for (Map.Entry<String, Integer> e : freq.entrySet()) {
            heap.offer(e);
            if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();     // drops the worst
        }

        // Draining gives worst-first, so reverse for the answer.
        LinkedList<String> out = new LinkedList<>();
        while (!heap.isEmpty()) out.addFirst(heap.poll().getKey());
        return out;
    }
}

703 · Kth Largest Element in a Stream min, size k

Path: storing every value and sorting on each add is O(n log n) per call. The stream has no known end, so O(k) memory is the actual requirement.

Delta: the same bounded min-heap, but as an instance field. Seed it from the constructor's array, then add is offer-then-trim-then-peek.

Watch for: the initial array may be shorter than k, so guard peek() until the heap has filled. This is the design question the problem is really asking.

973 · K Closest Points to Origin max, size k

Path: sort by distance and take k — O(n log n). The heap brings it to O(n log k), and quickselect on distance averages O(n).

Delta: you want the k smallest distances, so the heap flips to max: the farthest point sits at the root ready to be evicted.

Watch for: compare x² + y² directly. Math.sqrt is slower and introduces floating-point comparisons for no gain, since squaring preserves order on non-negative values.

347 · Top K Frequent Elements min on count

Path: count with a map, then a bounded min-heap keyed on the count gives O(n log k) — the expected answer.

Delta: then beat it. A frequency can never exceed n, so it can index an array directly: bucket the values by count and read downwards from n. That is O(n) with no comparator at all.

Watch for: new List[n + 1] raises an unchecked-generic-array warning. It is correct and idiomatic here — say so rather than working around it.

1046 · Last Stone Weight max, unbounded

Path: re-sorting after every smash is O(n² log n). The heap gives extract-max in O(log n), which is what the simulation needs.

Delta: this is not a top-k problem. The heap is unbounded and the loop repeatedly pulls the two largest, pushing back the difference when it is non-zero.

Watch for: loop while size > 1, and return 0 when the heap empties. Use Comparator.reverseOrder() for the max-heap — and with values bounded at 1000, a counting approach also works.

If you only drill twoDo 215 and 692. 215 fixes the direction rule — k largest means a min-heap — which is the error that costs people this whole family. 692 is the one that forces you to reason about why the comparator reads backwards, and once that clicks, writing a correct comparator for any two-key selection becomes mechanical.

Sort by one end, then a single pass decides everything

Interval problems are trivial once sorted and near-impossible before. The entire skill is choosing which end to sort by — start or end — because that one decision determines whether the following linear pass is correct.

The two sort keys, and when each is right

Sort by start
When you are building something: merging overlaps, inserting a new interval, counting simultaneous rooms. Processing in start order means each interval arrives exactly when it becomes relevant.
Sort by end
When you are keeping as many as possible: the classic activity-selection greedy. Finishing earliest leaves the most room for everything after it.

Get this backwards and the code still runs, still looks reasonable, and returns a wrong answer on the second test case. It is the only real decision in the pattern.

The overlap test

Two intervals a and b overlap when a.start <= b.end and b.start <= a.end. After sorting by start, the first condition is automatic, so the test collapses to b.start <= a.end.

Whether touching counts as overlapping is problem-specific. [1,2] and [2,3] merge in LC 56 but do not conflict in a meeting-room problem, where a room frees at the moment the meeting ends. That is <= versus <, and it decides correctness.

Read the statement for the word "touching", "adjacent", or an example with shared endpoints, and pick the operator deliberately.

Applies when

The input is a list of [start, end] pairs and the question is about overlap — merging, counting simultaneous, removing the fewest, or fitting the most.

Does not apply when

Intervals are inserted and queried dynamically — that wants a TreeMap or an interval tree. Also when you need per-point totals rather than interval structure, which is a range-update problem instead.

Complexity

O(n log n), dominated entirely by the sort; the pass itself is O(n). Space is O(n) for the output, or O(1) beyond it when you can sort in place.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"merge all overlapping intervals" · "insert a new interval and merge" · "can a person attend all meetings" · "the minimum number of conference rooms" · "remove the minimum number of intervals to make the rest non-overlapping" · "the minimum number of arrows". The last two are the same greedy, and both are activity selection in disguise.

LC 56 traced on [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]]

Merge everything that overlaps. After sorting by start, one pass suffices: either the current interval extends the last merged one, or it begins a new one. There is no third case.

currentlast mergedtestactionoutput
[1,3]——seed[[1,3]]

Why max and not just the new endConsider [[1,10],[2,3]]. After sorting, [2,3] overlaps [1,10] and merges into it — but its end is smaller. Writing last[1] = cur[1] shortens the merged interval to [1,3] and silently drops coverage. last[1] = Math.max(last[1], cur[1]) is the only correct form, and containment is exactly the case that exposes it.

Three skeletons, split by what the question wants

Merge (sort by start, extend or append), count simultaneous (sort by start, evict finished with a heap), and keep-the-most (sort by end, greedily accept). Each is under fifteen lines once the sort is chosen.

Skeleton A · merge overlapping (LC 56, 57)
// Sort by START. Then exactly two cases arise per interval.
int[][] merge(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

    List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();

    for (int[] cur : intervals) {
        int[] last = out.isEmpty() ? null : out.get(out.size() - 1);

        if (last != null && cur[0] <= last[1]) {
            // Overlap: extend. max() matters — cur may be CONTAINED
            // in last, and then cur[1] is smaller.
            last[1] = Math.max(last[1], cur[1]);
        } else {
            // Disjoint: start a new interval. Copy it — never alias
            // the input array, or a later merge mutates the source.
            out.add(new int[]{ cur[0], cur[1] });
        }
    }
    return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
}
Skeleton B · count simultaneous (LC 253)
// Sort by START; a min-heap of END times holds the rooms in use.
// The heap root is the meeting that frees up soonest.
int minMeetingRooms(int[][] meetings) {
    Arrays.sort(meetings, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

    PriorityQueue<Integer> endTimes = new PriorityQueue<>();

    for (int[] m : meetings) {
        // A room whose meeting ENDED by the time this one starts
        // can be reused. Note <= : a room frees AT its end time.
        if (!endTimes.isEmpty() && endTimes.peek() <= m[0]) {
            endTimes.poll();
        }
        endTimes.offer(m[1]);
    }
    return endTimes.size();       // peak concurrency
}
Skeleton C · keep the most / remove the fewest (LC 435, 452)
// Sort by END. The greedy: always take the interval that finishes
// earliest, because it leaves the most room for everything after.
//
// Exchange argument: any optimal set can have its first interval
// swapped for the earliest finisher without creating a conflict,
// so the greedy choice is never worse.
int maxNonOverlapping(int[][] intervals) {
    Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));

    int kept = 0;
    long lastEnd = Long.MIN_VALUE;

    for (int[] iv : intervals) {
        if (iv[0] >= lastEnd) {   // no conflict with what we kept
            kept++;
            lastEnd = iv[1];
        }
    }
    return kept;                  // removals = intervals.length - kept
}

Choosing the skeleton

"merge", "insert"
A. Sort by start; extend or append.
"how many rooms / how many at once"
B. Sort by start, heap of ends. Equivalently, sweep +1/−1 events — same answer, and worth naming as the alternative.
"remove the fewest", "the minimum arrows"
C. Sort by end, greedy accept. Both phrasings are the same problem.
"can one person attend all"
A, reduced: sort by start and return false at the first overlap.
The < versus <= decisionIn LC 56, [1,2] and [2,3] do merge — so the test is cur[0] <= last[1]. In LC 253, a meeting ending at 2 and another starting at 2 do not conflict, because the room frees at the end instant — so the reuse test is peek() <= start. In LC 452, an arrow at a shared endpoint does burst both balloons. Each of these is stated or implied by the examples; read them rather than guessing.
The three bugs that actually happenForgetting Math.max when extending — a contained interval shortens the merged end, and the failure only appears on inputs with nesting. Integer overflow in the comparator — a[0] - b[0] overflows when coordinates span the int range, which LC 452 tests directly; use Integer.compare. Sorting by the wrong end — sorting by start in an activity-selection problem picks a long early interval and loses several short ones, which passes the first example and fails the rest.

Six interval questions, three skeletons

56 and 57 merge. 252 and 253 count concurrency. 435 and 452 are the same greedy with different wording. Two of the six are behind LeetCode's paywall, and both have free equivalents noted below.

Anchor 1 · LC 56 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Repeatedly scan for any overlapping pair and fuse them, until a full pass changes nothing. O(n³) and awkward to write correctly.
The observation
Sorting by start makes overlap local: if an interval does not overlap the one immediately before it, it cannot overlap anything earlier either, because every earlier interval starts no later and has already been absorbed.
What that buys
Only the last emitted interval ever needs checking — so one pass with one comparison per element.
The two cases
cur.start <= last.end means extend; otherwise append. There is no third case, which is a useful thing to notice out loud.
The detail
last.end = max(last.end, cur.end). A contained interval such as [2,3] inside [1,10] would otherwise truncate the merge.
Edge cases
Touching intervals do merge here, so the test is <=. Copy each interval into the output rather than storing the input reference, or later mutation corrupts the source array.
LC 56 · O(n log n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int[][] merge(int[][] intervals) {
        // Sorting by start makes overlap local: only the previously
        // emitted interval can possibly overlap the current one.
        Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

        List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();

        for (int[] cur : intervals) {
            int[] last = out.isEmpty() ? null : out.get(out.size() - 1);

            if (last != null && cur[0] <= last[1]) {
                // Overlapping (touching counts here, hence <=).
                // max() because cur may be fully CONTAINED in last.
                last[1] = Math.max(last[1], cur[1]);
            } else {
                // Disjoint — copy, never alias the input row.
                out.add(new int[]{ cur[0], cur[1] });
            }
        }
        return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 253 — the path to the solution

Restating it
The number of rooms needed is the maximum number of meetings running at the same instant. Once phrased that way, the problem stops being about rooms.
Brute force
For each meeting, count how many others overlap it. O(n²).
Solution one — the heap
Sort by start. Keep a min-heap of end times: the root is the room freeing up soonest. For each meeting, reuse that room if it has already finished, otherwise open a new one. The heap size is the room count.
Solution two — the sweep
Split every meeting into a +1 at its start and a −1 at its end, sort all events by time, and track the running maximum. Same O(n log n), and often easier to explain.
The ordering detail
At equal timestamps, process the end before the start — a room genuinely frees at that instant. In the heap version this is the <= in the reuse test.
Why the heap is never bigger than needed
A room is only opened when every existing one is still busy, so the size never exceeds true peak concurrency.
LC 253 · O(n log n) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int minMeetingRooms(int[][] intervals) {
        if (intervals.length == 0) return 0;

        // Process meetings in the order they begin.
        Arrays.sort(intervals, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[0], b[0]));

        // Min-heap of END times: the root is the room that
        // becomes free soonest.
        PriorityQueue<Integer> rooms = new PriorityQueue<>();

        for (int[] m : intervals) {
            // <= because a room frees AT the end instant: a meeting
            // ending at 10 does not conflict with one starting at 10.
            if (!rooms.isEmpty() && rooms.peek() <= m[0]) {
                rooms.poll();          // reuse that room
            }
            rooms.offer(m[1]);         // occupy a room until m ends
        }
        // A room was only ever added when all others were busy,
        // so the size is exactly the peak concurrency.
        return rooms.size();
    }
}

57 · Insert Interval skeleton A

Path: appending and re-running LC 56 is O(n log n) and correct — say it. But the input is already sorted, so the sort is pure waste.

Delta: three phases in one pass. Copy everything ending before the new interval starts; absorb everything overlapping it by taking min of starts and max of ends; copy the rest.

Watch for: the new interval may overlap nothing, or everything. Both fall out of the three phases with no special case — which is why this structure is worth writing rather than branching.

252 · Meeting Rooms skeleton A Premium

Path: checking all pairs is O(n²). Sorting by start makes conflict local, exactly as in LC 56.

Delta: sort by start and return false the moment intervals[i][0] < intervals[i-1][1]. Strict < here: a meeting starting when another ends is fine.

Premium: paywalled. LC 56 covers the same reasoning, and 253 below is the strictly harder version — solving that one subsumes this entirely.

435 · Non-overlapping Intervals skeleton C

Path: "remove the minimum" is the same as "keep the maximum", which is classic activity selection. That restatement is the whole problem.

Delta: sort by end, then greedily accept any interval starting at or after the last accepted end. The answer is n − kept.

Watch for: sorting by start is the trap — it picks a long early interval and loses several short ones. Be ready to give the exchange argument for why earliest-finish-first is safe; that is the follow-up question.

452 · Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons skeleton C

Path: identical to 435 with the count inverted — instead of removals, you are counting the groups that survive.

Delta: sort by end; fire an arrow at the end of the first balloon, and skip every balloon whose start is at or before that point. The arrow count is the number of groups.

Watch for: coordinates span the full int range, so a[1] - b[1] in the comparator overflows and produces a wrong sort order. Use Integer.compare — LeetCode tests this case specifically.

If you only drill twoDo 56 and 435. Together they force the central decision: 56 sorts by start because it is building merged intervals, 435 sorts by end because it is keeping as many as possible. Once you can state why each is right, 57, 252, 253 and 452 are all short variations — and picking the wrong end is the only way this family goes wrong.

Take the locally best option — and be able to prove it is safe

A greedy algorithm commits to a choice and never reconsiders. That makes it fast and simple, and wrong far more often than people expect. The pattern is not "take the biggest"; it is finding the ordering under which the obvious choice is provably optimal, then saying why.

The exchange argument

Every correct greedy has the same proof shape. Take any optimal solution that differs from yours at the first choice. Show you can swap its choice for yours without making it worse. Repeat, and the optimal solution has been transformed into the greedy one — so the greedy is optimal too.

If you cannot construct that swap, the greedy is probably wrong. That failure is the signal to reach for dynamic programming instead.

Interviewers ask "why does that work?" on every greedy problem. The exchange argument is the answer, and it is usually two sentences.

The three shapes greedy takes here

Furthest reach
Track how far you can get, and commit only when forced. Jump problems.
Sort, then place
Find an order in which each item's position is forced once its predecessors are fixed. Reconstruction problems.
Bound then construct
Prove a lower bound on the answer from the most constrained element, then show it is achievable. Scheduling with cooldowns.

All three are O(n) or O(n log n), and all three are short — the difficulty is entirely in the justification.

Applies when

A locally optimal choice is provably safe: taking it never rules out an optimal completion. Usually visible after sorting, or when one element is so constrained that it dictates the answer.

Does not apply when

Choices interact — taking the biggest coin now may strand you later. That is the coin-change trap, and it is what dynamic programming exists for. If you cannot write the exchange argument, assume greedy is wrong.

Complexity

O(n) when no sort is needed, O(n log n) when there is one. Space is usually O(1). These are among the cheapest solutions in the deck — the cost is all in the reasoning.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the minimum number of jumps" · "can you reach the last index" · "partition the string into as many parts as possible" · "the least number of intervals" · "reconstruct the queue" · "the minimum time to finish all tasks with a cooldown" · "is there a starting point from which you can complete the circuit". The tell is an optimisation with no obvious subproblem structure — if a DP state is hard to define, look for a greedy and its proof.

LC 45 traced on [2,3,1,1,4]

The minimum jumps to reach the last index. The answer is 2. Watch that the algorithm never picks an index to jump from — it scans each reachable band, remembers the furthest point the band can reach, and increments the counter only when it runs out of band.

inums[i]i + nums[i]farthestbandEndat the band edge?jumps
02220 → 2yes — take a jump1
13442no1
21342 → 4yes — take a jump2
31444no2
Why this is optimal — the exchange argumentEvery index in band k is reachable in exactly k jumps and no fewer. When the scan reaches the band's edge it has seen every index in that band, so farthest is the true limit of band k+1. No alternative choice inside band k could reach further, because the scan already considered all of them. This is breadth-first search over layers, so the first band containing the target gives the minimum — and BFS optimality is the proof.

Three skeletons, and the proof that goes with each

Furthest reach for jumps and coverage, sort-then-place for reconstruction, and bound-then-construct for scheduling under a constraint. Each is short — write the justification in a comment so you remember why it is correct.

Skeleton A · furthest reach (LC 45, 55, 763)
/**
 * Scan a BAND of reachable positions, remembering the furthest
 * point anything in the band can reach. Commit to a jump only
 * when the band is exhausted.
 *
 * Optimality: this is BFS over layers. Band k is exactly the set
 * reachable in k jumps, so the first band containing the target
 * gives the minimum.
 */
int minJumps(int[] a) {
    int jumps = 0, bandEnd = 0, farthest = 0;

    // n - 1, NOT n: arriving at the last index means you are done,
    // so you never jump FROM it.
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length - 1; i++) {
        farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + a[i]);

        if (i == bandEnd) {          // band exhausted — must jump now
            jumps++;
            bandEnd = farthest;
        }
    }
    return jumps;
}

// Reachability only (LC 55) — no counter, just the frontier.
boolean canReach(int[] a) {
    int farthest = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
        if (i > farthest) return false;      // a gap we cannot cross
        farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + a[i]);
    }
    return true;
}
Skeleton B · sort, then place (LC 406)
/**
 * Find an order in which each item's position becomes FORCED once
 * its predecessors are fixed. Then a single insertion pass works.
 *
 * LC 406: people are [height, k] where k counts taller-or-equal
 * people in front. Process TALLEST first — shorter people inserted
 * later are invisible to them, so an already-placed person's k
 * value can never be disturbed. That invariance is the proof.
 */
int[][] reconstructQueue(int[][] people) {
    Arrays.sort(people, (a, b) ->
            a[0] != b[0] ? b[0] - a[0]     // taller first
                         : a[1] - b[1]);   // same height: smaller k first

    List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int[] p : people) {
        // Everyone already placed is >= this height, so putting p
        // at index p[1] puts exactly p[1] of them in front.
        out.add(p[1], p);
    }
    return out.toArray(new int[0][]);
}
Skeleton C · bound, then construct (LC 621)
/**
 * Prove a lower bound from the most constrained element, then show
 * it is achievable. The answer is the bound.
 *
 * LC 621: the most frequent task forces a skeleton of
 *     (maxFreq - 1) full blocks of width (n + 1), plus a tail
 *     holding every task that ties for maxFreq.
 * Nothing can beat that, and any leftover tasks slot into the gaps
 * without lengthening it — so the schedule length is
 *     max(that bound, tasks.length).
 */
int leastInterval(char[] tasks, int n) {
    int[] count = new int[26];
    int maxFreq = 0;
    for (char t : tasks) maxFreq = Math.max(maxFreq, ++count[t - 'A']);

    int tied = 0;                       // how many tasks hit maxFreq
    for (int c : count) if (c == maxFreq) tied++;

    int bound = (maxFreq - 1) * (n + 1) + tied;

    // If there are more tasks than slots, the gaps are already full
    // and no idling is needed at all.
    return Math.max(bound, tasks.length);
}

Which skeleton

"minimum jumps", "can you reach"
A. Track a frontier; increment only at the band edge.
"as many parts as possible"
A again — the part ends at the furthest last-occurrence seen so far.
"reconstruct", "rebuild the order"
B. Find the order in which each placement is forced, usually most-constrained first.
"minimum time with a cooldown"
C. Bound from the most frequent element, then show it is achievable.
"is there a valid starting point"
C in disguise: prove the total is feasible, then show the failure points identify the answer.
The three bugs that actually happenLooping to n − 1 in LC 45 — arriving at the last index ends the journey, so jumping from it counts a phantom step. Assuming greedy works without the exchange argument — LC 55 is greedy, but "pick the largest jump each time" is not correct for it; the frontier is. Comparator overflow in LC 406 — b[0] - a[0] is safe for heights under 10⁴, but build the habit of Integer.compare anyway.

Six greedies, six different proofs

55 and 45 share a frontier. 763 is a frontier over last-occurrences. 406 and 621 need constructions. 134 is the one where the proof is the entire problem.

45Jump Game IIMediumSame frontier, counting band edges. BFS without a queue.AO(n) / O(1)
763Partition LabelsMediumA part ends at the furthest last-occurrence seen so far.AO(n) / O(1)

Anchor 1 · LC 45 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Try every jump length from every index. Exponential, then O(n²) with memoisation — a fine first answer.
The reframing
This is a shortest-path problem on an unweighted graph, so BFS gives the minimum. Each BFS layer is a contiguous band of indices, because reachability from a band is an interval.
What that buys
Contiguous layers need no queue. Scan left to right, track the furthest reach of the current band, and advance the band boundary when you hit its edge.
Why you never choose an index
The scan visits every index in the band before committing, so it already has the best reach available. There is no decision to make — which is why the code has no max over candidates beyond the running one.
The off-by-one
Loop to n − 2. Arriving at the last index ends the journey; counting a jump from it inflates the answer by one.
Edge cases
A single-element array needs 0 jumps, which the loop bound handles for free. The problem guarantees the end is reachable, so no failure path is needed.
LC 45 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int jump(int[] nums) {
        int jumps = 0;
        int bandEnd = 0;     // last index reachable with `jumps` jumps
        int farthest = 0;    // furthest anything in this band can reach

        // n - 1: arriving at the last index finishes the journey,
        // so we never jump FROM it.
        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length - 1; i++) {

            farthest = Math.max(farthest, i + nums[i]);

            // Reached the edge of the current band, so the next step
            // must cost one more jump. `farthest` is the true limit
            // of that next band, since we scanned the whole band.
            if (i == bandEnd) {
                jumps++;
                bandEnd = farthest;
            }
        }
        return jumps;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 134 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Try every station as a start and simulate the full circuit. O(n²), and the natural first attempt.
Claim one — existence
If sum(gas) < sum(cost) no start can work, because the circuit is a closed loop and the total deficit is start-independent. If the total is non-negative, a valid start must exist.
Claim two — location
Suppose you start at s and run dry arriving at i. Then no station between s and i works either: each such start reaches i with less fuel than you had, since your running balance was non-negative throughout that stretch.
What that buys
On failure you skip the entire prefix in one move — restart at i + 1 rather than s + 1. So each station is examined once and the scan is O(n).
Why one pass proves it
The final candidate is the only one never invalidated, and claim one guarantees some start works. Therefore that candidate is the answer — no verification pass is needed.
Edge cases
Return −1 when the total is negative. The answer is unique, as the problem states, which is what makes the single candidate safe.
LC 134 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public int canCompleteCircuit(int[] gas, int[] cost) {
        int total = 0;      // whole-loop surplus: decides EXISTENCE
        int tank = 0;       // running surplus since the candidate start
        int start = 0;

        for (int i = 0; i < gas.length; i++) {
            int diff = gas[i] - cost[i];
            total += diff;
            tank  += diff;

            if (tank < 0) {
                // Ran dry arriving at i. Every station from `start`
                // to i also fails — each would reach i with even less
                // fuel, because tank was non-negative all the way here.
                // So skip the whole prefix in one move.
                start = i + 1;
                tank = 0;
            }
        }
        // Non-negative total guarantees a solution exists, and `start`
        // is the only candidate never invalidated.
        return total >= 0 ? start : -1;
    }
}

55 · Jump Game skeleton A

Path: the DP marks each index reachable or not in O(n²). The greedy needs only the frontier.

Delta: track farthest; if i > farthest you have hit a gap you cannot cross, so return false. Otherwise extend and continue.

Watch for: "always take the biggest jump" is not correct here — a large jump can overshoot a launchpad. The frontier is what works, and knowing why the obvious greedy fails is the point of the problem.

763 · Partition Labels skeleton A

Path: a letter must live entirely inside one part, so a part cannot end before the last occurrence of any letter it contains.

Delta: record each letter's last index in one pass. Then sweep, extending end = max(end, last[c]); when i == end, cut. The frontier is over last-occurrences instead of jump reaches.

Watch for: the part length is i − start + 1, and start must be reset to i + 1 after each cut.

406 · Queue Reconstruction by Height skeleton B

Path: trying orderings is factorial. The insight is choosing a processing order in which each placement is forced.

Delta: sort tallest first, ties by ascending k. Insert each person at index k. Because everyone already placed is at least as tall, inserting at k puts exactly k taller-or-equal people in front — and later, shorter insertions are invisible to them, so no earlier placement is ever disturbed.

Watch for: List.add(index, element) is O(n) per insert, giving O(n²) overall. That is accepted; say so rather than reaching for something exotic.

621 · Task Scheduler skeleton C

Path: simulating with a max-heap and a cooldown queue works and is O(n log 26) — a correct answer worth stating. The closed form is better and much shorter.

Delta: the most frequent task forces (maxFreq − 1) blocks of width (n + 1), plus a tail of every task tied at maxFreq. Take max(bound, tasks.length).

Watch for: the max with tasks.length is essential — when there are many distinct tasks the gaps are already full and no idling occurs, so the bound underestimates.

If you only drill twoDo 45 and 134. 45 teaches the frontier and the layered-BFS view that also solves 55 and 763. 134 is the one where the code is eight lines and the argument is the whole problem — and being able to give both claims out loud is exactly what an interviewer is probing for when they ask why a greedy is safe.

Rewire pointers without losing the rest of the list

Every one of these problems is the same physical act: change a next field. The difficulty is that overwriting cur.next destroys your only route to everything after it — so the discipline is save first, rewire second, and the tools are a dummy head and a fixed vocabulary of four moves.

The dummy head

Allocate one throwaway node that sits before the real head. Every "what if the head itself changes?" case vanishes, because the head is no longer special — it is just dummy.next.

Use it whenever the head might be removed, replaced, or reordered — which is most of this pattern. Return dummy.next, never the original head variable, since that node may no longer be first.

The cost is one node. The benefit is deleting an entire class of edge cases before they exist.

The four moves

Reverse
Three pointers, four lines, always in the same order: save next, flip the link, advance prev, advance cur.
Merge
A dummy plus a tail pointer. Repeatedly attach the smaller head and advance.
Split
Find a boundary node, then cut by setting its next to null — after saving what came after.
Interleave
Weave new nodes between existing ones so that position encodes a relationship, then unweave.

Everything in this family is a composition of those four. Naming which ones you need before writing anything is what keeps a Hard list problem tractable.

Applies when

You must restructure a list rather than just read it — reversing a section, merging, grouping, or deep-copying. Also when O(1) extra space is demanded, which rules out copying into an array.

Does not apply when

You only need to read values in order — copy them into a list and solve the array problem, unless the space constraint forbids it. Say that out loud before doing pointer surgery.

Complexity

O(n) for a single pass; merging k lists is O(n log k) with a heap. Space is O(1) for iterative solutions — prefer them, since recursion on a 10⁴-node list risks a stack overflow.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"reverse the nodes in k-group" · "merge two sorted lists" · "swap every two adjacent nodes" · "reverse between positions left and right" · "a deep copy of the list" · "you may not modify the values in the list's nodes — only the nodes themselves may be changed". That last sentence is decisive: it forbids the value-swapping shortcut and forces genuine pointer work.

LC 25 traced on 1→2→3→4→5, k = 3

Reverse each group of three; leave any short remainder alone. The result is 3→2→1→4→5. The whole problem is bookkeeping: for each group you need the node before it, its old head, and its old tail — because the old head becomes the new tail and must be reconnected.

StepWhat it doesWhy it is needed
Find kthWalk k steps from groupPrev.If it is null, fewer than k nodes remain — stop, leaving the tail alone.
Save nextGroupkth.next, before anything is rewired.The reversal overwrites it; without this the rest of the list is lost.
ReverseStandard three-pointer reverse, seeded with prev = nextGroup.Seeding with nextGroup instead of null performs the tail reconnection for free.
Reconnect frontgroupPrev.next = kth.kth is now the group's first node, so the preceding node must point at it.
AdvancegroupPrev = oldHead.The old head is now the group's last node, so it precedes the next group.
The trick worth stealingSeeding the reversal with prev = nextGroup rather than null means the old head's next already points at the following group when the reversal finishes. One of the two reconnections happens automatically, which removes a line and with it the most common place this problem goes wrong.

A dummy, a tail, and three saved pointers

Reverse and merge are the two primitives; everything else composes them. Write the reverse from muscle memory — its four lines never change order, and half this family is built on it.

Primitive A · reverse (LC 25, 92)
// Four lines, always in this order. Step 1 must come first or
// step 2 severs your only route to the rest of the list.
ListNode reverse(ListNode head) {
    ListNode prev = null, cur = head;

    while (cur != null) {
        ListNode next = cur.next;   // 1 · save what is ahead
        cur.next = prev;            // 2 · flip this link
        prev = cur;                 // 3 · advance prev
        cur = next;                 // 4 · advance cur
    }
    return prev;                    // the new head
}

// Reversing a SEGMENT: seed prev with the node that should follow
// the segment, and the tail reconnection happens for free.
ListNode reverseSegment(ListNode start, ListNode stopAfter) {
    ListNode prev = stopAfter, cur = start;
    while (cur != stopAfter) {
        ListNode next = cur.next;
        cur.next = prev;
        prev = cur;
        cur = next;
    }
    return prev;
}
Primitive B · merge two sorted lists (LC 21, 23)
// Dummy + tail. The dummy removes "which list starts the result?"
// and the tail removes "where do I append?".
ListNode merge(ListNode a, ListNode b) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0);
    ListNode tail = dummy;

    while (a != null && b != null) {
        if (a.val <= b.val) { tail.next = a; a = a.next; }
        else                { tail.next = b; b = b.next; }
        tail = tail.next;
    }

    // At most one list remains; attach it whole rather than looping.
    tail.next = (a != null) ? a : b;

    return dummy.next;
}
The composition — reverse in k-groups (LC 25)
/**
 * Per group you need THREE references:
 *   groupPrev  the node before the group (starts as the dummy)
 *   kth        the group's last node, which becomes its first
 *   nextGroup  the node after the group, saved before rewiring
 */
ListNode reverseKGroup(ListNode head, int k) {
    ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
    ListNode groupPrev = dummy;

    while (true) {
        ListNode kth = walk(groupPrev, k);
        if (kth == null) break;              // fewer than k left — leave it

        ListNode nextGroup = kth.next;       // SAVE before rewiring
        ListNode oldHead = groupPrev.next;   // becomes the group's new TAIL

        // Seeding prev with nextGroup reconnects the tail for free.
        ListNode prev = nextGroup, cur = oldHead;
        while (cur != nextGroup) {
            ListNode next = cur.next;
            cur.next = prev;
            prev = cur;
            cur = next;
        }

        groupPrev.next = kth;                // front reconnection
        groupPrev = oldHead;                 // old head now precedes the next group
    }
    return dummy.next;
}

/** The k-th node after `from`, or null if the list runs out. */
private ListNode walk(ListNode from, int k) {
    while (from != null && k > 0) { from = from.next; k--; }
    return from;
}

The knobs

Dummy or not
Use one whenever the head can change. The only problems here that do not need one are those that never touch the first node.
What to save
Before any rewiring, name every pointer you will still need afterwards. Writing those declarations first prevents almost every bug in this pattern.
Seed of the reversal
null for a whole list; the following node for a segment, which performs one reconnection for free.
Iterative or recursive
Iterative. Lists here reach 5×10⁴ nodes and recursion risks a stack overflow — mention that trade-off rather than assuming.
Values or nodes
If the statement says the values may not be modified, you must move nodes. Read for that sentence before choosing the easy path.
The three bugs that actually happenRewiring before saving — cur.next = prev written first loses the remainder of the list, and the output is a truncated list rather than a crash. Returning head instead of dummy.next — after any head change, head points into the middle of the result. Leaving a cycle — forgetting to terminate the final node produces an infinite loop in the judge's traversal, not in yours, which makes it hard to spot locally.

Six rewirings, two primitives

21 is the merge primitive; 23 applies it k times with a heap. 24 and 92 are bounded reversals. 25 is the general case. 138 is the odd one out — an interleave rather than a reversal.

#ProblemLevelThe twistPrimitiveComplexity
21Merge Two Sorted ListsEasyThe merge primitive. Attach the remainder whole, do not loop it.mergeO(n+m) / O(1)
24Swap Nodes in PairsMediumReverse in groups of exactly 2 — the simplest case of LC 25.reverseO(n) / O(1)
92Reverse Linked List IIMediumOne segment by position. A dummy removes the left == 1 case.reverseO(n) / O(1)
23Merge k Sorted ListsHardA heap of heads, or pairwise merging. Both are O(n log k).merge × kO(n log k) / O(k)
