Anchor 1 · LC 25 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Copy values into an array, reverse each block of k, write them back. O(n) time and O(n) space — but the statement forbids modifying values, so it is ruled out by the problem itself.
The decomposition
Two known procedures: find the k-th node ahead, and reverse a segment. Everything else is reconnecting the seam.
The three references
groupPrev (the node before the group), kth (its last node), and nextGroup (what follows). Naming these before writing any code is what makes the problem manageable.
The key fact
After reversing, the group's old head is its new tail. So it becomes groupPrev for the following iteration — no extra walk is needed.
The free reconnection
Seeding the reversal with prev = nextGroup leaves the old head already pointing at the next group, removing one of the two seam repairs.
Edge case
When fewer than k nodes remain, walk returns null and the loop exits, leaving the tail in its original order — exactly what the problem requires.
LC 25 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public ListNode reverseKGroup(ListNode head, int k) {
        ListNode dummy = new ListNode(0, head);
        ListNode groupPrev = dummy;

        while (true) {
            // The group's last node, or null if fewer than k remain.
            ListNode kth = walk(groupPrev, k);
            if (kth == null) break;            // leave the short tail alone

            ListNode nextGroup = kth.next;     // SAVE before any rewiring
            ListNode oldHead = groupPrev.next; // becomes the group's new TAIL

            // Seeding prev with nextGroup means oldHead ends up
            // pointing at the next group automatically.
            ListNode prev = nextGroup, cur = oldHead;
            while (cur != nextGroup) {
                ListNode next = cur.next;
                cur.next = prev;
                prev = cur;
                cur = next;
            }

            groupPrev.next = kth;    // kth is now the group's first node
            groupPrev = oldHead;     // oldHead is now its last
        }
        return dummy.next;
    }

    private ListNode walk(ListNode from, int k) {
        while (from != null && k > 0) { from = from.next; k--; }
        return from;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 138 — the path to the solution

Why it is hard
The random pointer may target a node you have not created yet, so a single naive pass cannot resolve it.
Solution one — a map
Pass 1 creates every copy and stores original → copy in a HashMap. Pass 2 sets copy.next and copy.random by looking up the originals. O(n) time, O(n) space, and completely correct. Give this first.
The follow-up
Do it in O(1) extra space. The map exists only to answer "which copy corresponds to this original?" — so encode that relationship in the list's own structure instead.
The interleave
Put each copy directly after its original: A → A' → B → B' → C → C'. Now the copy of any node x is simply x.next, which is O(1) with no storage at all.
Then three passes
Weave the copies in; set copy.random = original.random.next; unweave the two lists apart.
Edge cases
random may be null, so guard the second pass. The unweave must restore the original list exactly — leaving it damaged is a common and easily missed failure.
LC 138 · O(n) time, O(1) extra space
class Solution {
    public Node copyRandomList(Node head) {
        if (head == null) return null;

        // 1 · weave each copy in directly after its original,
        //     so copyOf(x) is always x.next — no map needed.
        for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next.next) {
            Node copy = new Node(cur.val);
            copy.next = cur.next;
            cur.next = copy;
        }

        // 2 · random pointers. The copy of cur.random is exactly
        //     cur.random.next, thanks to the interleaving.
        for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next.next) {
            cur.next.random = (cur.random != null) ? cur.random.next : null;
        }

        // 3 · unweave, restoring the original list intact.
        Node copyHead = head.next;
        for (Node cur = head; cur != null; cur = cur.next) {
            Node copy = cur.next;
            cur.next = copy.next;                       // restore original
            copy.next = (copy.next != null) ? copy.next.next : null;
        }
        return copyHead;
    }
}

21 · Merge Two Sorted Lists merge

Path: collecting all values, sorting and rebuilding is O(n log n) and wastes the fact that both inputs are already sorted.

Delta: the merge primitive verbatim. Dummy plus tail, attach the smaller head each step.

Watch for: when one list empties, attach the whole remainder with tail.next = a != null ? a : b. Looping the rest node by node works but is needless, and forgetting it entirely truncates the answer.

24 · Swap Nodes in Pairs reverse

Path: swapping the val fields is two lines and passes — but the follow-up forbids it, and the point is the pointer work.

Delta: this is LC 25 with k = 2. Writing the general version once covers both, and is barely longer than the special case.

Watch for: an odd-length list leaves a single trailing node untouched. The walk returning null handles that without a branch.

92 · Reverse Linked List II reverse

Path: one segment, given by 1-based positions left and right. Walk to the node before left, reverse right − left + 1 nodes, reconnect.

Delta: a dummy is what removes the left == 1 special case, where the head itself moves. With it, the code is uniform.

Watch for: positions are 1-based. Walking left steps instead of left − 1 reverses the wrong segment, and the off-by-one is invisible on symmetric test cases.

23 · Merge k Sorted Lists merge × k

Path: merging one at a time into an accumulator is O(n·k) — the accumulator is re-traversed each round. Say that, then improve it.

Delta: two ways to reach O(n log k). A min-heap of the k current heads, popping the smallest and pushing its successor; or pairwise merging in rounds, halving the list count each time. The heap is easier to explain; the pairwise version needs no extra structure.

Watch for: skip null lists when seeding the heap, or poll returns a null and throws on the first step.

If you only drill twoDo 25 and 138. 25 forces the full save-before-rewire discipline and the realisation that the old head becomes the new tail — after it, 24 and 92 are five-minute problems. 138 teaches the interleave trick, which is the one idea in this family that is not a reversal and the one most likely to appear as a follow-up you have not seen before.

Ask each node one question, and trust the recursion

Tree DFS is the shortest code in this deck and the hardest to reason about, because the recursive call does all the work. The discipline is to define exactly what the function returns for an arbitrary subtree, then write the body assuming the children already answered correctly.

The three-part contract

  1. Base case. What does a null node return? Almost always the identity for whatever you are combining — 0 for a depth, false for existence, MIN_VALUE for a maximum.
  2. Recurse. Call on both children. Do not think about what happens inside; assume the contract holds.
  3. Combine. Produce this node's answer from the two child answers and the node's own value.

Write the contract as a one-line comment before the body. Almost every wrong tree solution has a contract that changes meaning halfway through the function.

Return versus record — the distinction that matters

In the hardest problems here, what a node returns to its parent is not the same as the answer you are accumulating.

A path through a node — down one side, up through the node, down the other — cannot be extended by the parent, because the parent can only attach to one branch. So that value is recorded into a field, while the function returns the best single downward branch.

Conflating these two is the single biggest source of wrong answers in this pattern. When a problem mentions a path that "does not need to pass through the root", expect this split.

Applies when

The answer depends on subtree structure — depths, sums, paths, shapes. Any question phrased as "for every node…" or "the best path anywhere in the tree" is this pattern.

Does not apply when

You need level-by-level order, or the shallowest occurrence of something — DFS may find a deep answer first. Those want a breadth-first traversal instead.

Complexity

O(n) time, since each node is visited once. Space is O(h) for the call stack — O(log n) on a balanced tree but O(n) on a degenerate one, which is the case to mention.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the maximum depth" · "root-to-leaf path" · "the diameter" · "any path, not necessarily through the root" (the return/record split) · "invert the tree" · "return all paths that sum to" (backtracking on the path list) · "the number of nodes satisfying…". The phrase "not necessarily passing through the root" is the strongest signal that you need both a return value and a recorded one.

LC 124 traced on a five-node tree

Maximum path sum, where a path may start and end anywhere. The tree is -10 with children 9 and 20, and 20 has children 15 and 7. The answer is 42 — the path 15 → 20 → 7, which never touches the root.

nodegain from Lgain from Rrecorded (bends here)returned (one branch)best
150015 + 0 + 0 = 1515 + 0 = 1515
7007 + 0 + 0 = 77 + 0 = 715
2015720 + 15 + 7 = 4220 + max(15,7) = 3542
9009 + 0 + 0 = 99 + 0 = 942
−10935−10 + 9 + 35 = 34−10 + 35 = 2542
Why the child gains are clamped at zeroEach recursive result is wrapped in Math.max(0, …). A branch contributing a negative total should simply not be used — the path can stop at this node instead. Without the clamp, a tree of all-negative values propagates ever more negative sums and the answer is wrong. With it, the root above records 34 rather than being dragged down, and a single negative node correctly returns itself.

Three shapes: pure return, return plus record, and path backtracking

Decide which shape the problem needs before writing anything. The choice is forced by one question — can the parent extend this answer, or is it complete at this node?

Shape A · pure return (LC 104, 226, 112)
// The returned value IS the answer for that subtree, so there is
// no field and no accumulation. Three lines: base, recurse, combine.

// CONTRACT: the height of the subtree rooted here.
int maxDepth(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;                       // identity for max
    return 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(node.left), maxDepth(node.right));
}

// CONTRACT: this subtree, mirrored, and returns its new root.
TreeNode invert(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return null;
    TreeNode l = invert(node.left);
    node.left  = invert(node.right);
    node.right = l;                                   // save before overwrite
    return node;
}

// CONTRACT: does a root-to-LEAF path from here sum to `target`?
boolean hasPathSum(TreeNode node, int target) {
    if (node == null) return false;                   // NOT a leaf — false

    // A leaf has no children. Testing node == null instead would
    // accept a single-child node as if it were a leaf.
    if (node.left == null && node.right == null) return target == node.val;

    int rest = target - node.val;
    return hasPathSum(node.left, rest) || hasPathSum(node.right, rest);
}
Shape B · return one thing, record another (LC 124, 543)
// Used whenever a path may BEND at a node. The bent path is complete
// there, so it is banked in a field; the function returns the best
// single downward branch, which the parent can still extend.
private int best;

int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) {
    best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;     // values may all be negative
    gain(root);
    return best;
}

/** CONTRACT: the best sum of a path going DOWN from node, or 0. */
private int gain(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return 0;

    // Clamp at 0: a negative branch is better left unused.
    int l = Math.max(0, gain(node.left));
    int r = Math.max(0, gain(node.right));

    // RECORD the path that bends here — it uses BOTH branches,
    // so no parent can extend it.
    best = Math.max(best, node.val + l + r);

    // RETURN a single branch, which the parent CAN extend.
    return node.val + Math.max(l, r);
}
Shape C · path backtracking (LC 113)
// When the problem wants the paths themselves, carry a mutable
// list down the recursion and UNDO the addition on the way out.
List<List<Integer>> pathSum(TreeNode root, int target) {
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    dfs(root, target, new ArrayList<>(), out);
    return out;
}

private void dfs(TreeNode node, int remaining,
                 List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> out) {
    if (node == null) return;

    path.add(node.val);                       // choose

    if (node.left == null && node.right == null && remaining == node.val) {
        // COPY — `path` keeps mutating after this call returns.
        out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
    } else {
        dfs(node.left,  remaining - node.val, path, out);
        dfs(node.right, remaining - node.val, path, out);
    }

    path.remove(path.size() - 1);             // UNDO — the whole trick
}

Choosing the shape

Ask first
"Can my parent use what I return?" If yes, shape A. If the answer might bend at this node, shape B. If you need the path contents, shape C.
Base case
The identity of your combine operation: 0 for sums and depths, false for existence, null for structure.
Leaf test
node.left == null && node.right == null. A null check alone is not a leaf test, and that confusion is what breaks LC 112 on single-child chains.
Field or parameter
A field is simplest for the recorded value. An int[1] works too if you dislike fields — Java has no by-reference ints.
Copy on collect
Always new ArrayList<>(path). Adding the live list stores a reference that keeps changing.
The three bugs that actually happenReturning the bent path — the parent then builds an invalid path that visits a node twice, and the answer comes out too large. Treating null as a leaf — a node with one child looks like a leaf, so LC 112 accepts paths that stop mid-tree. Forgetting to undo in shape C — the path list grows without bound and every collected result is wrong.

Six traversals, three shapes

104, 226 and 112 are pure returns and should take two minutes each. 113 adds path backtracking. 543 and 124 need the return-versus-record split, and are the two worth real time.

Anchor 1 · LC 124 — the path to the solution

Brute force
For every node, compute the best path through it by exploring its whole subtree. O(n²) on a balanced tree and worse on a chain.
The definition
A path is a sequence of connected nodes with no repeats. Crucially it may bend at one node — down the left branch, up through the node, down the right.
The observation
Every path bends at exactly one node: its highest point. So if each node computes the best path bending at itself, the maximum over all nodes is the answer, and each node's computation uses only its two child results.
The split
The bent value val + l + r cannot be passed up — a parent attaching to it would revisit this node. So record it in a field, and return val + max(l, r), which the parent can extend.
The clamp
Math.max(0, childGain). A branch with a negative total should be dropped rather than included, since the path may simply end at this node.
Edge cases
Initialise best to Integer.MIN_VALUE, not 0 — a tree of all-negative values has a negative answer, and 0 would wrongly win.
LC 124 · O(n) time, O(h) space
class Solution {
    private int best;

    public int maxPathSum(TreeNode root) {
        // Values can all be negative, so 0 is not a safe floor.
        best = Integer.MIN_VALUE;
        gain(root);
        return best;
    }

    /** CONTRACT: best sum of a path descending from node, or 0. */
    private int gain(TreeNode node) {
        if (node == null) return 0;

        // A negative branch is better left unused — the path can
        // simply stop here instead of descending into it.
        int l = Math.max(0, gain(node.left));
        int r = Math.max(0, gain(node.right));

        // RECORD: the path bending at this node uses BOTH branches,
        // so it is complete here and no parent can extend it.
        best = Math.max(best, node.val + l + r);

        // RETURN: one branch only, so the parent can build on it.
        return node.val + Math.max(l, r);
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 113 — the path to the solution

The difference from LC 112
112 asks whether a path exists, so it can short-circuit. 113 wants every path, so it must explore the whole tree and carry the route it took.
The naive approach
Build a fresh list at every node and pass copies down. Correct, but it allocates O(n) lists and is wasteful.
Backtracking
Carry one mutable list. Add the node on the way down, recurse, then remove it on the way out. At any moment the list holds exactly the route from the root to the current node.
Why the undo is unconditional
It runs whether or not the subtree produced a result. Placing it inside an if leaves stale entries behind and corrupts every subsequent path.
Why the copy is mandatory
out.add(path) stores a reference to a list that keeps mutating — by the end every entry is the same empty list. new ArrayList<>(path) snapshots it.
Edge cases
The leaf test must check both children. A null root returns an empty list, which falls out of the base case.
LC 113 · O(n·h) time, O(h) space
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> pathSum(TreeNode root, int targetSum) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        dfs(root, targetSum, new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private void dfs(TreeNode node, int remaining,
                     List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (node == null) return;

        path.add(node.val);                    // CHOOSE

        if (node.left == null && node.right == null) {
            // A real leaf — both children absent.
            if (remaining == node.val) {
                // COPY: `path` keeps mutating after this returns.
                out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
            }
        } else {
            dfs(node.left,  remaining - node.val, path, out);
            dfs(node.right, remaining - node.val, path, out);
        }

        // UNDO — unconditionally, on every exit from this node.
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);
    }
}

104 · Maximum Depth shape A

Path: there is nothing to derive — this is the contract in its purest form, and its value is as a template for everything else in the pattern.

Delta: base case 0, combine with 1 + max(left, right). Three lines.

Watch for: the iterative version is a level-order traversal counting levels. Worth knowing if the interviewer asks you to avoid recursion because of stack depth.

226 · Invert Binary Tree shape A

Path: swap the children at every node. The recursion handles the rest.

Delta: the only care needed is saving one child before overwriting it — node.left = invert(node.right) destroys node.left if you have not stored it. This is the same save-before-rewire discipline that list problems require.

Watch for: a null root must return null rather than throwing. It is the base case, and it is easy to omit on a problem this short.

112 · Path Sum shape A

Path: subtract as you descend, and test at the leaves. The subtlety is entirely in what counts as a leaf.

Delta: a leaf has both children null. Testing node == null instead treats a single-child node as a leaf, so a path that stops halfway down is wrongly accepted — and the bug only appears on unbalanced trees.

Watch for: negative values mean you cannot prune when the remainder goes below zero. That optimisation is only valid when all values are positive.

543 · Diameter of Binary Tree shape B

Path: the diameter is the longest path between any two nodes, measured in edges. It need not pass through the root, which is the signal for the split.

Delta: identical structure to LC 124 with sums replaced by counts — record l + r (the bent path's edge count), return 1 + max(l, r).

Watch for: the answer counts edges, not nodes, so a single-node tree has diameter 0. Returning the node count gives an answer one too large everywhere. Solve this before 124 — it is the same idea with easier arithmetic.

If you only drill twoDo 543 and 124. They are the same problem twice, and together they fix the return-versus-record distinction that governs every hard tree question. 543 is gentler because the arithmetic is just counting; 124 adds negative clamping and an initial value that cannot be zero. Once both are automatic, 104, 226, 112 and 113 are mechanical.

Drain the queue one level at a time

A plain queue traversal visits nodes in level order but loses the level boundaries. The entire pattern is one line that recovers them: capture the queue's size before the inner loop. That snapshot is exactly one level, because everything added during the loop belongs to the next.

The invariant

At the top of each outer iteration, the queue contains precisely one complete level and nothing else.

So int size = queue.size() is the width of that level. Dequeuing exactly size nodes processes it fully, and the children enqueued during those size steps form the next level — restoring the invariant automatically.

Reading queue.size() inside the loop instead destroys this: the size grows as children are added, and the levels smear into one another.

What the level gives you

Once you can process a level as a unit, a whole family of questions becomes trivial variations on where you put one line:

  • The level's list — collect every value as you dequeue.
  • The last node of each level — the right-side view.
  • The level's max or average — fold over the level.
  • Alternating direction — reverse every other level, or push to the front.
  • The first level satisfying a condition — BFS finds the shallowest, which DFS cannot promise.

Applies when

The answer is organised by level, or you need the shallowest node satisfying something. BFS reaches nodes in non-decreasing depth order, which is a guarantee a depth-first traversal cannot make.

Does not apply when

The answer depends on subtree structure — depths, path sums, shapes. Those compose naturally bottom-up, which is a depth-first job; forcing them into BFS means rebuilding the tree in the queue.

Complexity

O(n) time — every node is enqueued and dequeued once. Space is O(w) where w is the widest level, which for a complete tree is about n/2. That is worse than DFS's O(h) and worth stating.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"level order traversal" · "return a list of lists, one per level" · "zigzag" or "alternate between left-to-right and right-to-left" · "the right side view" · "the largest value in each row" · "the average of each level" · "populate each next pointer to its right neighbour". The words "level", "row" or "depth" in the output description are decisive.

LC 102 traced on 3 / 9, 20 / null, null, 15, 7

Level order on the standard example. Three iterations of the outer loop produce three levels. Watch the queue contents at the top of each iteration — it always holds exactly one complete level, which is what makes the size snapshot correct.

iterationqueue at topsnapshotdrained in orderchildren addedlevel output
1[3]139, 20[3]
2[9, 20]29, 2015, 7[9, 20]
3[15, 7]215, 7none[15, 7]
—[]—loop ends—done
Filter nulls on enqueue, not on dequeueCheck if (node.left != null) before adding. The alternative — enqueuing nulls and skipping them on dequeue — makes the size snapshot meaningless, because a level's recorded width then includes phantom entries. The one exception is when you deliberately use null as a level separator, which is an alternative formulation of this pattern but does not mix with the size snapshot.

One loop, and a single line that changes per problem

The skeleton is identical across all six problems. What differs is which node of the drained level you keep, and whether the collected list gets reversed.

The template — level order
/**
 * INVARIANT: at the top of each outer iteration the queue holds
 * exactly one complete level.
 *
 * The size SNAPSHOT is the whole pattern — capture it before the
 * inner loop, because the queue grows as children are enqueued.
 */
List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
    List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
    if (root == null) return out;                 // empty tree, empty answer

    Queue<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();       // ArrayDeque, not LinkedList
    q.offer(root);

    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int size = q.size();                      // SNAPSHOT — never read live
        List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>(size);

        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            TreeNode node = q.poll();
            level.add(node.val);

            // Filter nulls HERE, so the snapshot stays meaningful.
            if (node.left  != null) q.offer(node.left);
            if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right);
        }
        out.add(level);
    }
    return out;
}
The one line that changes
// LC 102 — the whole level
level.add(node.val);

// LC 199 — right side view: keep only the LAST of each level
if (i == size - 1) out.add(node.val);

// LC 515 — the maximum per level
levelMax = Math.max(levelMax, node.val);

// LC 637 — the average per level. Sum in `long` or `double`:
// 2000 nodes of Integer.MAX_VALUE overflows int.
sum += node.val;             // long sum
// after the inner loop:  out.add((double) sum / size);

// LC 103 — zigzag: build normally, then reverse odd levels.
// Or use addFirst on a LinkedList, which avoids the reverse pass.
if (leftToRight) level.addLast(node.val);
else             level.addFirst(node.val);
Variant · O(1) space using the links you just built (LC 116)
// The queue costs O(w) space. But once a level's `next` pointers
// exist, that level is ITSELF a linked list — so you can walk it
// without a queue and wire up the level below.
Node connect(Node root) {
    Node leftmost = root;

    while (leftmost != null && leftmost.left != null) {
        // Walk the current level using the next pointers already set.
        for (Node head = leftmost; head != null; head = head.next) {

            head.left.next = head.right;              // within this node

            // Across the gap to the neighbour's subtree — this is
            // the step that needs the level's own next pointer.
            if (head.next != null) {
                head.right.next = head.next.left;
            }
        }
        leftmost = leftmost.left;                     // drop one level
    }
    return root;
}

The knobs

What you keep
All values, the last one, a running max, or a running sum. That single line is usually the entire difference between two problems in this family.
Direction
For zigzag, either reverse alternate levels afterwards or use addFirst on a LinkedList. The second is O(1) per insert and avoids a second pass.
Queue type
ArrayDeque, not LinkedList — faster and it rejects null elements, which surfaces a null-enqueue bug immediately instead of silently.
Null root
Return the empty answer before touching the queue. Enqueuing a null root throws on ArrayDeque.
Accumulator width
long or double for level sums. LC 637 has a test case that overflows int precisely here.
The three bugs that actually happenReading q.size() inside the inner loop — the levels merge, because the size grows as children are added. This breaks every problem in the pattern in the same way. Enqueuing nulls — the snapshot then counts phantom nodes, so level widths are wrong, and ArrayDeque throws outright. Summing level values in an int — LC 637's test set includes values near Integer.MAX_VALUE, and the average comes back negative.

Six levels, one skeleton

102, 199, 515 and 637 differ by a single line. 103 adds a direction flag. 116 is the one that abandons the queue entirely to meet an O(1) space requirement.

Anchor 1 · LC 102 — the path to the solution

First attempt
A plain queue traversal visits nodes in the right order but produces one flat list — the level boundaries are gone.
The failed fix
Tracking depth per node and grouping afterwards works, but it needs a parallel structure and is more code than the real solution.
The observation
At the moment the queue holds a complete level, its size is that level's width. Everything enqueued afterwards belongs to the next level, so the boundary is already in the data.
The one line
int size = q.size() before the inner loop. Draining exactly size nodes consumes one level and leaves the next in place — the invariant restores itself.
The DFS alternative
Recurse with a depth parameter and append to out.get(depth), creating the list when the depth is first reached. Also O(n), and worth mentioning — it uses O(h) space instead of O(w).
Edge cases
A null root returns an empty list. Filter null children on enqueue so the snapshot stays accurate.
LC 102 · O(n) time, O(w) space
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> levelOrder(TreeNode root) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        if (root == null) return out;

        Queue<TreeNode> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        q.offer(root);

        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            // SNAPSHOT: the queue currently holds exactly one level.
            // Reading q.size() inside the loop would swallow the next.
            int size = q.size();
            List<Integer> level = new ArrayList<>(size);

            for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
                TreeNode node = q.poll();
                level.add(node.val);

                // Filter nulls on ENQUEUE so the snapshot stays exact.
                if (node.left  != null) q.offer(node.left);
                if (node.right != null) q.offer(node.right);
            }
            out.add(level);
        }
        return out;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 116 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Level-order with the template, linking each node to the next in its level. O(n) time but O(w) space — and the follow-up demands O(1).
The observation
Once level k's next pointers are set, that level is itself a linked list. So you can traverse it without a queue — the structure you just built is the queue.
The two links per node
Walking a node on level k, you can set two pointers on level k+1: left.next = right within the node, and right.next = next.left across to the neighbour's subtree. The second is what needs the current level's own links.
Why perfection matters
The tree is stated to be perfect, so every node has either two children or none, and head.left and head.right always exist together. That is what makes the two-link step unconditional.
Descending
After wiring a level, drop to leftmost.left — the leftmost node of the next level, which is where the next sweep begins.
The general case
LC 117 removes the perfection guarantee, and then you must scan for the next non-null child. Mention it as the natural follow-up.
LC 116 · O(n) time, O(1) space
class Solution {
    public Node connect(Node root) {
        Node leftmost = root;

        // Stop at the last level — it has no children to wire.
        while (leftmost != null && leftmost.left != null) {

            // Walk this level using the next pointers ALREADY set.
            // The level is its own linked list, so no queue is needed.
            for (Node head = leftmost; head != null; head = head.next) {

                // 1 · within this node
                head.left.next = head.right;

                // 2 · across to the neighbour's subtree. This is the
                //     step that consumes the current level's links.
                if (head.next != null) {
                    head.right.next = head.next.left;
                }
            }
            leftmost = leftmost.left;    // descend one level
        }
        return root;
    }
}

199 · Binary Tree Right Side View template

Path: "what you see from the right" is the last node of each level — restating it that way turns the problem into the template.

Delta: one line. Inside the inner loop, if (i == size - 1) out.add(node.val).

Watch for: a DFS that visits right before left and records the first node at each new depth also works, in O(h) space. Worth offering when the tree is deep and narrow.

515 · Find Largest Value in Each Tree Row template

Path: a fold over each level rather than a collection.

Delta: replace the list with an int max, seeded to Integer.MIN_VALUE at the start of each level.

Watch for: seeding with 0 fails on a tree of all-negative values — a mistake that passes every example in the problem statement and fails the hidden tests.

637 · Average of Levels template

Path: another fold, this time summing and dividing by the snapshot — which is exactly the level's width, already at hand.

Delta: accumulate into a long, then out.add((double) sum / size).

Watch for: the overflow is real, not theoretical — a level of 2000 nodes each near Integer.MAX_VALUE is in the test set. Cast before dividing, or integer division truncates the result.

103 · Zigzag Level Order template + flag

Path: the instinct is to alternate the order in which children are enqueued. That does not work — it corrupts the ordering two levels down.

Delta: traverse normally and change only how the level list is built. Use a LinkedList with addFirst on right-to-left levels, or collect normally and Collections.reverse the odd ones.

Watch for: flip the flag once per level, outside the inner loop. Flipping per node produces an interleaving rather than a reversal.

If you only drill twoDo 102 and 116. 102 fixes the size snapshot, after which 199, 515, 637 and 103 are each a one-line edit. 116 is the one worth real thought: it asks you to notice that the structure you are building can replace the auxiliary structure you were using, which is a move that appears again in graph and matrix problems.

The ordering is the data structure — use it or you have a plain tree

A binary search tree guarantees that everything in the left subtree is smaller and everything on the right is larger. Two consequences follow, and every problem here is one of them: you can discard half the tree at each step, and an in-order traversal emits sorted values.

Consequence one — halving

Comparing a target against node.val tells you which side it must be on, so the other side is discarded outright. Searching, inserting, deleting and finding a lowest common ancestor are all O(h) rather than O(n).

On a balanced tree h is log n. On a degenerate one — values inserted in sorted order — it is n, and every operation degrades to a linear scan. Say that when asked about complexity.

Written iteratively, these are O(1) space, which is usually worth preferring.

Consequence two — in-order is sorted

Visit left, then the node, then right, and the values come out in ascending order. That single fact solves most of this family:

  • Validation — the sequence must be strictly increasing.
  • The k-th smallest — stop after k emissions.
  • Recovery — exactly two elements are out of order in a sorted sequence.

When a BST problem looks hard, ask what the in-order sequence would look like. The answer is usually the algorithm.

Applies when

The tree is stated to be a BST. That word is the licence to use ordering — without it you have an ordinary binary tree and must visit every node.

Does not apply when

The tree is unbalanced in a way that matters and you need guaranteed logarithmic bounds — that is an AVL or red-black tree. Also when duplicates are allowed, since the problem must then define which side they go on.

Complexity

O(h) for search, insert, delete and lowest common ancestor — log n balanced, n degenerate. O(n) for anything requiring a full in-order pass. Space is O(1) iteratively, O(h) recursively.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"a valid binary search tree" · "the k-th smallest element in a BST" · "exactly two nodes were swapped by mistake" · "the lowest common ancestor of a BST" (the BST version is far easier than the general one) · "delete a node" · "search in a BST". The phrase "without changing its structure" in LC 99 is what forces the in-order approach rather than a rebuild.

LC 98 traced on a tree that fails at depth two

The tree is 5 with children 1 and 4, where 4 has children 3 and 6. It looks locally valid everywhere, and a parent-only comparison accepts it. The range check rejects it at node 3.

nodeallowed rangeparent-only checkrange checkwhy they differ

1(−∞, 5)passes (1 < 5)passesboth agree on a direct child
4(5, +∞)passes (4 < 5 on the right? no)fails4 is in the right subtree so it must exceed 5

Why the bounds must be Long, not intSeeding with Integer.MIN_VALUE and Integer.MAX_VALUE breaks when the tree legitimately contains those values — a single node holding Integer.MIN_VALUE is a valid BST, but the check val > MIN_VALUE rejects it. Use Long bounds with null meaning unbounded, or pass Long.MIN_VALUE and Long.MAX_VALUE. LeetCode tests this exact case.

Two engines: range descent, and in-order with a previous pointer

Range descent covers search, insert, delete and ancestry. In-order with a remembered predecessor covers validation, selection and repair. Almost every BST question is one of the two.

Engine A · range descent (LC 700, 235, 450)
// Compare, discard a half, repeat. Iterative, so O(1) space.
TreeNode search(TreeNode root, int target) {
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null && cur.val != target) {
        cur = target < cur.val ? cur.left : cur.right;
    }
    return cur;
}

// LCA in a BST: the split point is the answer. While both targets
// lie on the SAME side, walk that way; the first node between them
// (or equal to one) is the lowest common ancestor.
TreeNode lca(TreeNode root, TreeNode p, TreeNode q) {
    TreeNode cur = root;
    while (cur != null) {
        if (p.val < cur.val && q.val < cur.val)      cur = cur.left;
        else if (p.val > cur.val && q.val > cur.val) cur = cur.right;
        else return cur;                    // they split here
    }
    return null;
}

// Validation carries a RANGE down, not a parent comparison.
// Long bounds: a node may legitimately hold Integer.MIN_VALUE.
boolean isValid(TreeNode node, long lo, long hi) {
    if (node == null) return true;
    if (node.val <= lo || node.val >= hi) return false;

    return isValid(node.left,  lo, node.val)    // tighten the upper bound
        && isValid(node.right, node.val, hi);   // tighten the lower bound
}
Engine B · in-order with a previous pointer (LC 98, 99, 230)
// In-order emits sorted values, so remembering the PREVIOUS node
// turns "is it sorted?" into a single comparison per step.
private TreeNode prev;

boolean isValidInOrder(TreeNode node) {
    if (node == null) return true;

    if (!isValidInOrder(node.left)) return false;

    // Strictly increasing — duplicates are invalid in a BST.
    if (prev != null && prev.val >= node.val) return false;
    prev = node;

    return isValidInOrder(node.right);
}

// The ITERATIVE in-order, which lets you stop early. This is what
// LC 230 needs: quit after k emissions instead of walking the tree.
int kthSmallest(TreeNode root, int k) {
    Deque<TreeNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>();
    TreeNode cur = root;

    while (cur != null || !stack.isEmpty()) {
        while (cur != null) {          // descend as far left as possible
            stack.push(cur);
            cur = cur.left;
        }
        cur = stack.pop();             // the next value in sorted order
        if (--k == 0) return cur.val;  // early exit — O(h + k), not O(n)
        cur = cur.right;
    }
    return -1;
}
Deletion — the three cases, and why the successor is chosen (LC 450)
/**
 * Descend to the node, then handle exactly three cases:
 *   0 or 1 child  ->  splice the child in
 *   2 children    ->  replace the value with the IN-ORDER SUCCESSOR,
 *                     then delete that successor from the right subtree
 *
 * The successor is the smallest value greater than this node, so it
 * is the unique value that preserves the ordering for BOTH subtrees.
 * The predecessor works equally well; pick one and be consistent.
 */
TreeNode deleteNode(TreeNode root, int key) {
    if (root == null) return null;

    if      (key < root.val) root.left  = deleteNode(root.left,  key);
    else if (key > root.val) root.right = deleteNode(root.right, key);
    else {
        // Found it. Cases 0 and 1: hand the single child upward.
        if (root.left  == null) return root.right;
        if (root.right == null) return root.left;

        // Case 2: the successor is the leftmost node on the right.
        TreeNode succ = root.right;
        while (succ.left != null) succ = succ.left;

        root.val = succ.val;                                 // overwrite
        root.right = deleteNode(root.right, succ.val);       // remove the dup
    }
    return root;
}

Which engine

"find", "insert", "delete", "LCA"
Engine A. Compare and descend; never visit both children.
"is it valid", "k-th smallest", "two nodes swapped"
Engine B. Think about what the in-order sequence looks like, then detect the property on that sequence.
Early exit needed
The iterative in-order with an explicit stack. The recursive version cannot stop cleanly partway.
Bounds type
long, or Integer objects with null for unbounded. Never bare int sentinels.
The three bugs that actually happenComparing against the parent instead of a range — accepts trees that are locally fine and globally invalid, exactly as in the trace. int sentinels in the range check — a node legitimately holding Integer.MIN_VALUE is rejected. Deleting a two-child node by promoting an arbitrary child — the ordering breaks; only the in-order successor or predecessor preserves it, and the duplicate must then be removed from the subtree.

Six BST questions, two engines

700, 235 and 450 descend. 98, 230 and 99 read the in-order sequence. 99 is the one that combines both ideas and is worth the most time.

Anchor 1 · LC 98 — the path to the solution

The wrong first attempt
Check left.val < node.val < right.val at every node. This is the single most common wrong answer in the whole BST family, and it passes the problem's own first example.
Why it fails
The BST property is about entire subtrees, not immediate children. A node can satisfy its parent while violating an ancestor several levels up, exactly as in the traced tree.
Solution one — the range
Carry (lo, hi) down. Descending left tightens hi to the current value; descending right tightens lo. Every node must lie strictly inside its inherited interval.
Solution two — in-order
A valid BST emits a strictly increasing in-order sequence, so keep a prev pointer and fail the moment prev.val >= node.val. Same complexity, and it generalises to LC 99.
The overflow trap
Use long bounds. A tree consisting of one node holding Integer.MIN_VALUE is valid, but val > Integer.MIN_VALUE rejects it — and that case is in the test set.
Duplicates
Invalid by LeetCode's definition, so the comparisons are strict on both sides.
LC 98 · O(n) time, O(h) space
class Solution {
    public boolean isValidBST(TreeNode root) {
        // long bounds: a node may legitimately hold Integer.MIN_VALUE
        // or Integer.MAX_VALUE, which int sentinels would reject.
        return valid(root, Long.MIN_VALUE, Long.MAX_VALUE);
    }

    private boolean valid(TreeNode node, long lo, long hi) {
        if (node == null) return true;

        // Strict on both sides — duplicates are not allowed.
        if (node.val <= lo || node.val >= hi) return false;

        // Descending LEFT tightens the upper bound to this value;
        // descending RIGHT tightens the lower bound. That inherited
        // bound is what a parent-only comparison cannot see.
        return valid(node.left,  lo, node.val)
            && valid(node.right, node.val, hi);
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 99 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Collect the in-order values, sort a copy, compare position by position, and swap back the two that differ. O(n log n) time and O(n) space — correct, and worth stating first.
The reframing
The in-order sequence should be sorted. Swapping two elements of a sorted sequence creates a very specific defect, so you do not need to sort anything — just find it.
The two cases
If the swapped nodes are non-adjacent in the sequence, there are exactly two inversions: take the first element of the first and the second element of the last. If they are adjacent, there is exactly one inversion, and both culprits are in it.
Handling both uniformly
On the first inversion, record first = prev and second = node. On any later inversion, overwrite second = node only. That single rule covers both cases with no branching.
The final step
Swap the two values. The statement forbids changing the structure, so moving nodes is not allowed.
Edge cases
Exactly two nodes are swapped, as guaranteed. The O(1)-space follow-up is Morris traversal — mention it, but the stack version is what to write.
LC 99 · O(n) time, O(h) space
class Solution {
    private TreeNode first, second, prev;

    public void recoverTree(TreeNode root) {
        inorder(root);
        // Swap VALUES — the structure must not change.
        int tmp = first.val;
        first.val = second.val;
        second.val = tmp;
    }

    private void inorder(TreeNode node) {
        if (node == null) return;

        inorder(node.left);

        // In-order should be strictly increasing. An inversion here
        // means one of the two swapped nodes is involved.
        if (prev != null && prev.val > node.val) {
            // First inversion: BOTH candidates come from it.
            if (first == null) first = prev;
            // Every inversion updates `second`. If the nodes were
            // adjacent there is only one inversion, and this line
            // still captures the right node.
            second = node;
        }
        prev = node;

        inorder(node.right);
    }
}

700 · Search in a BST engine A

Path: scanning the whole tree is O(n) and ignores the ordering. One comparison per level discards half the remaining tree.

Delta: a three-line while loop. Prefer the iterative form — it is O(1) space, and the recursive version buys nothing here.

Watch for: return the node, not a boolean. The subtree rooted there is the expected answer, and returning null when absent is correct rather than an error.

235 · Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST engine A

Path: the general-tree algorithm is O(n) and works, but ignores the ordering entirely. The BST version is O(h) and much shorter.

Delta: while both targets are on the same side of the current node, walk that way. The first node where they split — or that equals one of them — is the answer.

Watch for: a node is permitted to be its own ancestor, so stop when cur.val equals either target. Forgetting that descends past the correct answer.

230 · Kth Smallest Element in a BST engine B

Path: a full in-order into a list then index k−1 is O(n) time and space. The observation is that you can stop as soon as k values have been emitted.

Delta: the iterative in-order with an explicit stack, decrementing k on each pop and returning at zero. That is O(h + k), which matters when k is small and the tree is large.

Watch for: the follow-up asks what changes if the tree is modified often. The answer is to store a subtree size in each node, making selection O(h) — worth naming even without coding it.

450 · Delete Node in a BST engine A

Path: descend to the node using the ordering, then handle the removal. The descent is easy; the removal has three cases.

Delta: zero or one child means returning that child upward — the parent's assignment splices it in. Two children means overwriting the value with the in-order successor, then deleting that successor from the right subtree.

Watch for: the successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, not simply root.right. It is the unique smallest value greater than the deleted one, which is what keeps both subtrees ordered.

If you only drill twoDo 98 and 99. 98 corrects the parent-comparison instinct, which is the error that quietly breaks more BST solutions than anything else. 99 then forces you to reason about what a swap does to the in-order sequence — and that habit of asking "what would the sorted order look like?" is what makes the rest of this family straightforward.

Choose, explore, un-choose

Backtracking builds a candidate one element at a time and walks back the instant it cannot lead anywhere. The code is always the same three lines wrapped in a loop — and the entire difficulty is the start index, which decides whether you enumerate combinations or permutations.

The three lines

  1. Choose — add a candidate to the partial solution.
  2. Explore — recurse with the state updated.
  3. Un-choose — remove it, restoring the state exactly as it was.

Step 3 is what makes it backtracking rather than plain recursion. Every mutation on the way down must have a matching undo on the way up, so the state at any point describes only the current branch.

Write the undo immediately after the recursive call, before anything else — the same discipline as pairing admit with evict.

The start index decides everything

i + 1
Combinations. Each element may be used once, and order does not matter, because a fixed left-to-right sweep never revisits earlier positions.
i
Combinations with reuse. The same element may be chosen repeatedly, but still no reordering.
from 0, with a used[]
Permutations. Every position is reachable at every depth, so order matters and you need explicit tracking of what is already in the path.

Nothing else distinguishes 46, 77, 78 and 39. One parameter.

Applies when

The problem asks you to enumerate — return all subsets, all permutations, all combinations summing to a target. The plural in "return all" is the signal.

Does not apply when

Only a count or the best one is wanted. Enumerating to count is exponential when a dynamic-programming recurrence would be polynomial — that distinction decides the whole approach.

Complexity

O(n·2ⁿ) for subsets, O(n·n!) for permutations — the output itself is that large, so it cannot be beaten. Space is O(n) for the path plus the recursion stack, excluding the output.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"return all possible subsets" · "all permutations" · "all combinations of k numbers" · "all unique combinations that sum to target" · "the solution set must not contain duplicates" (the dedup rule) · "you may return the answer in any order". The constraint bound is confirmation: n ≤ 20 or smaller means an exponential answer is intended.

LC 78 traced on [1,2,3]

All eight subsets. Every node of the recursion tree is recorded on entry — there is no base case that filters, because the empty set and every partial prefix are legitimate answers. Watch the path shrink back as each call returns.

callstartloop rangepath on entryrecorded

32i = 2[1,2][1,2]
43empty — loop does not run[1,2,3][1,2,3]

Why there is no explicit base caseThe recursion terminates because start eventually reaches nums.length and the loop body never executes. Adding if (start == n) return; would be harmless but redundant — the loop is its own base case. Problems that do need one, such as combinations of a fixed size k, use it to decide when to record rather than when to stop.

One skeleton, three parameters, one dedup rule

The body never changes. Where you record, what you pass as start, and whether you skip duplicates at the same depth — those three decisions cover all six problems.

The skeleton — choose, explore, un-choose
/**
 * KNOB 1 · where to record   — every node, leaves only, or depth == k
 * KNOB 2 · the start index   — i+1, i, or 0 with used[]
 * KNOB 3 · duplicate skip    — needed only when the input has repeats
 */
void backtrack(int[] nums, int start, List<Integer> path,
               List<List<Integer>> out) {

    // KNOB 1 · subsets record EVERY node, so there is no filter here.
    out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));      // COPY — path keeps mutating

    for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {

        path.add(nums[i]);                          // 1 · choose
        backtrack(nums, i + 1, path, out);          // 2 · explore  (KNOB 2)
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);               // 3 · un-choose
    }
}
Knob 2 — the start index, and what it produces
// COMBINATIONS — each element once, order irrelevant (LC 78, 77, 90)
backtrack(nums, i + 1, ...);

// WITH REUSE — the same element may repeat (LC 39)
backtrack(nums, i, ...);          // note: i, not i + 1

// PERMUTATIONS — order matters, so every index is reachable
// at every depth and you must track what is already used.
for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    if (used[i]) continue;
    used[i] = true;
    path.add(nums[i]);

    backtrack(nums, 0, path, out);    // start is always 0

    path.remove(path.size() - 1);
    used[i] = false;                  // undo BOTH mutations
}

// FIXED SIZE k — record at the right depth instead of at every node
if (path.size() == k) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); return; }
Knob 3 — the duplicate rule, and why it is written that way
// The input must be SORTED first, so equal values sit adjacent.
Arrays.sort(nums);

// COMBINATIONS with duplicates (LC 90, 40):
// skip a repeated value when it is not the FIRST choice at this depth.
for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {
    if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i - 1]) continue;
    ...
}
// `i > start`, NOT `i > 0`. Using i > 0 would also block the
// legitimate second copy at a DEEPER level, so [1,1] would vanish.

// PERMUTATIONS with duplicates (LC 47):
// only let the leftmost unused copy be chosen at each depth.
for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    if (used[i]) continue;
    if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]) continue;
    ...
}
// !used[i-1] means the previous equal copy was already undone at
// THIS depth — so choosing this one would repeat the same branch.

The three knobs in one table

Wantrecordstartdedup

The three bugs that actually happenAdding path instead of a copy — every entry in the output ends up being the same list, empty by the time you return. Always new ArrayList<>(path). Forgetting to undo — or undoing only one of two mutations in the permutation case, where both path and used[i] must be restored. i > 0 instead of i > start in the combination dedup — this drops legitimate results such as [1,1], and the failure appears only on inputs with repeats.

Six enumerations, one skeleton

78 and 77 differ by where you record. 39 changes the start index to allow reuse. 46 switches to a used array. 90 and 47 add the two dedup rules — which are different from each other, and that difference is the point.

Anchor 1 · LC 78 — the path to the solution

The bitmask alternative
For n ≤ 20, loop a mask from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 and include element j when bit j is set. Iterative, no recursion, and a genuinely good answer — offer it.
The recursive view
At each element there are two choices: include it or not. That binary tree has 2ⁿ leaves, one per subset.
The loop formulation
Rather than an explicit include/exclude branch, loop over the remaining candidates. Each iteration is the include branch; moving to the next iteration is the exclude branch.
Why every node counts
Each partial path is itself a valid subset, so record on entry rather than at leaves. That is what makes subsets simpler than combinations.
Why order is not duplicated
start = i + 1 means the sweep only ever moves right, so [2,1] is unreachable. No sorting or set is needed for distinct input.
Edge case
The empty subset is included automatically — it is the very first recorded value, at the root.
LC 78 · O(n·2ⁿ) time, O(n) space beyond the output
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> subsets(int[] nums) {
        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        backtrack(nums, 0, new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private void backtrack(int[] nums, int start,
                           List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        // EVERY node is a valid subset, including the empty one,
        // so record on entry with no filter at all.
        out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));    // COPY, not the live list

        for (int i = start; i < nums.length; i++) {

            path.add(nums[i]);                          // choose

            // i + 1: the sweep only moves right, so [2,1] can never
            // be generated and no de-duplication is needed.
            backtrack(nums, i + 1, path, out);          // explore

            path.remove(path.size() - 1);               // un-choose
        }
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 47 — the path to the solution

The lazy fix
Generate all n! permutations and push them through a HashSet. Correct, but it does the full exponential work and then discards most of it. Say it, then do better.
The right approach
Prune duplicate branches before exploring them, so the identical work is never done.
The rule
Sort first so equal values are adjacent. Then at each depth, among a run of equal values, allow only the leftmost unused copy to be chosen.
Why !used[i-1]
If the previous equal copy is currently in use, we are deeper in a branch that already took it — so this copy is a legitimate second occurrence. If it is not in use, it was already tried and undone at this depth, so choosing this copy would repeat an identical branch.
Why the other rule does not work here
The combination rule i > start relies on a left-to-right sweep. Permutations revisit every index at every depth, so there is no start to compare against — hence a different test.
Edge case
The sort is mandatory. Without it, equal values are not adjacent and the rule silently does nothing.
LC 47 · O(n·n!) worst case, O(n) space beyond the output
class Solution {
    public List<List<Integer>> permuteUnique(int[] nums) {
        Arrays.sort(nums);                 // MANDATORY: equal values adjacent

        List<List<Integer>> out = new ArrayList<>();
        backtrack(nums, new boolean[nums.length], new ArrayList<>(), out);
        return out;
    }

    private void backtrack(int[] nums, boolean[] used,
                           List<Integer> path, List<List<Integer>> out) {
        if (path.size() == nums.length) {
            out.add(new ArrayList<>(path));
            return;
        }

        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
            if (used[i]) continue;

            // Among equal values, only the LEFTMOST unused copy may be
            // chosen at this depth. If nums[i-1] is not used, it was
            // already tried and undone here — taking nums[i] now would
            // repeat an identical branch.
            if (i > 0 && nums[i] == nums[i - 1] && !used[i - 1]) continue;

            used[i] = true;
            path.add(nums[i]);

            backtrack(nums, used, path, out);

            path.remove(path.size() - 1);      // undo BOTH mutations
            used[i] = false;
        }
    }
}

77 · Combinations record at depth k

Path: the same tree as subsets, but only nodes at depth k are answers.

Delta: move the record into a base case — if (path.size() == k) { collect; return; }.

Watch for: the pruning is worth adding. If fewer than k − path.size() candidates remain, the branch cannot complete, so bound the loop at n - (k - path.size()) + 1. It converts a slow solution into a fast one on the larger inputs.

39 · Combination Sum start = i

Path: candidates are distinct but each may be reused without limit, and the target bounds the depth.

Delta: recurse with i instead of i + 1, which permits reuse while still forbidding reorderings. Record when the remaining target reaches exactly 0, and abandon the branch when it goes negative.

Watch for: sorting first lets you break rather than continue once a candidate exceeds the remainder — every later candidate is larger, so the whole rest of the loop is dead.

46 · Permutations used[]

Path: order matters, so the left-to-right sweep no longer applies — every unused index is a candidate at every depth.

Delta: drop start entirely, loop from 0, and guard with a boolean[] used. Record at depth n.

Watch for: there are now two mutations to undo — the path entry and the used flag. Restoring only one is the classic failure, and it produces too few permutations rather than an obvious crash.

90 · Subsets II i > start

Path: subsets of an input with repeats. Collecting into a set works but does the full work first.

Delta: sort, then if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;. This lets the first copy at a given depth through and blocks the rest.

Watch for: i > start, not i > 0. With i > 0 the second copy is blocked even one level deeper, so [1,1] never appears — and the answer is missing entries rather than having extra ones.

If you only drill twoDo 78 and 47. 78 fixes the skeleton and the copy-on-record habit that every problem here depends on. 47 is where the two dedup rules become distinguishable — being able to explain why combinations use i > start while permutations use !used[i-1] is the difference between remembering two lines and understanding them.

Prune early, and make the feasibility test O(1)

Plain enumeration explores the whole tree. Constrained backtracking kills a branch the moment it becomes impossible — and the difference between a solution that finishes and one that times out is almost always how cheaply you can ask "is this still legal?".

Two kinds of pruning

Feasibility
This branch violates a rule now — a queen attacks another, a cell is already on the path, the remaining sum went negative. Cut immediately.
Bound
This branch cannot possibly reach a solution even if everything goes well — not enough candidates remain, or the smallest remaining value already exceeds the target. Cut on arithmetic rather than on a rule.

Both belong at the top of the loop body, before the choose step. Pruning after recursing does the work you were trying to avoid.

Make the test O(1)

A feasibility check that scans the partial solution turns an already exponential search into something far worse. Maintain incremental state instead, updated on choose and restored on un-choose.

For N-Queens, three boolean arrays — column, and the two diagonals keyed by r + c and r − c + n — turn an O(n) scan into three array reads. For a grid walk, mutating the board itself records the visited set with no extra memory at all.

Identifying that state is the real work in this pattern. The recursion is unchanged.

Applies when

Enumeration plus rules: a grid path that cannot revisit cells, a partition where every piece must satisfy a predicate, placements that must not conflict. Constraints are what keep the exponential search tractable.

Does not apply when

Only a count or an optimum is wanted and subproblems repeat — that is dynamic programming. Backtracking re-explores overlapping states; DP solves each once.

Complexity

Worst case still exponential — O(m·n·4^L) for a grid word search, O(n!) for N-Queens — but pruning makes the practical running time far smaller. State the worst case, then say what the pruning buys.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"return all unique combinations" where each number is used once · "the same letter cell may not be used more than once" · "partition so that every substring is a palindrome" · "place n queens such that no two attack each other" · "all letter combinations the number could represent". The tell is enumerate plus an explicit rule that candidates must satisfy.

LC 79 traced on a 3×4 board searching "ABCCED"

The board's first row is A B C E, second S F C S, third A D E E. The word is found along a path that turns twice. The visited set is the board itself — each cell is temporarily overwritten and restored on the way out.

depthcellletter neededoutcomewhat the marking prevents
0(0,0)Amatch, mark, descend—
1(0,1)Bmatch, mark, descendreturning left to (0,0)
2(0,2)Cmatch; right fails, down succeedsreturning left to (0,1)
3(1,2)Cmatch, mark, descendreturning up to (0,2)
4(2,2)Ematch, mark, descendreturning up to (1,2)
5(2,1)Dword complete — return true—
Why the cell must be restored even on successThe board is the interviewer's input, and leaving it full of '#' corrupts it for any later call — LC 212 calls this routine thousands of times on the same grid. Restore in a finally-like position: compute the result, put the character back, then return. Restoring only on failure is the subtle version of this bug, and it passes a single-call test.

The same skeleton, with the guard moved to the top

Choose, explore, un-choose is unchanged. What is added is a guard clause before the choose, and incremental state that keeps that guard O(1).

Grid backtracking — the board as its own visited set (LC 79)
private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

boolean exist(char[][] board, String word) {
    for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
            if (dfs(board, word, r, c, 0)) return true;
    return false;
}

private boolean dfs(char[][] b, String w, int r, int c, int k) {
    if (k == w.length()) return true;                 // whole word matched

    // GUARD — bounds, then the letter test. Marked cells hold '#',
    // which never equals a real letter, so one check covers both
    // "already on the path" and "wrong letter".
    if (r < 0 || r >= b.length || c < 0 || c >= b[0].length) return false;
    if (b[r][c] != w.charAt(k)) return false;

    char saved = b[r][c];
    b[r][c] = '#';                                    // choose

    for (int[] d : DIRS) {
        if (dfs(b, w, r + d[0], c + d[1], k + 1)) {
            b[r][c] = saved;      // RESTORE even on success — the
            return true;          // caller's board must stay intact
        }
    }

    b[r][c] = saved;                                  // un-choose
    return false;
}
Placement with O(1) conflict tests (LC 51, 52)
// One queen per row, so only the COLUMN is chosen at each depth.
// Three boolean arrays make every conflict test a single read.
private boolean[] col, diag, anti;
private int n, count;

void solve(int row, List<String> board, List<List<String>> out) {
    if (row == n) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(board)); return; }

    for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
        int d = row + c;              // constant along one diagonal
        int a = row - c + n;          // + n shifts the range into [0, 2n)

        // GUARD before choosing — O(1), no board scan.
        if (col[c] || diag[d] || anti[a]) continue;

        col[c] = diag[d] = anti[a] = true;            // choose
        board.add(rowString(c));

        solve(row + 1, board, out);                   // explore

        board.remove(board.size() - 1);               // un-choose
        col[c] = diag[d] = anti[a] = false;           // ALL THREE
    }
}
Partitioning — the guard is a predicate on the piece (LC 131)
// Cut the string at every position; keep a cut only when the piece
// to the left satisfies the rule.
void partition(String s, int start, List<String> path,
               List<List<String>> out) {
    if (start == s.length()) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(path)); return; }

    for (int end = start; end < s.length(); end++) {

        // GUARD — this piece must be legal before we commit to it.
        if (!isPalindrome(s, start, end)) continue;

        path.add(s.substring(start, end + 1));        // choose
        partition(s, end + 1, path, out);             // explore
        path.remove(path.size() - 1);                 // un-choose
    }
}

// Two pointers, O(len). Precomputing an isPal[i][j] table in O(n^2)
// makes the guard O(1) and is the standard optimisation here.
private boolean isPalindrome(String s, int i, int j) {
    while (i < j) if (s.charAt(i++) != s.charAt(j--)) return false;
    return true;
}

The knobs

Guard position
Top of the loop body, before the choose. Pruning after recursing has already paid the cost.
Visited state
Mutate the input when it is allowed and restorable — a board cell, a used flag. Otherwise a separate structure, updated and undone in step.
Conflict encoding
Find an O(1) key. For diagonals, r + c and r − c + n. For sets, a bitmask. Scanning the partial solution is what turns a passing solution into a timeout.
Record point
At full depth for placements and partitions, or the moment the target is met for sum problems.
Precomputation
When the guard is expensive and called repeatedly on the same ranges, compute a table first. That is the standard LC 131 improvement.
The three bugs that actually happenRestoring only on failure — the board or flags stay dirty after a successful branch, which breaks any repeated call. Undoing some of the state — N-Queens has three arrays plus the path, and missing one produces too few solutions rather than a crash. A guard that scans — checking every placed queen is O(n) per test and turns a fast solution into a slow one; the array encoding is what makes it O(1).

Six constrained searches

17 has no pruning at all and is the gentle start. 40 adds the dedup rule. 131 guards on a predicate. 79 mutates the grid. 51 and 52 are the same search with different outputs.
