Anchor 1 · LC 79 — the path to the solution

The shape
From every cell, try to walk the word. Each step moves to one of four neighbours, and the search is depth-first because a path must be followed to its end before an alternative is tried.
The constraint
A cell may not be reused within one path — but it is free again once that path is abandoned. So the visited set is per-branch, not global, which is exactly what backtracking provides.
The space trick
Instead of a separate boolean[][], overwrite the cell with a sentinel such as '#'. Since the sentinel never equals a real letter, the existing letter comparison also rejects visited cells — one check does two jobs.
Restoring
Put the character back before returning, on both the success and failure paths. The grid belongs to the caller.
Pruning that matters
The letter check at the top is the pruning — most starting cells fail at depth 0 or 1, which is why the exponential bound is rarely approached.
Worth mentioning
If the first letter is rarer than the last, searching the reversed word is faster. It is a small optimisation that signals you thought about the search shape.
LC 79 · O(m·n·4^L) worst case, O(L) space
class Solution {
    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

    public boolean exist(char[][] board, String word) {
        for (int r = 0; r < board.length; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < board[0].length; c++)
                if (dfs(board, word, r, c, 0)) return true;
        return false;
    }

    private boolean dfs(char[][] b, String w, int r, int c, int k) {
        if (k == w.length()) return true;          // matched everything

        // GUARD first: bounds, then the letter. A visited cell holds
        // '#', which matches no real letter, so this single test also
        // enforces "do not revisit".
        if (r < 0 || r >= b.length || c < 0 || c >= b[0].length) return false;
        if (b[r][c] != w.charAt(k)) return false;

        char saved = b[r][c];
        b[r][c] = '#';                             // choose

        for (int[] d : DIRS) {
            if (dfs(b, w, r + d[0], c + d[1], k + 1)) {
                b[r][c] = saved;                   // restore on SUCCESS too
                return true;
            }
        }

        b[r][c] = saved;                           // un-choose
        return false;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 51 — the path to the solution

Brute force
Place queens on any of n² squares in all combinations. Astronomically large and entirely unnecessary.
Observation one
Exactly one queen per row, since two in a row always attack. So the search has depth n and each level chooses only a column — the problem collapses from C(n², n) to at most n!.
Observation two
Two queens share a ↘ diagonal exactly when r − c is equal, and a ↗ diagonal exactly when r + c is equal. Both are computable in O(1).
The encoding
Three boolean arrays: col[n], diag[2n] indexed by r + c, and anti[2n] indexed by r − c + n. The + n shifts a range that would otherwise be negative.
Why it is fast in practice
Conflicts appear early, so most branches die in the first few rows. The n! bound is never approached for the n ≤ 9 the problem allows.
LC 52
Identical search, incrementing a counter instead of building boards. Write 51 and you have both.
LC 51 · O(n!) worst case, O(n) space beyond the output
class Solution {
    private int n;
    private boolean[] col, diag, anti;
    private List<List<String>> out;

    public List<List<String>> solveNQueens(int n) {
        this.n = n;
        col  = new boolean[n];
        diag = new boolean[2 * n];      // indexed by r + c
        anti = new boolean[2 * n];      // indexed by r - c + n
        out  = new ArrayList<>();

        solve(0, new ArrayList<>());
        return out;
    }

    private void solve(int row, List<String> board) {
        if (row == n) { out.add(new ArrayList<>(board)); return; }

        for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            int d = row + c;            // constant along a diagonal
            int a = row - c + n;        // + n keeps the index non-negative

            // O(1) guard — three reads, no board scan.
            if (col[c] || diag[d] || anti[a]) continue;

            col[c] = diag[d] = anti[a] = true;
            board.add(rowOf(c));

            solve(row + 1, board);

            board.remove(board.size() - 1);
            col[c] = diag[d] = anti[a] = false;    // undo ALL THREE
        }
    }

    private String rowOf(int queenCol) {
        char[] row = new char[n];
        Arrays.fill(row, '.');
        row[queenCol] = 'Q';
        return new String(row);
    }
}

17 · Letter Combinations no pruning

Path: a Cartesian product over the digit-to-letter mapping. Every branch is valid, so there is nothing to prune — which makes it the cleanest place to practise the skeleton.

Delta: depth equals the number of digits, and the branching factor is 3 or 4. Record at full depth.

Watch for: an empty input must return an empty list, not a list containing one empty string. Guard before recursing — it is the only edge case, and it is the one the tests check.

40 · Combination Sum II dedup + sum guard

Path: each candidate may be used at most once, and the input contains duplicates, so both the start index and the dedup rule matter.

Delta: sort, recurse with i + 1, and skip with if (i > start && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;. Prune with if (nums[i] > remaining) break; — after sorting, every later candidate is larger too.

Watch for: break rather than continue on the sum prune. Using continue is correct but pointlessly scans the rest of the sorted range.

131 · Palindrome Partitioning predicate guard

Path: a cut position at every index, with each resulting piece required to be a palindrome. The guard is the palindrome test.

Delta: loop end from start, check the piece, and recurse from end + 1. Record when start reaches the end of the string.

Watch for: the same substring is tested many times. Precomputing isPal[i][j] with an O(n²) DP makes the guard O(1) and is the expected optimisation if asked to improve it.

52 · N-Queens II same search

Path: identical to 51. The only question is whether you notice that building the boards is wasted work when only a count is needed.

Delta: drop the board list and increment a counter at row == n. Everything else is unchanged.

Watch for: the bitmask version — three integers instead of three arrays, with Integer.lowestOneBit to iterate free columns — is meaningfully faster and a good thing to mention. Correctness first, then offer it.

If you only drill twoDo 79 and 51. 79 teaches per-branch state that lives in the input itself, and the restore-on-every-path discipline that goes with it. 51 teaches the move that defines this pattern: recognising that a constraint can be encoded so the feasibility test is O(1), which is what separates a search that finishes from one that does not.

A grid is a graph — and the choice of traversal is the answer

Every cell has up to four neighbours, which makes a grid an implicit graph with no adjacency list to build. The only real decision is DFS or BFS, and it is forced by the question: DFS for "what is connected", BFS for "how far".

The choice, and why it is not a preference

DFS
Counting components, measuring a region's size, flood-filling. Order does not matter because you visit everything reachable regardless.
BFS
Shortest path in an unweighted graph, or elapsed time in a spreading process. BFS reaches every cell in non-decreasing distance order, which is a guarantee DFS cannot make.

Using DFS for a shortest path is not slow — it is wrong. It may reach the target by a long route first and report that length.

On a large grid, prefer iterative DFS or BFS: recursion on 10⁶ cells overflows the stack.

Marking visited, and when

Mark a cell when you enqueue it, never when you dequeue it. Otherwise the same cell is added many times before its first visit, and the queue blows up — the classic BFS memory failure.

If the grid may be mutated, overwrite the cell itself and skip the extra array entirely. Say out loud that you are modifying the input; it is usually fine and interviewers like the space saving, but it should be a stated choice.

Unlike backtracking, these marks are never undone — a cell belongs to exactly one component, so revisiting it is always waste.

Applies when

Cells or nodes with neighbours, and a question about connectivity or distance. Grids, mazes, spreading processes, and region counting all reduce to this.

Does not apply when

Edges carry different weights — BFS assumes every step costs the same, so a weighted shortest path needs a priority queue instead. Also when the order must respect prerequisites, which is a different traversal entirely.

Complexity

O(rows × cols) — every cell is enqueued and dequeued once. Space is O(rows × cols) worst case for the queue or the recursion stack, which for a full grid is the entire grid.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the number of islands" · "the maximum area of an island" · "flood fill" · "the minimum number of minutes until no cell has a fresh orange" · "the length of the shortest clear path" · "a closed island" (surrounded on all four sides — check the border). The word "shortest" or "minimum steps" forces BFS; anything about counting or sizing permits DFS.

LC 994 traced on a 3×3 grid of oranges

The grid is 2 1 1 / 1 1 0 / 0 1 1, where 2 is rotten, 1 is fresh and 0 is empty. Rot spreads to orthogonal neighbours each minute. The answer is 4 — and the count comes from the number of BFS levels, not from any per-cell arithmetic.

leveldequeuednewly rottenfresh remainingminutes
seed——60
1(0,0)(0,1), (1,0)41
2(0,1), (1,0)(0,2), (1,1)22
3(0,2), (1,1)(2,1)13
4(2,1)(2,2)04
5(2,2)nothing04 — not incremented
Two details that decide correctnessCount the fresh oranges up front and decrement as they rot. At the end, a non-zero count means some orange was unreachable — return −1. Checking "are any 1s left?" by rescanning the grid also works but is an extra pass. Only increment the minute counter when a level actually rotted something, or the final drain level inflates the answer by one.

Two traversals, one direction array

The DIRS constant and the bounds check are shared. Everything else is the choice between a stack of recursive calls and an explicit queue with level counting.

DFS — connectivity, counting, sizing (LC 200, 695, 733, 1254)
private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

// Count components: one DFS per unvisited start.
int numIslands(char[][] g) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++)
            if (g[r][c] == '1') { count++; sink(g, r, c); }
    return count;
}

/** Marks the whole component. Returns its size, which LC 695 needs. */
private int sink(char[][] g, int r, int c) {
    // One guard covers bounds AND "not part of this component".
    if (r < 0 || r >= g.length || c < 0 || c >= g[0].length) return 0;
    if (g[r][c] != '1') return 0;

    g[r][c] = '0';           // mark visited — NEVER undone, unlike backtracking

    int size = 1;
    for (int[] d : DIRS) size += sink(g, r + d[0], c + d[1]);
    return size;
}
BFS — distance and elapsed time (LC 994, 1091)
// Multi-source: seed EVERY start before the loop, then one pass
// reaches each cell from its nearest source automatically.
int spread(int[][] g) {
    Queue<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    int fresh = 0;

    for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++) {
            if (g[r][c] == 2) q.offer(new int[]{r, c});   // every source
            else if (g[r][c] == 1) fresh++;
        }

    int minutes = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty() && fresh > 0) {
        int size = q.size();              // SNAPSHOT — one level = one minute

        for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
            int[] cur = q.poll();
            for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                int nr = cur[0] + d[0], nc = cur[1] + d[1];
                if (nr < 0 || nr >= g.length || nc < 0 || nc >= g[0].length) continue;
                if (g[nr][nc] != 1) continue;

                g[nr][nc] = 2;            // mark on ENQUEUE, not on dequeue
                fresh--;
                q.offer(new int[]{nr, nc});
            }
        }
        minutes++;      // guarded by fresh > 0, so a drain level never counts
    }
    return fresh == 0 ? minutes : -1;     // unreachable fresh cells
}
The border trick — for "surrounded" questions (LC 1254)
// "Closed" means not touching the edge. Rather than tracking that
// during each traversal, ELIMINATE the open ones first: flood every
// component that touches a border, then count what remains.
int closedIslands(int[][] g) {
    int rows = g.length, cols = g[0].length;

    // Sink everything reachable from the border.
    for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++) { sink(g, r, 0); sink(g, r, cols - 1); }
    for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++) { sink(g, 0, c); sink(g, rows - 1, c); }

    // Whatever land is left cannot touch an edge.
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < cols; c++)
            if (g[r][c] == 0) { count++; sink(g, r, c); }   // 0 is LAND here
    return count;
}

The knobs

Traversal
DFS for connectivity, BFS for distance. Forced by the question, not chosen.
Marking
Mutate the grid when allowed — no extra array, and the guard doubles as the visited test. Otherwise a boolean[][].
When to mark
On enqueue in BFS. Marking on dequeue lets the same cell enter the queue many times.
Level counting
The size snapshot, exactly as in a level-order tree traversal. Guard the increment so a level that changes nothing does not count.
Diagonals
Eight directions instead of four when the problem says "8-directionally", as LC 1091 does. Read for that word.
Recursion depth
A 10⁶-cell grid overflows the stack. Say so and switch to an explicit stack if the constraints are large.
The three bugs that actually happenMarking on dequeue — cells are enqueued repeatedly before their first visit, and the queue grows far beyond the grid. Using DFS for a shortest path — it terminates and returns a number, just not the minimum one. Incrementing the level counter unconditionally — the final drain level adds a phantom step, which is exactly the off-by-one in LC 994.

Six grids, one decision

733, 200, 695 and 1254 are DFS — count, size, fill. 994 and 1091 are BFS because both ask for a minimum number of steps. Choosing wrongly gives a wrong answer, not a slow one.

Anchor 1 · LC 200 — the path to the solution

The reframing
An island is a connected component of land cells. Counting islands is counting components, which is the most standard graph question there is.
The algorithm
Scan every cell. On finding unvisited land, increment the counter and traverse its entire component, marking as you go. Every land cell is then visited exactly once across the whole run.
Why the count is right
The counter increments only at the first cell of each component, because every other cell of that component is marked before the scan reaches it.
The space saving
Overwrite '1' with '0' instead of keeping a boolean[][]. The existing land test then doubles as the visited test. State that you are mutating the input.
DFS or BFS
Either works — the question is about connectivity, not distance. DFS is shorter; BFS avoids deep recursion on a large grid.
Edge cases
An empty grid returns 0. The grid is character-based, so compare against '1', not 1.
LC 200 · O(mn) time, O(mn) space worst case
class Solution {
    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

    public int numIslands(char[][] grid) {
        int count = 0;

        for (int r = 0; r < grid.length; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < grid[0].length; c++) {
                if (grid[r][c] == '1') {
                    // First cell of a new component — everything else
                    // in it gets marked before the scan reaches it.
                    count++;
                    sink(grid, r, c);
                }
            }
        }
        return count;
    }

    private void sink(char[][] g, int r, int c) {
        // One guard: out of bounds, water, or already visited.
        if (r < 0 || r >= g.length || c < 0 || c >= g[0].length) return;
        if (g[r][c] != '1') return;

        g[r][c] = '0';        // mark — never undone, unlike backtracking

        for (int[] d : DIRS) sink(g, r + d[0], c + d[1]);
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 994 — the path to the solution

Why not DFS
The question asks for elapsed time, which is a shortest distance. DFS may reach a cell by a long route and record that, so it is wrong rather than slow.
Why not one BFS per source
That is O(sources × cells) and needs a minimum across runs. Unnecessary work.
Multi-source BFS
Seed every rotten orange into the queue before the loop starts. A single pass then reaches each cell from its nearest source, because all sources expand in lockstep.
Time from levels
One BFS level is one minute. The size snapshot separates the levels, exactly as in a level-order tree traversal.
The two details
Count fresh oranges up front and decrement as they rot, so a leftover non-zero count means unreachable cells and the answer is −1. And guard the minute increment with fresh > 0, or the final drain level adds a phantom minute.
Edge case
Zero fresh oranges at the start returns 0 immediately, even if there are no rotten ones at all.
LC 994 · O(mn) time, O(mn) space
class Solution {
    private static final int[][] DIRS = {{1,0},{-1,0},{0,1},{0,-1}};

    public int orangesRotting(int[][] grid) {
        Queue<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        int fresh = 0;

        // Seed EVERY source before the loop — that is what makes one
        // pass compute the distance to the nearest source.
        for (int r = 0; r < grid.length; r++)
            for (int c = 0; c < grid[0].length; c++) {
                if (grid[r][c] == 2)      q.offer(new int[]{r, c});
                else if (grid[r][c] == 1) fresh++;
            }

        int minutes = 0;

        // `fresh > 0` stops the loop before a level that rots nothing,
        // so the counter is never inflated by the final drain.
        while (!q.isEmpty() && fresh > 0) {
            int size = q.size();          // one level == one minute

            for (int i = 0; i < size; i++) {
                int[] cur = q.poll();

                for (int[] d : DIRS) {
                    int nr = cur[0] + d[0], nc = cur[1] + d[1];

                    if (nr < 0 || nr >= grid.length) continue;
                    if (nc < 0 || nc >= grid[0].length) continue;
                    if (grid[nr][nc] != 1) continue;

                    grid[nr][nc] = 2;     // mark on ENQUEUE
                    fresh--;
                    q.offer(new int[]{nr, nc});
                }
            }
            minutes++;
        }
        return fresh == 0 ? minutes : -1;   // leftovers were unreachable
    }
}

733 · Flood Fill DFS

Path: recolour the connected region sharing the starting colour. The bare traversal with a colour test as the guard.

Delta: almost none — but there is one real trap. If the new colour equals the starting colour, marking changes nothing and the recursion never terminates.

Watch for: guard with if (image[sr][sc] == color) return image; before starting. It is the single line that separates a passing solution from an infinite loop.

695 · Max Area of Island DFS

Path: identical to LC 200, except the traversal reports how many cells it visited.

Delta: make sink return 1 + the sum of its four recursive calls, and take the maximum across all starts.

Watch for: the base cases must return 0, not simply return. Writing 200 and 695 as one function that returns a size, and ignoring the result in 200, covers both problems with one piece of code.

1254 · Number of Closed Islands DFS + border

Path: a closed island touches no edge. Tracking that flag during each traversal works but is fiddly — a cleaner approach removes the disqualified components first.

Delta: flood every component reachable from a border cell, then count what remains. Any surviving component is closed by construction.

Watch for: the polarity is inverted here — 0 is land and 1 is water, the opposite of LC 200. Reading that from the statement is most of the difficulty.

1091 · Shortest Path in Binary Matrix BFS

Path: shortest path in an unweighted grid, so BFS from the top-left corner, counting levels until the bottom-right is reached.

Delta: the statement says 8-directionally connected, so DIRS has eight entries including the diagonals. Using four silently returns a longer path or −1.

Watch for: check that both the start and the end cells are 0 before beginning. A blocked start is a valid input and must return −1 rather than throwing. Path length counts cells, so the start counts as 1.

If you only drill twoDo 200 and 994. 200 fixes the component-counting shape that 695 and 1254 reuse almost verbatim. 994 teaches multi-source BFS and level-as-time, which is the idea that turns a whole class of "how long until everything is X" problems into a single pass — and the two off-by-ones it contains are the ones interviewers watch for.

Repeatedly take whatever has nothing left blocking it

Given tasks with prerequisites, produce an order in which every task comes after everything it depends on. The algorithm is one sentence: keep a set of tasks with zero remaining prerequisites, take any of them, and decrement its dependents. If you run out before finishing, there is a cycle.

Kahn's algorithm — the invariant

indegree[v] counts how many prerequisites of v are still unprocessed. The queue holds exactly those nodes whose count has reached zero.

Processing a node decrements each of its dependents; any that hit zero join the queue. Each edge is examined once, so the whole thing is O(V + E).

Cycle detection is free: if fewer than V nodes were emitted, the remainder form a cycle — every one of them is still waiting on another, so none can ever reach zero.

Edge direction is the thing to get right

The input usually reads [a, b] meaning "to take a you must first take b". That is an edge from b to a — the prerequisite points at what it unlocks — and indegree[a] is what increments.

Building it backwards produces a perfectly plausible order that is exactly reversed. Write one concrete example on paper before coding: it takes ten seconds and prevents the most common failure in this pattern.

The DFS alternative uses three colours and produces the order reversed on the way out. Kahn's is easier to reason about and gives cycle detection without extra state.

Applies when

Directed dependencies and a question about ordering or feasibility — course schedules, build systems, recipe ingredients, task graphs. Also for detecting a cycle in a directed graph.

Does not apply when

The graph is undirected — "cycle" means something different there, and union-find is the tool. Also when edges have weights and you want a shortest path rather than an order.

Complexity

O(V + E) time: each node is enqueued once and each edge relaxed once. Space is O(V + E) for the adjacency list plus O(V) for the indegree array and queue.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"prerequisites[i] = [a, b] means you must take b before a" · "can you finish all courses" (feasibility, so only the count matters) · "return the ordering of courses" · "eventual safe states" (reverse the edges) · "which recipes can you create" · "build order". The phrase "if it is impossible, return an empty array" is the cycle case being handed to you.

LC 210 traced on 4 courses with [[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2]]

Each pair reads "to take the first, finish the second". So course 0 unlocks 1 and 2, and course 3 needs both. A valid order is 0, 1, 2, 3 — and watch course 3's indegree fall twice before it becomes available.

stepqueue beforetakendependents decrementedindegree afterorder so far
seed[0]——[0,1,1,2][ ]
1[0]01 → 0 ✓ freed, 2 → 0 ✓ freed[0,0,0,2][0]
2[1,2]13 → 1, still blocked[0,0,0,1][0,1]
3[2]23 → 0 ✓ freed[0,0,0,0][0,1,2]
4[3]3none[0,0,0,0][0,1,2,3]
What a cycle looks like in this traceAdd the prerequisite [0,3] and every indegree starts at 1 or more, so the queue is empty before the loop begins and nothing is ever emitted. With a cycle buried deeper, the loop runs for a while and then stalls with nodes still unprocessed. Either way the test is the same: emitted count versus V. Return an empty array when they differ — the problem defines that as "impossible".

Build, seed, drain, check

Four phases, and the first is where the mistakes live. Get the edge direction right and the rest is mechanical.

Kahn's algorithm — the template
/**
 * [a, b] means "b must come before a", so the edge runs b -> a
 * and indegree[a] counts how many prerequisites a is still waiting on.
 *
 * Returns a valid order, or an empty array when a cycle exists.
 */
int[] topoSort(int n, int[][] pairs) {
    // 1 · BUILD — adjacency plus indegree, in one pass
    List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());

    int[] indeg = new int[n];
    for (int[] p : pairs) {
        int after = p[0], before = p[1];
        adj.get(before).add(after);     // before UNLOCKS after
        indeg[after]++;                 // after is BLOCKED by one more
    }

    // 2 · SEED — every node that starts unblocked
    Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.offer(i);

    // 3 · DRAIN
    int[] order = new int[n];
    int idx = 0;

    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int cur = q.poll();
        order[idx++] = cur;

        for (int next : adj.get(cur)) {
            // A node is freed exactly when its LAST blocker is removed.
            if (--indeg[next] == 0) q.offer(next);
        }
    }

    // 4 · CHECK — anything unemitted is part of a cycle
    return idx == n ? order : new int[0];
}
Variant · the DFS colouring form
// Three states. GRAY means "on the current recursion path", so
// meeting a GRAY node is a back edge — that is the cycle.
// The order comes out REVERSED, because a node is appended only
// after all its descendants are finished.
private static final int WHITE = 0, GRAY = 1, BLACK = 2;

boolean dfs(int u, List<List<Integer>> adj, int[] color, Deque<Integer> out) {
    color[u] = GRAY;

    for (int v : adj.get(u)) {
        if (color[v] == GRAY) return false;             // back edge → cycle
        if (color[v] == WHITE && !dfs(v, adj, color, out)) return false;
        // BLACK means already finished — safe to skip
    }

    color[u] = BLACK;
    out.push(u);        // push, so the final stack reads in topo order
    return true;
}
Variant · reverse the edges (LC 802)
// "Safe" means every path from the node leads to a terminal.
// Equivalently: the node reaches no cycle. Kahn's peels away nodes
// with OUTdegree zero — so build the graph BACKWARDS and use
// outdegree where indegree normally goes.
List<Integer> eventualSafeNodes(int[][] graph) {
    int n = graph.length;
    List<List<Integer>> rev = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) rev.add(new ArrayList<>());

    int[] outdeg = new int[n];
    for (int u = 0; u < n; u++) {
        outdeg[u] = graph[u].length;
        for (int v : graph[u]) rev.get(v).add(u);       // reversed edge
    }

    Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (outdeg[i] == 0) q.offer(i);   // terminals

    boolean[] safe = new boolean[n];
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll();
        safe[u] = true;
        for (int p : rev.get(u)) if (--outdeg[p] == 0) q.offer(p);
    }

    List<Integer> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (safe[i]) out.add(i);
    return out;      // already ascending, as the problem requires
}

The knobs

Edge direction
Prerequisite points at what it unlocks. Write one example out before coding — this is where the pattern goes wrong.
What you return
The order, or just whether the count reached V. Feasibility questions need nothing else.
Queue or priority queue
A plain queue gives any valid order. Swap in a PriorityQueue when the problem wants the lexicographically smallest one.
Reversed graph
When the question is about reaching terminals rather than being reachable, build the graph backwards and peel by outdegree.
Non-integer nodes
Map string names to indices with a HashMap, or keep the adjacency and indegree keyed on the string directly.
The three bugs that actually happenReversed edges — the algorithm runs happily and emits a plausible order that is backwards, which passes a symmetric test case and fails the rest. Seeding after the loop — the queue must be filled with all zero-indegree nodes before draining; a disconnected component with its own start is otherwise never reached. Skipping the count check — without it a cyclic input returns a partial order instead of the required empty array.

Six orderings, one algorithm

207 and 210 are the template with different return types. 802 reverses the graph. 2115 keys it on strings. 1462 asks about reachability, and 1203 nests two sorts inside each other.

Anchor 1 · LC 210 — the path to the solution

The restatement
Courses are nodes, prerequisites are directed edges, and a valid schedule is a topological order. Saying that out loud is most of the solution.
Reading the input
[a, b] means "take b before a", so the edge is b → a and indegree[a] increments. Getting this backwards is the failure mode for this whole family.
Why indegree and not removal
A course with three prerequisites must wait for all three. A counter that decrements handles that naturally; removing edges from a set would need extra bookkeeping.
Seeding
Every course with no prerequisites starts available. There may be several, and there may be disconnected groups — so seed them all before draining.
Cycle detection
Free. If fewer than n courses were emitted, the remainder are mutually blocking, and the problem asks for an empty array in that case.
Edge cases
No prerequisites at all means every course is immediately available and any order works. A self-loop [a, a] is a cycle of length one and is handled with no special case.
LC 210 · O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space
class Solution {
    public int[] findOrder(int numCourses, int[][] prerequisites) {
        // 1 · BUILD. [a, b] = "take b before a", so the edge is b -> a.
        List<List<Integer>> adj = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < numCourses; i++) adj.add(new ArrayList<>());

        int[] indeg = new int[numCourses];
        for (int[] p : prerequisites) {
            int after = p[0], before = p[1];
            adj.get(before).add(after);     // finishing `before` unlocks `after`
            indeg[after]++;                 // `after` has one more blocker
        }

        // 2 · SEED every initially-unblocked course, not just one.
        Queue<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < numCourses; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.offer(i);

        // 3 · DRAIN
        int[] order = new int[numCourses];
        int idx = 0;

        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            int cur = q.poll();
            order[idx++] = cur;

            for (int next : adj.get(cur)) {
                // Freed exactly when its last prerequisite is done.
                if (--indeg[next] == 0) q.offer(next);
            }
        }

        // 4 · CHECK. Unemitted courses are mutually blocking: a cycle.
        return idx == numCourses ? order : new int[0];
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 2115 — the path to the solution

The restatement
A recipe is a node; each ingredient it needs is a prerequisite edge. Supplies are nodes that start satisfied. "Which recipes can I make?" is "which nodes does the topological sort reach?".
The naive approach
Loop repeatedly over all recipes, making any whose ingredients are all available, until a full pass changes nothing. Correct, but O(n²) in the number of recipes.
The change from LC 210
Nodes are strings, and not every ingredient is a recipe — some are raw supplies with no dependencies of their own.
Handling that
Give each recipe an indegree equal to its ingredient count, minus the ones already in supplies. Or more simply: seed the queue with every supply, and let an ingredient that is not a recipe simply never appear as a node.
The structure
Map<String, List<String>> from ingredient to the recipes it feeds, plus Map<String, Integer> for indegrees. Everything else is the template.
Why cycles matter
Two recipes can require each other. Neither ever reaches indegree zero, so neither is emitted — which is the correct answer with no extra code.
LC 2115 · O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space
class Solution {
    public List<String> findAllRecipes(String[] recipes, List<List<String>> ingredients,
                                       String[] supplies) {
        // ingredient -> recipes that need it
        Map<String, List<String>> adj = new HashMap<>();
        Map<String, Integer> indeg = new HashMap<>();

        for (int i = 0; i < recipes.length; i++) {
            String recipe = recipes[i];
            indeg.put(recipe, ingredients.get(i).size());

            for (String ing : ingredients.get(i)) {
                adj.computeIfAbsent(ing, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(recipe);
            }
        }

        // SEED with the supplies — they are the zero-indegree nodes.
        Queue<String> q = new ArrayDeque<>(Arrays.asList(supplies));

        List<String> made = new ArrayList<>();

        while (!q.isEmpty()) {
            String have = q.poll();

            // An ingredient nobody needs simply has no entry here.
            for (String recipe : adj.getOrDefault(have, List.of())) {
                if (indeg.merge(recipe, -1, Integer::sum) == 0) {
                    made.add(recipe);      // every ingredient satisfied
                    q.offer(recipe);       // and it can feed other recipes
                }
            }
        }
        // Mutually-dependent recipes never reach zero and are excluded,
        // which is exactly the required behaviour.
        return made;
    }
}

207 · Course Schedule Kahn

Path: "can you finish all courses" is "is this graph acyclic". The order itself is never needed.

Delta: the template with return count == numCourses; and no output array. The DFS three-colour version is equally valid and slightly shorter if you prefer recursion.

Watch for: solve 210 instead and return order.length > 0 — one implementation covers both problems, and 210 is the one that exercises the edge direction.

802 · Find Eventual Safe States reversed

Path: a node is safe when every path from it ends at a terminal — equivalently, it can reach no cycle. Kahn's peels nodes with no outgoing edges rather than no incoming ones.

Delta: build the reversed graph and use outdegree where indegree normally goes. Seed with the terminals, and everything the peeling reaches is safe.

Watch for: the answer must be in ascending order. Collecting by scanning the safe[] array gives that for free; collecting in processing order does not.

1462 · Course Schedule IV closure

Path: answering each query with its own traversal is O(Q·(V+E)) and too slow. The queries need the transitive closure, not a single order.

Delta: run Kahn's while propagating a boolean[n] or BitSet of ancestors — when node u is processed, every dependent inherits u's ancestor set plus u itself. With n ≤ 100, Floyd–Warshall over a reachability matrix is also acceptable and easier to write.

Watch for: propagation must happen in topological order, or a node's ancestor set is incomplete when it is read.

1203 · Sort Items by Groups Kahn × 2

Path: two levels of ordering — groups must be ordered relative to each other, and items within a group must be ordered too.

Delta: assign every ungrouped item its own unique group first, so the group graph is well defined. Then topologically sort the groups, sort the items inside each group, and concatenate.

Watch for: that first step is what makes the problem tractable — without it, items with group == -1 are all lumped together and their mutual ordering is lost. A cycle in either sort means the answer is empty.

If you only drill twoDo 210 and 802. 210 fixes the edge direction and the count-based cycle check, which 207, 2115 and 1203 all reuse unchanged. 802 forces you to notice that reversing the graph turns "what depends on me" into "what do I depend on" — and that reversal is the move that makes several otherwise awkward graph problems fall out immediately.

Answer "are these two connected?" in almost constant time

A traversal can tell you the components of a graph you already have. Union-find handles the harder case: edges arriving one at a time, with connectivity queries interleaved. Each element points at a parent; the root of that chain names the component.

Two operations, two optimisations

find(x)
Walk parent links to the root. Path compression re-points every node on the way directly at the root, so the next walk is one step.
union(a, b)
Find both roots; if they differ, attach one to the other. Union by size attaches the smaller tree under the larger, keeping the structure shallow.

Either optimisation alone is good; together they give O(α(n)) amortised — the inverse Ackermann function, which is below 5 for any input that fits in memory. Call it "effectively constant" rather than claiming O(1).

Without them, a chain of unions builds a linked list and every find is O(n).

The return value that does the work

Make union return a boolean: true if it merged two distinct components, false if they were already connected.

That single value answers most problems in this family directly. A false means the edge closed a cycle. Counting the true results tells you how many merges happened, so components = n − merges with no second pass.

Keeping a live component counter inside the structure is even simpler: start at n and decrement on every successful union.

Applies when

Edges arrive incrementally and you need connectivity as you go, or the question is about components, redundant edges, or merging equivalence classes. Also the core of Kruskal's spanning-tree algorithm.

Does not apply when

Edges are removed — union-find cannot split a set, and the standard workaround is to process the timeline backwards so deletions become insertions. Also when you need the path itself, not just whether one exists.

Complexity

O(α(n)) amortised per operation with both optimisations, so O(E·α(n)) overall — effectively linear. Space is O(n) for the parent and size arrays.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the number of provinces" or "connected components" · "return the edge that can be removed" · "the minimum number of cables to connect" · "are these equations satisfiable" · "you may swap characters at these index pairs" · "keep the graph fully traversable". The tell is grouping by equivalence, or edges arriving as a list you process one by one.

LC 684 traced on [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]]

Find the edge that creates a cycle. Three nodes, three edges — one too many for a tree. The first two unions succeed; the third finds both endpoints already in the same component, and that is the answer.

edgeroot of aroot of bunionparent array aftercomponents
———initial[_, 1, 2, 3]3
[1,2]12true — merged[_, 1, 1, 3]2
[1,3]13true — merged[_, 1, 1, 1]1
[2,3]11false — cycleunchanged1
Why union-find and not a traversalDFS also detects the cycle, but it must re-examine the graph built so far after every edge, giving O(E²) if you want the last redundant edge. Union-find processes each edge once and answers immediately, because the connectivity state is carried forward rather than recomputed. That incremental property is the whole reason this structure exists.

Twenty lines you should be able to type from memory

Write the class once, correctly, and every problem in this family becomes four or five lines of driver code. Both optimisations are one line each and neither is optional.

The class — path compression and union by size
class DSU {
    private final int[] parent;
    private final int[] size;
    private int components;      // live count, so no second pass is needed

    DSU(int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        size   = new int[n];
        components = n;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; }
    }

    /** Root of x's component, flattening the path on the way. */
    int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];   // point at the grandparent
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    /** true if two distinct components were merged; false if already joined. */
    boolean union(int a, int b) {
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return false;          // this edge would close a cycle

        // Attach the SMALLER tree under the larger, keeping depth low.
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
        parent[rb] = ra;
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        components--;
        return true;
    }

    boolean connected(int a, int b) { return find(a) == find(b); }
    int componentCount()            { return components; }
    int componentSize(int x)        { return size[find(x)]; }
}
The driver is always four or five lines
// LC 547 — count components from an adjacency MATRIX
DSU dsu = new DSU(n);
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
        if (isConnected[i][j] == 1) dsu.union(i, j);
return dsu.componentCount();

// LC 684 — the last edge that closes a cycle
for (int[] e : edges)
    if (!dsu.union(e[0] - 1, e[1] - 1)) return e;   // 1-indexed input

// LC 1319 — cables to connect everything
// You need n-1 edges minimum; spares are the redundant ones.
if (connections.length < n - 1) return -1;
for (int[] c : connections) dsu.union(c[0], c[1]);
return dsu.componentCount() - 1;    // moves = components - 1

// LC 990 — equalities first, then check the inequalities
for (String e : equations)
    if (e.charAt(1) == '=') dsu.union(e.charAt(0) - 'a', e.charAt(3) - 'a');
for (String e : equations)
    if (e.charAt(1) == '!' && dsu.connected(e.charAt(0)-'a', e.charAt(3)-'a'))
        return false;
return true;
Variant · grouping, then sorting within groups (LC 1202)
// Swappable index pairs form components. Within a component ANY
// permutation is reachable, so each component's characters can be
// sorted freely among its own positions.
String smallestStringWithSwaps(String s, List<List<Integer>> pairs) {
    DSU dsu = new DSU(s.length());
    for (List<Integer> p : pairs) dsu.union(p.get(0), p.get(1));

    // Bucket the indices by root.
    Map<Integer, List<Integer>> groups = new HashMap<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++)
        groups.computeIfAbsent(dsu.find(i), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(i);

    char[] out = s.toCharArray();

    for (List<Integer> idx : groups.values()) {
        // idx is ascending already, since i increased as we inserted.
        char[] chars = new char[idx.size()];
        for (int i = 0; i < idx.size(); i++) chars[i] = s.charAt(idx.get(i));
        Arrays.sort(chars);

        // Smallest characters into the smallest positions.
        for (int i = 0; i < idx.size(); i++) out[idx.get(i)] = chars[i];
    }
    return new String(out);
}

The knobs

Index mapping
Nodes must be 0..n−1. Subtract 1 for 1-indexed input, or map characters with c - 'a', or strings through a HashMap.
What to carry
A size array for balancing, a live component count, and sometimes a per-component aggregate such as a maximum. Update all of them inside union.
Edge order
Process in the given order when the problem asks for the last qualifying edge; sort by weight when building a minimum spanning tree.
Two DSUs
Some problems need separate connectivity views — LC 1579 runs one for each traveller and shares the type-3 edges between them.
Rank or size
Either balances correctly. Size is more useful, because it also answers "how big is this component?".
The three bugs that actually happenComparing the nodes instead of their roots — if (a == b) rather than if (find(a) == find(b)) misses every cycle that is not a self-loop. Forgetting to initialise parent[i] = i — Java zero-fills the array, so every node claims 0 as its root and the whole graph starts connected. Omitting both optimisations — the code is still correct, but a path-shaped union sequence makes each find O(n) and the solution times out on the large tests.

Six groupings, one class

547, 684 and 1319 are the class with a four-line driver. 990 and 1202 map non-integer elements onto indices. 1579 is the one that needs two structures at once.

Anchor 1 · LC 684 — the path to the solution

The setup
A tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges. The input has n, so precisely one edge closes a cycle, and you must return the last such edge in the input order.
The DFS approach
After adding each edge, check whether the graph now has a cycle. Correct, but each check is O(V + E), so the whole thing is O(E²).
The observation
An edge closes a cycle exactly when its two endpoints are already in the same component. That is a connectivity query, and union-find answers it incrementally without re-examining anything.
Why the first false is the last edge
Edges are processed in input order and exactly one is redundant, so the first failure is that edge. Return immediately.
Indexing
Nodes are labelled 1 to n, so either size the arrays n + 1 and ignore index 0, or subtract 1 everywhere. Pick one and be consistent.
Edge case
The problem guarantees a solution exists, so no fallback return is needed — though returning an empty array keeps the compiler quiet.
LC 684 · O(n·α(n)) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int[] findRedundantConnection(int[][] edges) {
        int n = edges.length;                 // n nodes, n edges
        int[] parent = new int[n + 1];        // nodes are 1-indexed
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) parent[i] = i;   // MUST initialise

        for (int[] e : edges) {
            // Already connected means this edge closes a cycle.
            // Processing in input order makes the first such edge
            // the LAST one in the input that qualifies.
            if (!union(parent, e[0], e[1])) return e;
        }
        return new int[0];                    // guaranteed unreachable
    }

    private int find(int[] parent, int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];    // path compression
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    private boolean union(int[] parent, int a, int b) {
        int ra = find(parent, a), rb = find(parent, b);
        if (ra == rb) return false;           // compare ROOTS, not a and b
        parent[rb] = ra;
        return true;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 1579 — the path to the solution

The restatement
Keep the fewest edges such that Alice can reach everything and Bob can too. "Remove the maximum" is "keep the minimum", so the answer is total − kept.
The structure
Two separate connectivity views — one per traveller. Type 3 edges belong to both; type 1 to Alice only; type 2 to Bob only.
The ordering insight
Process type 3 first. A shared edge serves both travellers, so it is never worse than two single-type edges doing the same job. Taking them first is a greedy choice, and the exchange argument is that swapping a type-3 edge in can only reduce the count.
Counting kept edges
A type-3 edge counts once if it merged in either DSU. Type 1 and type 2 edges count when they merge in their own DSU.
The feasibility check
At the end both DSUs must have exactly one component. If either does not, some node is unreachable for that traveller and the answer is −1.
Edge case
Nodes are 1-indexed again, and duplicate edges appear in the test set — they union to false and are correctly discarded.
LC 1579 · O(E·α(n)) time, O(n) space
class Solution {
    public int maxNumEdgesToRemove(int n, int[][] edges) {
        DSU alice = new DSU(n + 1), bob = new DSU(n + 1);
        int kept = 0;

        // TYPE 3 FIRST: a shared edge does two jobs, so taking it can
        // never be worse than taking two single-type edges instead.
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            if (e[0] != 3) continue;
            boolean a = alice.union(e[1], e[2]);
            boolean b = bob.union(e[1], e[2]);
            if (a || b) kept++;          // useful to at least one traveller
        }

        // Then the private edges, each in its own structure.
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            if (e[0] == 1 && alice.union(e[1], e[2])) kept++;
            if (e[0] == 2 && bob.union(e[1], e[2]))   kept++;
        }

        // Component 0 is unused (1-indexed), so a fully connected graph
        // leaves 2 components: the real one plus the dummy node 0.
        if (alice.componentCount() != 2 || bob.componentCount() != 2) return -1;

        return edges.length - kept;
    }
}

547 · Number of Provinces count

Path: DFS over the adjacency matrix counting components is equally valid and equally fast — say so. Union-find is the natural choice if the edges were arriving over time.

Delta: iterate the upper triangle only (j > i); the matrix is symmetric, so the lower half is duplicated work.

Watch for: isConnected[i][i] is always 1 and must not be unioned — starting j at i + 1 handles that for free.

1319 · Operations to Make Network Connected count

Path: connecting k components needs k − 1 moves, and each move requires a spare cable — one that currently connects two already-connected computers.

Delta: check connections.length >= n - 1 first and return −1 otherwise; below that threshold there are not enough cables no matter how they are arranged. Then union everything and return componentCount() - 1.

Watch for: you never need to count the redundant cables explicitly. If there are at least n − 1 edges, there are always enough spares — proving that to yourself is the insight.

990 · Satisfiability of Equality Equations two-pass

Path: equality is an equivalence relation, which is exactly what union-find models. Inequality is a constraint checked afterwards.

Delta: two passes, and the order matters. Merge every == first, then verify that no != pair shares a root. Doing them in one pass fails when an equality appears after the inequality it contradicts.

Watch for: variables are single lowercase letters, so the universe is 26 elements — c - 'a' is the whole mapping, and "a!=a" must correctly return false.

1202 · Smallest String With Swaps group + sort

Path: the key realisation is that swaps are transitive. If you may swap (0,1) and (1,2), you can achieve any arrangement of positions 0, 1 and 2 — so a component's characters can be rearranged freely within its own positions.

Delta: union all pairs, bucket indices by root, then sort each bucket's characters and write the smallest into the smallest index.

Watch for: the indices in each bucket are already ascending if you collect them with an increasing loop, so only the characters need sorting — not both.

If you only drill twoDo 684 and 1202. 684 fixes the class itself and the boolean-returning union that most of this family depends on. 1202 is the one that teaches the modelling step — noticing that swap pairs are transitive, and therefore an equivalence relation — which is the move that makes a problem look like union-find when it did not at first.

Always expand the closest unfinished node

When every edge costs the same, a queue suffices. When edges carry different weights, a queue is no longer in distance order — so replace it with a priority queue. That one substitution is Dijkstra's algorithm, and it is the whole of this pattern.

The invariant

When a node is popped from the priority queue, its recorded distance is final. Nothing still in the queue can offer a shorter route, because every remaining path starts from something at least as far away.

That argument requires non-negative weights. With a negative edge, a longer-looking route could later become shorter, and the invariant collapses — which is why Dijkstra is simply wrong on such graphs rather than slow.

So: pop, finalise, relax the neighbours, repeat.

Lazy deletion

Java's PriorityQueue cannot decrease a key. The standard workaround is to push a new entry whenever a shorter distance is found, leaving the stale one in place.

Then skip stale entries on pop: if the popped distance exceeds the recorded one, discard it and continue. The queue may hold up to E entries, which is where the O(E log E) bound comes from.

Without that skip the algorithm still terminates and still returns the right answer — but it re-expands finalised nodes and wastes a great deal of time.

Applies when

Edges carry non-negative weights and you want the cheapest route. The cost need not be a distance — it can be time, effort, or a probability treated multiplicatively.

Does not apply when

Weights can be negative — use Bellman-Ford. Or when a constraint such as "at most k stops" means a cheaper partial route is not always better; then the state must carry that constraint.

Complexity

O(E log E) with a binary heap and lazy deletion. Bellman-Ford is O(V·E), and the k-bounded variant O(k·E). Floyd–Warshall is O(V³), which is fine when V ≤ 100.

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the time it takes for all nodes to receive the signal" · "the cheapest price with at most k stops" (the constraint dimension) · "maximise the probability" (multiplicative, so use a max-heap) · "minimise the maximum absolute difference along a path" (minimax, not a sum) · "how many cities are reachable within a threshold" (all-pairs, so Floyd–Warshall) · "the number of ways to arrive in the shortest time".

Why the stale check is written as d > dist[node]When a shorter route to a node is found, a new entry is pushed and the old one is left behind. The old entry carries a distance larger than the recorded one, so that single comparison identifies it. Using != would also work, but > reads as what it means: "this entry describes a route we have already beaten." A visited[] array is an equally valid alternative — pick one, not both.

One heap loop, and three ways to change what "shorter" means

The skeleton is fixed. What varies is the comparator, how costs combine, and whether the state needs an extra dimension for a constraint.

Dijkstra — the template
/**
 * Shortest distances from `src`. Requires NON-NEGATIVE weights:
 * the correctness argument is that a popped node can never be
 * improved by anything still in the queue.
 *
 * Lazy deletion: Java's PriorityQueue cannot decrease a key, so we
 * push a new entry and skip the stale one when it surfaces.
 */
int[] dijkstra(int n, List<int[]>[] adj, int src) {
    int[] dist = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[src] = 0;

    // (node, distance), ordered by distance
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq =
            new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
    pq.offer(new int[]{src, 0});

    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = pq.poll();
        int node = cur[0], d = cur[1];

        // STALE: a better route to this node was already recorded.
        if (d > dist[node]) continue;

        for (int[] e : adj[node]) {
            int next = e[0], w = e[1];
            int cand = d + w;

            if (cand < dist[next]) {
                dist[next] = cand;
                pq.offer(new int[]{next, cand});   // push, never update
            }
        }
    }
    return dist;
}
Changing what "shorter" means
// MAXIMISE a PRODUCT — probabilities (LC 1514).
// Max-heap, and costs MULTIPLY instead of adding.
PriorityQueue<Object[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(
        (a, b) -> Double.compare((double) b[1], (double) a[1]));
double cand = prob * edgeProb;
if (cand > best[next]) { best[next] = cand; pq.offer(...); }

// MINIMISE a MAXIMUM — minimax paths (LC 1631, 778).
// The path cost is the WORST single step, not the sum.
int cand = Math.max(effortSoFar, Math.abs(h[next] - h[cur]));
if (cand < dist[next]) { dist[next] = cand; pq.offer(...); }

// COUNT the shortest paths (LC 1976).
// Carry a ways[] alongside dist[]:
if (cand < dist[next]) {
    dist[next] = cand;
    ways[next] = ways[cur];                    // a strictly better route
    pq.offer(...);
} else if (cand == dist[next]) {
    ways[next] = (ways[next] + ways[cur]) % MOD;   // another equally short one
}
Bellman-Ford — when a constraint bounds the hops (LC 787)
/**
 * "At most k stops" breaks Dijkstra's invariant: a MORE expensive
 * route that uses fewer stops may still win later, so a single
 * distance per node is not enough information.
 *
 * Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge k+1 times. After round r, dist[]
 * holds the cheapest cost reachable using AT MOST r edges — so the
 * hop limit falls out of the round count for free.
 */
int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
    int[] dist = new int[n];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    dist[src] = 0;

    for (int round = 0; round <= k; round++) {
        // Relax from a SNAPSHOT: without it, a route found earlier in
        // this same round could be extended again, using more than
        // `round + 1` edges and breaking the hop bound.
        int[] prev = dist.clone();

        for (int[] f : flights) {
            int from = f[0], to = f[1], price = f[2];
            if (prev[from] == Integer.MAX_VALUE) continue;

            dist[to] = Math.min(dist[to], prev[from] + price);
        }
    }
    return dist[dst] == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : dist[dst];
}

Choosing the algorithm

Unweighted
Plain BFS. A priority queue is wasted effort when every edge costs 1.
Non-negative weights
Dijkstra. O(E log E), and the default choice.
A hop or step limit
Bellman-Ford with the round count as the limit, or Dijkstra over (node, stepsUsed) states.
All pairs, small V
Floyd–Warshall. Three nested loops, O(V³), and trivial to write correctly when V ≤ 100.
Minimax rather than sum
Dijkstra with max in place of +. Union-find with sorted edges also solves these, and is worth naming.
The three bugs that actually happenOverflow when relaxing — dist[u] + w overflows when dist[u] is Integer.MAX_VALUE; skip unreachable nodes first, or use a large finite sentinel. Omitting the stale skip — still correct, but finalised nodes are re-expanded and the solution times out on dense graphs. Relaxing in place in Bellman-Ford — without the clone(), one round can chain several edges and the hop limit is silently violated, which is the classic LC 787 wrong answer.

Six shortest paths, four cost models

743 is textbook Dijkstra. 1514 maximises a product, 1631 minimises a maximum, 1976 counts the optima. 787 needs a hop limit, and 1334 is all-pairs on a graph small enough for Floyd–Warshall.

Anchor 1 · LC 743 — the path to the solution

The restatement
The signal reaches a node along its shortest path, so the time for all nodes is the maximum shortest-path distance from the source. Two standard pieces, composed.
Why not BFS
Edge weights differ, so a queue no longer produces nodes in distance order. BFS would report hop counts rather than travel times.
The substitution
Replace the queue with a priority queue ordered by distance. Everything else about BFS is unchanged, which is a useful way to remember Dijkstra.
Lazy deletion
Java cannot decrease a key, so push a new entry on improvement and skip stale ones with if (d > dist[node]) continue;.
The answer
The maximum over dist[1..n]. If any entry is still infinite, that node is unreachable and the answer is −1.
Edge cases
Nodes are 1-indexed, so size the arrays n + 1 and ignore index 0. Multiple edges between the same pair are fine — the relaxation keeps the best.
LC 743 · O(E log E) time, O(V + E) space
class Solution {
    public int networkDelayTime(int[][] times, int n, int k) {
        // node -> list of (neighbour, weight). 1-indexed, so n + 1.
        List<int[]>[] adj = new List[n + 1];
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) adj[i] = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int[] t : times) adj[t[0]].add(new int[]{t[1], t[2]});

        int[] dist = new int[n + 1];
        Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
        dist[k] = 0;

        PriorityQueue<int[]> pq =
                new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]));
        pq.offer(new int[]{k, 0});

        while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
            int[] cur = pq.poll();
            int node = cur[0], d = cur[1];

            // Stale entry: we already recorded a shorter route here.
            if (d > dist[node]) continue;

            for (int[] e : adj[node]) {
                int next = e[0], cand = d + e[1];
                if (cand < dist[next]) {
                    dist[next] = cand;
                    pq.offer(new int[]{next, cand});   // push, not update
                }
            }
        }

        int worst = 0;
        for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
            if (dist[i] == Integer.MAX_VALUE) return -1;   // unreachable
            worst = Math.max(worst, dist[i]);
        }
        return worst;
    }
}

Anchor 2 · LC 787 — the path to the solution

Why Dijkstra fails
Its invariant is that a popped node is final. With a stop limit that breaks: reaching a node cheaply but using all your stops can be worse than reaching it expensively with stops to spare. A single distance per node no longer captures the state.
Fix one — add a dimension
Run Dijkstra over (node, stopsUsed) pairs. Correct, and worth mentioning, but the state space is larger and the bookkeeping is fiddlier.
Fix two — Bellman-Ford
Relax every edge, k + 1 times. After round r, dist[] holds the cheapest cost using at most r edges — so the hop limit is simply the number of rounds. Much simpler to get right.
Why k + 1
k stops means k + 1 flights. Off-by-one here is the most common wrong answer on this problem.
Why the snapshot
prev = dist.clone() before each round. Relaxing in place lets a route discovered earlier in the same round be extended again, chaining two edges in one round and exceeding the hop bound.
Edge case
Skip relaxation from unreachable nodes, or MAX_VALUE + price overflows into a negative and looks like a bargain.
LC 787 · O(k·E) time, O(V) space
class Solution {
    public int findCheapestPrice(int n, int[][] flights, int src, int dst, int k) {
        int[] dist = new int[n];
        Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
        dist[src] = 0;

        // k STOPS means k + 1 FLIGHTS, hence k + 1 rounds.
        for (int round = 0; round <= k; round++) {

            // Snapshot: relaxing in place would let a route found
            // earlier in THIS round be extended again, using more
            // edges than the round count permits.
            int[] prev = dist.clone();

            for (int[] f : flights) {
                int from = f[0], to = f[1], price = f[2];

                // Unreachable so far — and MAX_VALUE + price overflows.
                if (prev[from] == Integer.MAX_VALUE) continue;

                dist[to] = Math.min(dist[to], prev[from] + price);
            }
        }
        return dist[dst] == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : dist[dst];
    }
}

1514 · Path with Maximum Probability Dijkstra, max

Path: maximise a product of probabilities rather than minimise a sum. Since every factor is in [0,1], extending a path can only shrink it — which is the same monotonicity Dijkstra relies on, just mirrored.

Delta: a max-heap on probability, double[] best initialised to 0, and prob * edgeProb in place of d + w. Return as soon as the destination is popped.

Watch for: the graph is undirected, so add both directions. Taking -log of each probability turns it back into a standard minimisation — a nice thing to mention, though the direct version is simpler.

1631 · Path With Minimum Effort minimax

Path: the cost of a path is its worst single step, not the total. That is still monotone — extending a path can only keep or raise the maximum — so Dijkstra applies unchanged.

Delta: cand = max(effortSoFar, |h[next] − h[cur]|) replaces the addition. The grid is the graph, with four-directional neighbours.

Watch for: binary search on the answer plus a connectivity check is an equally good alternative, as is union-find over edges sorted by weight. Naming all three shows you see the shape rather than one recipe.

1334 · City With Smallest Number of Neighbors Floyd–Warshall

Path: you need distances between all pairs. Running Dijkstra from every node is O(V·E log E) and works; with n ≤ 100 there is something much shorter.

Delta: Floyd–Warshall — three nested loops with k outermost, relaxing d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j]). Then count reachable cities per node and take the smallest count, breaking ties by the largest index.

Watch for: k must be the outer loop — it is the "intermediate vertex allowed" dimension, and reordering the loops silently produces wrong distances. Use a finite sentinel such as 10⁹ rather than MAX_VALUE to avoid overflow in the addition.

1976 · Number of Ways to Arrive at Destination Dijkstra + count

Path: ordinary Dijkstra finds the shortest time; the question additionally asks how many distinct routes achieve it.

Delta: carry long[] ways next to dist[]. On a strictly shorter route, replace the count with the predecessor's. On an equally short one, add it. Take everything modulo 10⁹+7.

Watch for: times sum to more than int range, so dist[] must be long. And the equal-distance branch must not push to the heap again — the node's distance has not changed, so re-expanding it would double-count.

If you only drill twoDo 743 and 787. 743 fixes the heap loop, the lazy-deletion skip, and the habit of reading Dijkstra as "BFS with a priority queue". 787 is the one that teaches the boundary of the pattern — recognising that an added constraint invalidates the finality invariant, and that the fix is either an extra state dimension or a different algorithm entirely.

Connect everything for the least total cost

A minimum spanning tree touches every node using exactly n − 1 edges at the lowest possible total weight. Two algorithms build it, both greedy, and both justified by the same fact: the cheapest edge crossing any split of the graph is always safe to take.

The cut property — why greedy is correct

Split the nodes into any two non-empty groups. The cheapest edge crossing that split belongs to some minimum spanning tree.

The proof is an exchange argument: take an MST without that edge, add it, and a cycle appears. That cycle must cross the split somewhere else, at an edge no cheaper. Remove it and the tree is still spanning, and no more expensive.

That one property licenses both algorithms — which is why they never need to reconsider a choice.

Kruskal and Prim

Kruskal
Sort all edges by weight, then take each one whose endpoints are not already connected. Union-find answers that test. O(E log E), best when the graph is sparse or you already have an edge list.
Prim
Grow one tree from an arbitrary start, repeatedly taking the cheapest edge leaving it. A priority queue supplies that edge. O(E log V), best when the graph is dense or implicit — as with points where every pair is connected.

Both give the same total weight. Choose by what the input looks like, and say why.

Applies when

Connect every node at minimum total cost — cables, roads, pipes. Also the minimax path family, where sorting edges and unioning until two nodes connect gives the smallest possible bottleneck.

Does not apply when

You want the shortest path between two nodes. An MST minimises the total edge weight, not any individual route — the MST path between two nodes is often longer than their shortest path.

Complexity

O(E log E) for Kruskal, dominated by the sort. O(E log V) for Prim with a heap. On a complete graph of n points, E is n², so both are about O(n² log n).

Recognition cues — the literal words in the statement"the minimum cost to connect all points" · "connect all cities with the minimum cost" · "every house must have water" (the virtual-node trick) · "critical and pseudo-critical edges" · "the least time until you can swim from corner to corner" (minimax) · "maximise the minimum value along a path" (minimax, mirrored). Two tells: "connect all", and an answer that is a total rather than a route.

LC 1584 traced on four points

Points are (0,0), (2,2), (3,10), (5,2) with Manhattan distance. Kruskal sorts all six candidate edges and takes the first three that merge distinct components — one fewer than the number of points.

Why stopping at n − 1 edges is safeA spanning tree on n nodes has exactly n − 1 edges, so once that many have been accepted every node is connected and any further edge would close a cycle. Breaking there saves scanning the tail of the sorted list — with n = 1000 points that is roughly 500,000 edges, of which only 999 are ever taken.

Sort and union, or grow and pop

Kruskal is union-find with a sorted edge list. Prim is Dijkstra with the distance replaced by the single edge weight. Both are short; the choice between them is about the input shape.

Kruskal — sort, then take non-cycling edges (LC 1584, 1135)
/**
 * Sort every edge, take each one whose endpoints are not yet
 * connected. Union-find answers that test in near-constant time.
 * Stop at n-1 edges: the tree is then complete.
 */
int kruskal(int n, int[][] edges) {       // edges: {u, v, w}
    Arrays.sort(edges, (a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[2], b[2]));

    DSU dsu = new DSU(n);
    int total = 0, taken = 0;

    for (int[] e : edges) {
        // false means the endpoints already share a component,
        // so this edge would close a cycle.
        if (dsu.union(e[0], e[1])) {
            total += e[2];
            if (++taken == n - 1) break;     // spanning tree complete
        }
    }
    return taken == n - 1 ? total : -1;      // -1 if the graph is disconnected
}
Prim — grow one tree from any start (LC 1584 on points)
/**
 * Better when the graph is DENSE or IMPLICIT — with n points every
 * pair is an edge, so materialising all n^2/2 of them is wasteful.
 *
 * This is Dijkstra with one change: the key is the single edge
 * weight, not the accumulated distance.
 */
int primOnPoints(int[][] points) {
    int n = points.length;
    boolean[] inTree = new boolean[n];
    int[] best = new int[n];                 // cheapest edge into the tree
    Arrays.fill(best, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    best[0] = 0;

    int total = 0;

    for (int iter = 0; iter < n; iter++) {
        // Pick the cheapest node not yet in the tree. With n <= 1000
        // a linear scan is O(n^2) overall and simpler than a heap.
        int u = -1;
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++)
            if (!inTree[v] && (u == -1 || best[v] < best[u])) u = v;

        inTree[u] = true;
        total += best[u];

        // Relax: the key is the EDGE weight, not best[u] + weight.
        for (int v = 0; v < n; v++) {
            if (inTree[v]) continue;
            int d = Math.abs(points[u][0] - points[v][0])
                  + Math.abs(points[u][1] - points[v][1]);
            if (d < best[v]) best[v] = d;
        }
    }
    return total;
}
The virtual node — turning a per-node cost into an edge (LC 1168)
/**
 * Each house can either dig its OWN well at cost wells[i], or lay a
 * pipe to a neighbour. Two different kinds of cost, which is not an
 * MST — until you notice the trick.
 *
 * Invent node 0 as "the water source". A well at house i becomes an
 * EDGE from 0 to i with weight wells[i]. Now every cost is an edge,
 * and the answer is an ordinary MST over n+1 nodes.
 */
int minCostToSupplyWater(int n, int[] wells, int[][] pipes) {
    List<int[]> edges = new ArrayList<>();

    // Wells become edges from the virtual source.
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) edges.add(new int[]{0, i + 1, wells[i]});

    // Pipes are ordinary edges.
    for (int[] p : pipes) edges.add(new int[]{p[0], p[1], p[2]});

    edges.sort((a, b) -> Integer.compare(a[2], b[2]));

    DSU dsu = new DSU(n + 1);        // +1 for the virtual node
    int total = 0, taken = 0;

    for (int[] e : edges) {
        if (dsu.union(e[0], e[1])) {
            total += e[2];
            if (++taken == n) break;  // n+1 nodes, so n edges span them
        }
    }
    return total;
}

Choosing, and the variants

Edge list given
Kruskal. The sort is already the natural first move.
Points or a dense graph
Prim with a linear scan when n ≤ 1000, avoiding the n² edge list entirely.
Two kinds of cost
Look for a virtual node that converts the odd one into an edge. It is the single most reusable trick here.
Minimax path
Sort edges ascending and union until the two endpoints connect. The last edge added is the smallest possible bottleneck.
Critical edges
Compute the MST weight, then for each edge: force-exclude it and see whether the weight rises (critical), or force-include it and see whether the weight is unchanged (pseudo-critical).
The three bugs that actually happenForgetting the disconnected case — if fewer than n − 1 edges are accepted the graph cannot be spanned, and the answer is −1 rather than a partial total. Off-by-one with a virtual node — the DSU must be sized n + 1 and the stopping count becomes n, not n − 1. Treating Prim's key as a distance — relaxing with best[u] + weight makes it Dijkstra and produces a shortest-path tree, which is a different and more expensive tree.

Six connection problems

1584 and 1135 are plain MSTs. 1168 needs the virtual node. 1489 runs the MST repeatedly. 778 and 1102 are minimax rather than total-weight, and both yield to sorted edges with union-find. Three of the six are behind LeetCode's paywall, with free equivalents noted.
